# THE LÖWDIN CHALLENGE — THE OUTSIDE LITERATURE

*Compiled 2026-08-11 by live search. Every claim here is attributed; where a
paper's own abstract states a limitation, that limitation is quoted in substance
rather than softened. Nothing in this file is a result of this work.*

---

## 1 · THE CHALLENGE AS POSED

**Löwdin, P.-O. (1969).** *Some comments on the Periodic System of Elements.*
Int. J. Quantum Chem. Symp. **IIIS**, 331–334. Points out that the Madelung
(n+ℓ, n) rule has not been derived from quantum mechanics. This became "the
Löwdin challenge."

**Klechkovskii, V. M. (1951).** *(n+ℓ) groups in successive filling of atomic
electron configurations.* Doklady Akademii Nauk **80**, 603–606. The rule's
Russian originator; proposed an explanation in 1962. **Madelung, E. (1936).**
*Die Mathematischen Hilfsmittel des Physikers*, 3rd ed., p. 359. And earlier
still, **Janet (1928/1929)**, whose left-step table is the rule made a table —
unrecognised until Stewart (2010), which is why it carries Madelung's name.

---

## 2 · THE PRINCIPAL ATTEMPT, AND THE OBJECTION TO IT

**Demkov, Yu. N. & Ostrovsky, V. N. (1971/72).** *(n+ℓ) filling rule in the
Periodic System and focusing potentials.* Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. **62**, 125–132
[Sov. Phys. JETP **35**, 66–69, 1972].

The potential **U(r) ∝ −r⁻¹(r + R)⁻²** — a "focusing" potential closely
resembling the Thomas–Fermi potential — produces **additional degeneracy for
levels with identical N = n + ℓ at energy E = 0**. This is the closest thing in
the literature to a derivation, and it is what most later work builds on or
argues against. Related: Ostrovsky (2001, 2003) on what physics contributes to
the periodic law; Rosu *et al.* (1995) on the supersymmetry of the DO potentials;
the κ = ½ member of the family is the one obeying Madelung, κ = 1 being the
Maxwell fish-eye.

**THE OBJECTION.** Thyssen & Ceulemans (*Shattered Symmetry*, OUP 2017) conclude
that although the Demkov–Ostrovsky results reproduce the Madelung rule correctly,
**the way they were obtained cannot be considered a solution of the Löwdin
challenge — because the effective potential was GUESSED.** Kholodenko & Kauffman
(2019) make the same point: DO obtained correct results without rigorous
justification of the potential.

*This objection applies with equal force to any posited ordering functional,
including ν. See §6.*

---

## 3 · THE OTHER CLAIMANTS

**Allen, L. C. & Knight, E. T. (2002/2003).** *The Löwdin challenge: Origin of
the n+ℓ, n (Madelung) rule…* Int. J. Quantum Chem. **90**, 80–88. Treats the
table as an s/p framework internally perturbed by d and f electrons; a
perturbation operator locates the blocks; verified against Desclaux's 1973
Dirac–Fock calculations for Z = 1–118. **Scerri's commentary (2006) concludes the
explanation is inadequate on several grounds.**

**Kholodenko, A. L. & Kauffman, L. H. (2019); Kholodenko (2020).** *How the
modified Bertrand theorem explains regularities of the periodic table* (arXiv
1906.05278) and *…Regularities and Anomalies…* (arXiv 2002.12128). Uses Perlick's
extension of Bertrand's theorem to static spherically symmetric spacetimes
supporting closed orbits; shows the Tietz-type Schrödinger equation (Tietz 1956)
describes quantum motion in Bertrand spacetimes; claims an **analytic solution of
the Löwdin challenge.**

**Their own stated limitation:** the solution is **not universal** — the Madelung
exceptions among transition metals, lanthanides and actinides are **not described
in detail**, though they argue the method is capable of it.

**Group-theoretic approaches.** Kibler (2007), SO(4,2) ⊗ SU(2). Fet (2016),
Varlamov (2018). Thyssen (2013 dissertation) and Thyssen & Ceulemans (2017, 2020)
— SO(4,2) broken to the anti-de Sitter SO(3,2) explains period doubling, and the
Madelung rule is **rationalised via nonlinear Lie algebras reflecting the
screening of the Coulomb hole**. A 2026 arXiv preprint extends this to SO(4,4)
double towers. These approaches generally require some empirical input
(Ostrovsky's own assessment).

**Tangour, B. (2015).** *Beyond the Madelung–Klechkowski rule.* World J. Chem.
Educ. **3**(6), 160–167. Proposes a descriptor **K(ZX) built from all four
quantum numbers n, ℓ, mℓ, ms of the most recently added electron**, incrementing
with Z, claiming **no exceptions remain**, and connecting it to the first
ionisation energy. *Closest in spirit to putting the occupancy inside the
ordering functional.*

---

## 4 · THE DISSENTING POSITION

**Schwarz, W. H. E.** (and Cao, Hu, Li, Schwarz, *Pure Appl. Chem.* **91**,
1969–1999, 2019; Schwarz & Rich 2010). Argues the Madelung rule **does not truly
reflect the order of orbital occupation** in the way generally believed. The
(n+ℓ, n) rule was originally used by spectroscopists to remember which
*differentiating* orbital is added in free neutral atoms as Z increases; chemical
educators then applied it to ions, where it is a different claim. **The rule
usually fails where d and f orbitals are involved.**

*This is the objection that bears most directly on this work's own results: the
walk is precisely the neutral-atom differentiating-orbital reading, and its
failures are concentrated in d and f contests.*

---

## 5 · THE FIELD'S CONSENSUS

**Scerri, E. R. (2020).** *Recent attempts to change the periodic table.* Phil.
Trans. R. Soc. A **378**, 20190300. States that **numerous authors claim to have
met the challenge, but the generally held opinion is that no such derivation has
succeeded in the way Löwdin intended.**

Scerri was for many years the leading proponent of the "not derived" position and
has more recently said he has **somewhat changed his mind** (Inference Review,
2021). Others hold that the rule is empirical and that a first-principles
derivation would be surprising, and that obtaining configurations from first
principles is "a mathematical experiment rather than a mathematical deduction."

**So the challenge is open by consensus, with two live claimants (Bertrand
spacetimes; group theory) and one standing objection to the premise (Schwarz).**

---

## 6 · WHERE THIS WORK SITS

**Different in kind.** Every attempt above seeks a POTENTIAL or a SYMMETRY GROUP
from which the n+ℓ ordering follows. This work posits an ordering functional
directly — ν(n, ℓ, q) = n − a√(n−ℓ−1 + q/2(2ℓ+1)) — and tests it by whether the
resulting corridor is non-empty at each element.

**The guessed-potential objection applies to ν too**, and must be answered rather
than dodged. The answer available here is not that ν is derived but that it is
FALSIFIABLE in a way a guessed potential is not: the same corridor construction
applied to the nuclear shell ordering gives an EMPTY feasible set (registers
1367–1371, 1394), while the atomic corridor is non-empty at 106 of 106. A form
that can fail and does not is a different epistemic object from a form fitted to
succeed. *That is a defence of the method, not a derivation of ν.*

**Points of contact worth pursuing.**

- Demkov–Ostrovsky locate their content at **degeneracy at E = 0 for equal
  N = n+ℓ**. This work locates its content at **crossings** — the values of a
  where two orderings become indistinguishable, the nineteen surds. Both say the
  physics lives where the ordering is degenerate. Whether these are the same
  degeneracy in two languages is a concrete question and has not been asked.
- Tangour's K(ZX) puts the occupancy of the newly added electron into the
  descriptor; ν puts q into the radicand as the Pauli fraction q/cap. Two
  attempts to remove the exceptions by carrying occupancy. **His claim of no
  exceptions should be checked against our 93 of 100.**
- Schwarz's objection predicts failures concentrated in d and f. Ours are: Mn,
  Tc, Gd, Cm are all s-vs-d or d-vs-f contests, and the half-capacity mechanism
  is a d and f phenomenon. **The objection and our miss classification agree**,
  which is either a confirmation of his reading or a symptom of the same cause.

**What appears NOT to be in the literature.** No source found reports an
**out-of-sample generation test against a Madelung null**. The claimants ask
whether the rule FOLLOWS from their formalism; none appears to ask how far past
the record their formalism can DERIVE, or to score it against plain Madelung
run under identical conditions. This work has measured that:

    conditional, one step ahead      law 90 · Madelung 96   (of 106)
    free-running from hydrogen       law 72 · Madelung 94
    forward horizon from a prefix    law mean 3.9 · Madelung mean 6.0 steps

**On that measurement the law currently loses to the rule it seeks to explain.**
That is a negative result, but the MEASUREMENT is the thing not previously made,
and it converts the challenge from a yes/no into a distance.

---

## 7 · WHAT TO READ NEXT, IN ORDER

1. **Demkov & Ostrovsky 1972** in full — whether their E = 0 degeneracy is our
   crossing condition is the single most valuable comparison available.
2. **Kholodenko 2020 (arXiv 2002.12128)** — the most recent claimed solution;
   read specifically for how it treats the exceptions, which is where it concedes.
3. **Thyssen & Ceulemans 2017, ch. 13** — contains a literature study of
   Demkov–Ostrovsky and the statement of the guessed-potential objection.
4. **Tangour 2015** — the no-exceptions claim, checkable against our 93 of 100.
5. **Schwarz, Cao, Hu, Li 2019** — the case that the rule is not what it is
   taken to be, which if right narrows what the challenge even asks.

  physics lives where the ordering is degenerate. Whether these are the same
  degeneracy in two languages is a concrete question and has not been asked.
- Tangour's K(ZX) puts the occupancy of the newly added electron into the
  descriptor; ν puts q into the radicand as the Pauli fraction q/cap. Two
  attempts to remove the exceptions by carrying occupancy. **His claim of no
  exceptions should be checked against our 93 of 100.**
- Schwarz's objection predicts failures concentrated in d and f. Ours are: Mn,
  Tc, Gd, Cm are all s-vs-d or d-vs-f contests, and the half-capacity mechanism
  is a d and f phenomenon. **The objection and our miss classification agree**,
  which is either a confirmation of his reading or a symptom of the same cause.

**What appears NOT to be in the literature.** No source found reports an
**out-of-sample generation test against a Madelung null**. The claimants ask
whether the rule FOLLOWS from their formalism; none appears to ask how far past
the record their formalism can DERIVE, or to score it against plain Madelung
run under identical conditions. This work has measured that:

    conditional, one step ahead      law 90 · Madelung 96   (of 106)
    free-running from hydrogen       law 72 · Madelung 94
    forward horizon from a prefix    law mean 3.9 · Madelung mean 6.0 steps

**On that measurement the law currently loses to the rule it seeks to explain.**
That is a negative result, but the MEASUREMENT is the thing not previously made,
and it converts the challenge from a yes/no into a distance.

---

## 7 · WHAT TO READ NEXT, IN ORDER

1. **Demkov & Ostrovsky 1972** in full — whether their E = 0 degeneracy is our
   crossing condition is the single most valuable comparison available.
2. **Kholodenko 2020 (arXiv 2002.12128)** — the most recent claimed solution;
   read specifically for how it treats the exceptions, which is where it concedes.
3. **Thyssen & Ceulemans 2017, ch. 13** — contains a literature study of
   Demkov–Ostrovsky and the statement of the guessed-potential objection.
4. **Tangour 2015** — the no-exceptions claim, checkable against our 93 of 100.
5. **Schwarz, Cao, Hu, Li 2019** — the case that the rule is not what it is
   taken to be, which if right narrows what the challenge even asks.

content.text:
**The field is open by consensus, there are two live claimants, and the nearest neighbour to our approach carries an objection that applies to us too.**

**Demkov and Ostrovsky (1972)** is the closest thing to a derivation: a focusing potential U(r) ∝ −r⁻¹(r+R)⁻², closely resembling Thomas–Fermi, which produces **additional degeneracy for levels of equal N = n+ℓ at exactly E = 0**. Everything since either builds on it or argues with it.

**And the standing objection to it is the one we have to answer.** Thyssen and Ceulemans conclude that although it reproduces Madelung correctly, it cannot count as a solution **because the potential was guessed**. Kholodenko and Kauffman say the same. That objection transfers directly to ν — we posited the form.

**The answer available to us is not that ν is derived, but that it is falsifiable in a way a guessed potential is not.** The same corridor construction applied to the nuclear shell ordering gives an *empty* feasible set — six pairs collapsing onto 4β + α with three demanding each sign — while the atomic corridor is non-empty at 106 of 106. A form that could fail and didn't is a different object from a form fitted to succeed. That is a defence of the *method*, not a derivation of ν, and it should be stated that carefully.

**Two things in the literature bear on our own results.** Tangour (2015) proposes a descriptor built from all four quantum numbers of the newly added electron and claims **no exceptions remain** — the same move as putting q in the radicand, and checkable against our 93 of 100. And Schwarz argues the rule **doesn't reflect actual orbital occupation** and usually fails where d and f are involved — which is precisely where our misses are. His objection and our miss classification agree, and that's either confirmation or a shared symptom.

**What I could not find anywhere is our measurement.** Every claimant asks whether the rule *follows* from their formalism. Nobody appears to ask how far past the record their formalism can *derive*, or to score it against plain Madelung under identical conditions. The 90-against-96, the 72-against-94, and the 3.9-against-6.0 forward horizon look like a kind of test the field hasn't run.

**On closing half the queue, the honest read.** We are not closing Löwdin on these numbers, and neither is anyone else — Kholodenko's own abstract concedes the exceptions aren't described, and Allen and Knight were judged inadequate. But the queue may be closeable from a different direction than a derivation: if the challenge's answer is a **horizon** rather than a proof, then what we have is a new way of posing it, and the items that depend on "the walk generates" would need restating rather than solving.

The single highest-value next read is Demkov and Ostrovsky in full — **whether their E = 0 degeneracy is our crossing condition**. Both locate the content at degeneracy. If they are the same object in two languages, that is a bridge to fifty years of work and it would be worth more than another placement rule.

content.thinking:
I'm looking at the Demkov-Ostrovsky paper now—this is a significant reference. The key structure involves a potential family with exact focusing properties for zero-energy particles, though the OCR rendering is a bit unclear on the mathematical details. There's a crucial statement about specific values of ν that seems to be cut off, but this comparison to our work should help clarify the theoretical framework. The Demkov-Ostrovsky combination n_r + 2ℓ is exactly what we're using—the radial node count plus twice the angular momentum quantum number. Their Z_N formula predicts the effective charge where each n+ℓ group first appears, and the numerical values match observations quite well across the table.

Now I'm working through the second part of the filling rule for equal N values. There's a tension here: the paper claims that larger n at fixed N corresponds to deeper, more bound levels that should fill first, but Madelung's rule says smallest n fills first. I need to reconcile what "deeper" means in this context—whether it refers to binding energy or something else—and check what the paper actually states about the filling order.

The Appendix clarifies that s-terms (smallest ℓ, largest n at fixed N) lie highest in energy, meaning they're least bound and fill last. This confirms that smallest n (largest ℓ) is deepest and fills first, which aligns with Madelung. So the apparent contradiction seems to be a translation or OCR issue in how the paper phrased it.

The paper also notes 18 exceptions to the rule—16 deviations by one electron and 2 by two electrons—with the caveat that excited states usually satisfy the rule even when ground states don't.

The crucial limitation they acknowledge is that their potential neglects the Coulomb tail at large r, so reliable results only appear in a narrow binding energy range of several electron volts.

Comparing their approach to mine: they use n_r + 2ℓ (where n_r = n − ℓ − 1), a linear combination of node count and angular momentum. My radicand is n_r plus a Pauli fraction that depends on ℓ through the degeneracy factor 2ℓ+1, so the ℓ-dependence is more intricate than theirs.

Their degeneracy occurs when n_r + 2ℓ stays constant across states. My crossing condition is when ν(A) = ν(B), which gives a = (n_A − n_B)/(√r_A − √r_B). In the q-zero limit where my radicand reduces to just p = n_r, the crossing formula becomes a = Δn/(√p_A − √p_B), so there's a structural parallel—both involve balancing node count differences against some measure of the radial parameter.

Now I'm testing whether my "same corridor" condition maps onto their "same N" degeneracy. Taking concrete examples: 4s and 3d have N = 4 and N = 5 respectively, so they're not degenerate by their criterion. But 4s and 3p both have N = 4, with radial nodes p = 3 and p = 1, giving a crossing at a = 1/(√3 − 1).

Looking at the N = 5 group (3d, 4p, 5s), I'm computing all pairwise crossings and finding they match my surd values exactly: 1/√2, 1, and 1.7071 appear consistently across different orbital pairs within the same N level.…

from collections import defaultdict
L="spdfg"
subs=[(n,l) for n in range(1,9) for l in range(min(n,5))]

# our crossing in the q-zero slice

    d=math.sqrt(p(*A))-math.sqrt(p(*B))

       2.4409104:"1/(√7−√5)",3.7320508:"1/(√4−√3)",4.2360680:"1/(√5−√4)"}
byrel=defaultdict(set)
for A,B in itertools.combinations(subs,2):
    x=cross(A,B)
    if x is None or x<=0 or x>6: continue
    byrel[N(*B)-N(*A)].add(round(x,7))
print("  DEMKOV–OSTROVSKY'S GROUPING AGAINST OUR CROSSINGS\n")
print("  D-O: at E = 0 the levels depend only on n_r + 2ℓ = N − 1, so subshells")

print("  become indistinguishable. Are they the same event?\n")
print(f"    {'ΔN':>4}  crossings")
for d in sorted(byrel):
    v=sorted(byrel[d])
    tag=", ".join(NAMES.get(x,f"{x:.4f}") for x in v[:8])
    print(f"    {d:>4}  {len(v):>3}   {tag}")
print("\n  THE SAME-N PAIRS EXPLICITLY (ΔN = 0) — Madelung's own groups\n")
for Nv in range(2,9):
    g=[s for s in subs if N(*s)==Nv]
    if len(g)<2: continue
    out=[]
    for A,B in itertools.combinations(g,2):
        x=cross(A,B)
        if x and 0<x<6: out.append(f"{A[0]}{L[A[1]]}/{B[0]}{L[B[1]]}={NAMES.get(round(x,7),f'{x:.4f}')}")
    print(f"    N={Nv}: " + "  ".join(out))

import math, itertools
L="spdfg"
p=lambda n,l:n-l-1
def cross(A,B):
    d=math.sqrt(p(*A))-math.sqrt(p(*B))
    return None if abs(d)<1e-12 else (A[0]-B[0])/d
print("  THE SHIFT (n, ℓ) -> (n+1, ℓ+1)\n")
print("    p = n − ℓ − 1 is INVARIANT under it, and so is Δn.")
print("    Therefore every crossing is invariant, and N = n+ℓ increases by 2.\n")
ok=True
for (nA,lA),(nB,lB) in [((2,1),(3,0)),((3,2),(4,1)),((3,2),(5,0)),((4,1),(5,0))]:
    x1=cross((nA,lA),(nB,lB)); x2=cross((nA+1,lA+1),(nB+1,lB+1))
    x3=cross((nA+2,lA+2),(nB+2,lB+2)) if lB+2<5 and lA+2<5 else None
    same = abs(x1-x2)<1e-12 and (x3 is None or abs(x1-x3)<1e-12)
    ok &= same
    s=f"{nA}{L[lA]}/{nB}{L[lB]} = {x1:.6f}   ->   {nA+1}{L[lA+1]}/{nB+1}{L[lB+1]} = {x2:.6f}"
    if x3 is not None: s+=f"   ->   {nA+2}{L[lA+2]}/{nB+2}{L[lB+2]} = {x3:.6f}"
    print(f"    {s}   identical: {same}")
print(f"\n    invariant in every case: {ok}")
print("\n  SO THE CROSSING SET HAS PERIOD 2 IN N — WHICH IS THE PERIOD DOUBLING.\n")
subs=[(n,l) for n in range(1,9) for l in range(min(n,5))]
from collections import defaultdict
g=defaultdict(set)
for A,B in itertools.combinations(subs,2):
    if A[0]+A[1]!=B[0]+B[1]: continue
    x=cross(A,B)
    if x and 0<x<6: g[A[0]+A[1]].add(round(x,7))
print(f"    {'N':>3}  block length  distinct internal crossings")
BL={1:2,2:2,3:8,4:8,5:18,6:18,7:32,8:32}
for Nv in sorted(g):
    print(f"    {Nv:>3}  {BL.get(Nv,'?'):>11}   {sorted(g[Nv])}")
print("\n    N and N+2 share their crossing sets exactly:",
      all(g[k]<=g[k+2] or g[k+2]<=g[k] for k in (3,4,5,6) if k+2 in g))

**The bridge holds, and it produces something I don't think either side has.**

**Demkov and Ostrovsky's fundamental combination is n_r + 2ℓ, where n_r = n − ℓ − 1.** That is the node count and the angular momentum — our two coordinates, exactly. Their whole construction turns on levels being degenerate at E = 0 when that combination is fixed, which is N = n + ℓ constant. So both approaches locate the content in the same place, in the same variables.

**And our surds are the crossings between subshells of equal N — Madelung's own groups.**

    N=3   2p/3s = 1/√2
    N=4   3p/4s = 1/(√3−1)
    N=5   3d/4p = 1/√2 · 3d/5s = 1 · 4p/5s = 1+1/√2
    N=6   4d/5p = 1/(√3−1) · 4d/6s = φ · 5p/6s = 1/(√5−√3)
    N=7   4f/5d = 1/√2 · 4f/6p = 1 · 5d/6p = 1+1/√2 · …
    N=8   5f/6d = 1/(√3−1) · 5f/7p = φ · 6d/7p = 1/(√5−√3) · …

Every named value in the nineteen appears here, including 1.6180 — the golden ratio, and mercury's recorded a of 0.8090 is exactly half of it.

**Then the structural reason, which is elementary arithmetic.** The shift **(n, ℓ) → (n+1, ℓ+1) leaves p = n − ℓ − 1 invariant and leaves Δn invariant**, so it leaves every crossing invariant — while raising N by two. Verified: 2p/3s, 3d/4p, 4f/5d and 5g/6f all give 1/√2 identically. 3d/5s, 4f/6p, 5g/7d all give 1.

**So the crossing sets are nested with period two in N, and the odd-N and even-N families are disjoint.** N = 3, 5, 7, 9 build on {1/√2, 1, 1+1/√2, …}; N = 4, 6, 8, 10 build on {1/(√3−1), φ, 1/(√5−√3), …}. Two interleaved families, never meeting, each group's crossings contained in the group two later.

**That is a two-fold structure in N arising from node-count invariance.** Period doubling in the block *lengths* — 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 — is standard and comes from N and N+1 carrying the same number of subshells. This is a *different* periodicity, pairing N with N+2, and it's the one Thyssen and Ceulemans reach for SO(4,2) broken to SO(3,2) to explain. Here it falls out of the fact that the node count doesn't notice the shift.

**What I'd claim and what I wouldn't.** The invariance is trivial arithmetic once seen, and I'd expect it to be known somewhere even if I haven't found it. What looks new is the *identification*: that the corridor's nineteen surds are precisely the intra-group crossings of Demkov–Ostrovsky's degenerate sets, and that they organise into two disjoint families by the parity of N. That is a statement connecting our object to theirs, and it is checkable in ten lines.

Worth registering, and worth putting to Thyssen or Ceulemans if you ever want an outside reader — it's in their language as much as ours.

# 2 The Madelung Rule

As is known, as the charge of the atomic nucleus Z increases in the periodic table, the filling of orbitals in a neutral atom is set in a certain sequence, which is traditionally called the Aufbau scheme [1]. Obviously, the Aufbau circuit is determined by a sequence of single-electron levels $\varepsilon_{nl}$ on the energy scale. This sequence depends on the properties of the effective one-electron central field (Coulomb field with potential -Z/r). The lengths of the periods in the hydrogen-like Aufbau scheme correspond to hydrogen n shells: $2n^2 = 2, 8, 18, 32, 50, \ldots$ A comparison with detailed numerical quantum calculations for multielectronic systems and empirical data shows that for highly ionized atoms, the (n, l) ordering really works [21].

However, the structure of *neutral atoms* is of paramount importance when it comes to the periodic table. The (n, l) rule is not satisfied here. 

This means that the effective potential is very different from the Coulomb potential, which leads to a significant restructuring of the spectrum. There is an overlap between groups of energy levels with different principal quantum numbers n. The n-grouping of levels disappears and new types of regularities appear [22, 21, 23].

Empirically, it has been observed that the periodic table is well described by the Madelung rule (n+l,n): orbitals are filled in ascending order of the sum $N \equiv n+l$ , and for a fixed N - in ascending order of n. The advantage of the (n+l,n) scheme in comparison with the rule (n,l) is especially clearly seen from the graphical construction given by Demkov and Ostrovsky [22].

## 2 The Madelung [n+l, n]-rule

We get an exact expression for the Mendeleev periods and other properties of the Mendeleev table with the Madelung [n + l, n]-rule [22]).

The [n+l,n]-rule asserts: with growth of atomic charge Z the electrons fill up in atom consecutively the one-particle states with the least possible value of the quantum number n+l; and, for a given value n+l, the electrons fill up states with the least possible value of the quantum number n.

Here it is reasonable to introduce the quantum number

$$M = n + l = n_r + 2l + 1.$$

The [n+l,n]-rule is in fact an algorithm for consecutive building-up of atoms<sup>2</sup>. 

 $\mu(x) = x \mod(2) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \text{ is odd,} \\ 0, & x \text{ is even.} \end{cases}$ 

Relations for $Z_{n+l}$ and $_{n+l}Z$ are exact. Other relations are exact up to exclusions pointed out above. For example, for $l=0,1,\ldots$ , we have $Z_l=1,5,21,57,\ldots$ , that is, according to the Madelung rule, the onset of the 4f block starts with La (Z=57). But, according to the IUPAC data<sup>3</sup> on electron configurations in atoms, the onset of the 4f block starts with Ce (Z=58).

The [n+l,l]-rule defines essential characteristics of the Mendeleev periodic system.

In the Mendeleev periodic system, the table rows are enumerated by the Mendeleev number M which is a linear function of the Madelung number M [15]:

$$M = M - 1 + \delta_{l,0} = n + l - 1 + \delta_{l,0}$$

where $\delta_{j,k}$ is the Kronecker delta.

It is easy to show that the number of elements in the Mendeleev M-th period of the periodic system according to the [n+l, n]-rule is equal to

content.title: Group Theoretical Description of Mendeleev Periodic System
content.text:
<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>8</sup>Erwin Madelung was the first to apply "hydrogen" quantum numbers n, l, m, s to the numbering of elements of the periodic table. It should be noted that the numbers n, l, m, s are not quantum numbers in Bohr's model, because in this model there is no single quantum-mechanical description of the system of elements, the latter is assigned an atomic number Z, distinguishing rather than combining individual quantum systems. The resulting classification of elements Madelung called "empirical", because he cold not connect it with the Bohr model. Apparently, it was because of the lack of theoretical justification at the time (20-ies of the last century), he published it as a reference material in [20]. Theoretical justification (understanding of the nature of Madelung numbers) was later given by Fet [18] from the position of group-theoretic vision. 

The history of Madelung numbers was also developed in a slightly different direction in the works of Kleczkowski [21], where the filling of the electronic levels of the atom was considered according to the rule of sequential filling of (n+l)-groups (the so-called Madelung-Kleczkowski groups).

- 1) elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number Z;
- 2) collections $(\nu, \lambda, \mu, s, s')$ are arranged in increasing order of $\nu$ ; at the given $\nu$ in increasing order of s'; at the given $\nu$ , s' in decreasing order of $\lambda$ ; at the given $\nu$ , s', $\lambda$ in increasing order of $\mu$ ; at the given $\nu$ , s', $\lambda$ , $\mu$ in increasing order of s;
 - 3) Z-th element corresponds to Z-th collection.

The introduction of the fifth quantum number leads to another (second) "doubling" of the representation space. In this space we have the Rumer-Fet group

content.title: Madelung Rules: Orbital Filling Order
content.text:
Madelung Rules are a set of principles that define the electron orbital filling order based on the sum (n+ℓ) and the principal quantum number n. Analytic derivations reveal their foundation in central potentials with hidden O(4) symmetry, which explains observed energy degeneracies and periodic trends. Recent studies incorporate topological perspectives and account for electron correlations and relativistic effects, clarifying exceptions in d- and f-block elements. The Madelung rules, also known as the (n + ℓ, n) principle or Aufbau principle, formalize the empirically observed ordering in which electronic subshells (atomic orbitals) are filled in atoms. This filling sequence underpins the structure of the periodic table, the energetic ordering of orbitals, and a broad range of atomic properties. 

The Madelung rule asserts: orbitals are filled in order of increasing sum n + ℓ, where n is the principal quantum number and ℓ is the azimuthal quantum number; when two orbitals have the same 

In summary, the Madelung rules arise from a confluence of dynamical symmetry (O(4)), analytic properties of central potentials (Tietz or deformed fish-eye forms), conformal geometry, and topological field theory. Their predictive power remains central to both atomic structure theory and the rational design of advanced materials. Exceptions and anomalies are analytically understood as consequences of symmetry breaking, relativistic reordering, and many-body effects, setting the stage for precise modeling of both known and as-yet-unknown elements (Belokolos, 2017, Kholodenko et al., 2019, Kumar, 15 Jun 2026, Loza et al., 2012, Kholodenko, 2020). ... ## 6 · ATTRIBUTION OF THE 2026-08-11 "BRIDGE" FINDINGS

*Searched specifically to test whether the connections found in this session are
already in the literature. THEY LARGELY ARE, and the attributions are older and
more explicit than the session's claims assumed. Recorded here so that nothing
downstream repeats them as new.*

**The coordinates are not ours.** Demkov & Ostrovsky (1972) write the E = 0
degeneracy condition as **N − 1 = n_r + 2ℓ, where n_r = n − ℓ − 1 is the radial
quantum number** — the node count. Belokolos (2017) states it as an identity:

> **M = n + ℓ = n_r + 2ℓ + 1**

So the pair (node count, angular momentum) is the standard coordinate system of
this literature, not a discovery of this work. That ν's radicand is built from
n − ℓ − 1 places it in the same variables the field has used since 1972.

**The period-2 structure in N is not ours either.** Belokolos gives the period
lengths in closed form:

> **L_M = 2( ⌊M/2⌋ + 1 )²**, yielding 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, …

The floor function ⌊M/2⌋ IS the period-two structure. The session's observation —
that (n, ℓ) → (n+1, ℓ+1) leaves n − ℓ − 1 and Δn invariant while raising N by
two, so the crossing sets repeat with period two — is a restatement of the same
arithmetic in a different object. It is correct and it is not new.

**The odd/even N split** appears in the Rumer–Fet / SO(4,2) line: the SO(4,4)
double-tower construction marks rings of odd n+ℓ separately, and the "doubling of
the representation space" is the same parity distinction.

**What this session's search did NOT find in the literature.** No source located
reports (i) the corridor construction — an interval L(Z) < a < U(Z) on a carried
ordering parameter, with endpoints as exact surds in node counts; (ii) a
falsification test of the ordering form against a case where the corridor is
EMPTY, as the nuclear shell ordering is; or (iii) an out-of-sample or
forward-horizon measurement of a proposed rule against a Madelung null.
**Absence from these searches is not absence from the literature**, and (i) in
particular should be searched again with better terms before any claim is made.

**The corrected reading of the "bridge".** This work has independently arrived at
the coordinate system the field has used for fifty years. That is a validation of
the coordinates and it makes comparison possible — it is not a contribution.
Belokolos additionally states an intention to compare his spectra against the
NIST Atomic Spectra Database, which is the same test this work has been running.

quantum number n.

Belokolos shows that central potentials have O(4) dynamical symmetry, and the frequency degeneracy condition qω_r = pω_θ relates the energy to quantum numbers through a key relationship where α = q/p equals the negative derivative of the radial action with respect to the angular action.

Solving Abel's integral equation yields a family of potentials, but requiring Coulomb behavior at small distances forces α = 2 and β = ZR, giving the Tietz potential. This constraint produces a beautiful result: the energy becomes E = E(n_r + 2ℓ) = E(M − 1), which is exactly the Madelung formula. The spectrum vanishes at E = 0 when √(2ZR) = M, corresponding to Z = M³/6.

I'm noticing a structural parallel here—both Belokolos's result and our frequency law involve square roots of something, and the frequency ratio α = 2 appears as a fundamental constraint.

Now looking at the Demkov-Ostrovsky connection: the radial period is twice the azimuthal period, which explains the factor of 2 in n_r + 2ℓ. The scaled radial quantum number ν_r = n_r/(ℓ+½) relates to η_l = 2ZR/(ℓ+½)², and there's a quantity J_0 involving √(η_l − 2), though the exact form is a bit ambiguous in the notation.

Working through the spectrum formula, I can see that (ℓ+½)√η_l − 2ℓ − 1 − n_r simplifies to (ℓ+½)√η_l − (n+ℓ) because n_r + 2ℓ + 1 = n + ℓ. This means (ℓ+½)√η_l = √(2ZR), which is a clean relationship since η_l = 2ZR.

The key insight is that the semiclassical quantum number M = n + ℓ equals √(2ZR), and I'm trying to understand how this connects to our ν formula with its parameter a and the Belokolos spectrum—specifically whether the level crossings in our two-subshell system correspond to where the Belokolos energy becomes zero. With M = 2n − p − 1, I can express ν = n − a√p in terms of M by substituting p = 2n − M − 1, which gives dν/dn = 1 − a/√p. For Madelung's ordering to work—where within each M group the smallest n comes first—ν needs to increase with n, requiring a < √p across all members of a group.

But this breaks down at p = 0 where the derivative becomes undefined, and the constraint a < √p can't hold universally. The key insight is that Madelung's M is a linear combination of our coordinates (M = 2n − p − 1), while ν involves the square root of p—so they're fundamentally different types of functions on the same lattice.

What's striking is that the coefficient 2 in Madelung's relation directly corresponds to Belokolos's frequency ratio: the radial frequency is exactly twice the angular frequency. That's where the 2 comes from—it's not arbitrary, it's the degeneracy ratio built into the system. Now I'm checking the 19 exceptions Belokolos lists against our donor steps — we have 12 that match (Cr, Cu, Nb, Ru, Pd, Pt among them), but there are discrepancies I need to resolve. The relation M = 2n − p − 1 connects his formulation to our coordinate system, and I should verify this holds before comparing against NIST data. Looking at the electron configurations…

content.text:
**Belokolos closes the gap that sank Demkov–Ostrovsky, and I want to be clear about how.**

His chain: any central potential carries a dynamical O(4) symmetry, not just the Coulomb one. Frequency degeneracy qω_r = pω_θ forces the energy to depend only on **p·n_r + q·ℓ**. Solving the resulting Abel integral equation gives a whole family of potentials indexed by α = q/p. Then — and this is the step that matters — **requiring the potential to be Coulombic as r → 0 forces α = 2**, which yields the Tietz potential and E = E(n_r + 2ℓ).

**So the "2" is derived, not guessed.** Demkov and Ostrovsky picked μ = ½ from their family and got the right answer; Thyssen and Ceulemans object that the choice was unjustified. Belokolos derives it from the nuclear singularity. That is a materially stronger position, and it means the field's strongest claim is better than the consensus summary suggests.

**And his coordinates are ours, exactly.** M = n + ℓ = n_r + 2ℓ + 1, so with our node count p = n_r:

**M = 2n − p − 1**, verified on every subshell.

Madelung's number is **linear** in our two coordinates. Our ν = n − a√p is the same lattice with a square root in it — a nonlinear deformation of a linear ordering. And **the 2 in that linear form is his frequency ratio ω_r = 2ω_θ**, the radial oscillation running twice per revolution. That is where our factor of two comes from, and it has a derivation.

**On the exceptions, his list contains ours.** His nineteen — Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, La, Ce, Gd, Pt, Au, Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Cm — is a strict superset of register 1395's eleven, adding Mo, Rh, Pd, La, Au, Th, Pa, U. Our twelve donor steps intersect his in seven and contribute five he doesn't list: Pr, Tb, Pu, Bk, Rf.

**Two things he leaves open that we have.** His E = 0 condition gives **Z = M³/6**, an ordering-onset prediction, but he does not carry the exceptions — the paper says the anomalies are outside the treatment. And his conclusion states an *intention* to compare against the NIST Atomic Spectra Database, in future tense. That comparison is what we've been running all evening.

So the honest positioning: he has the derivation we lack, and we have the measurement he hasn't made.

What stood out to you?

**Belokolos supplies the group.** His frequency degeneracy ω_r = 2ω_θ — forced, not guessed, by the Coulomb singularity at the origin — makes the energy a function of n_r + 2ℓ alone, so at E = 0 every member of a Madelung group is degenerate. **The group exists; its internal order does not.** He lifts it by going to E < 0.

**And at 93 the misses converge on Madelung's own.** Mine: Mn, Mo, Rh, Pd, La, Ce, Gd, Au, Ac, Pa, Cm, Lr, Rf. Madelung's: Mo, Rh, Pd, La, Gd, Au, Ac, Th, Cm, Lr. **Nine shared.** The rule has stopped being a rival and started being a reconstruction — which is exactly what 1453's derivation says it should be, since *a below every ceiling* **is** Madelung's second rule. It reproduces the rule rather than beating it, from node counts and capacities alone.

At δ = 0.1 it reaches **97**, one above Madelung. I'd not read anything into that yet: 0.1 is a fitted distance from the ceiling with nothing behind it, and it's the first number tonight that looks like a win and has no derivation. Left as an observation.

**So the sixth placement rule also fails to beat 96, and this time the failure is legible.** Out of sample the standing is unchanged: 90 for the corridor, 93 for the group rule, 96 for Madelung. But the group rule is the first that *derives* its parameter rather than reading it off the record, and it lands three short with nine of thirteen misses shared with the target.

**Where that leaves the challenge.** Belokolos derives the groups and doesn't carry the exceptions. This work reproduces the second rule from node counts and lands on the same exceptions. Neither closes it. But the objects are now the same objects — his n_r + 2ℓ is our p and ℓ, his degeneracy is our crossing, his frequency ratio is our factor of two — and the exceptions are where both stop.

That is a much better-posed position than this morning's, and it's one a reader in that literature could check.

"""register_1450_1453.py — the literature bridge and the join."""
import pathlib, re, sys, textwrap

ENTRIES = [
(1450, "THE OUTSIDE LITERATURE, SEARCHED AT LAST, AND OUR COORDINATES ARE FIFTY YEARS OLD.",
 "*A precedent search on the Löwdin challenge itself, owed since the work began.* **The challenge is open "
 "by consensus — Scerri, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 378, 20190300 (2020): numerous authors claim to have met "
 "it and the generally held opinion is that none has succeeded as Löwdin intended.** *The principal "
 "attempt is Demkov & Ostrovsky, Sov. Phys. JETP 35, 66 (1972): the focusing potential U(r) ∝ "
 "−r⁻¹(r+R)⁻², closely resembling Thomas–Fermi, gives additional degeneracy for levels of identical "
 "N = n+ℓ at E = 0. Thyssen & Ceulemans (Shattered Symmetry, OUP 2017) object that it cannot count as a "
 "solution BECAUSE THE POTENTIAL WAS GUESSED — an objection that transfers directly to ν, which this "
 "work posited.* **And the coordinates are not ours. Demkov & Ostrovsky write the degeneracy as "
 "N − 1 = n_r + 2ℓ with n_r = n − ℓ − 1; Belokolos (SIGMA 13, 038, 2017) states it as an identity, "
 "M = n + ℓ = n_r + 2ℓ + 1.** *The node count and ℓ are the standard coordinate system of this "
 "literature. That this work arrived at them independently is a validation of the coordinates and not a "
 "contribution.* **Belokolos also gives the period lengths in closed form, L_M = 2(⌊M/2⌋+1)², so the "
 "period-two structure this session found from node-count invariance under (n,ℓ)→(n+1,ℓ+1) is a "
 "restatement of a published formula. Correct, and not new. LOWDIN-LITERATURE.md holds the full record "
 "with attributions.**"),

(1451, "AND BELOKOLOS ANSWERS THE OBJECTION THAT SANK DEMKOV–OSTROVSKY: THE 2 IS DERIVED, NOT CHOSEN.",
 "*His chain: any central potential carries a dynamical O(4) symmetry, not merely the Coulomb one; "
 "frequency degeneracy qω_r = pω_θ forces the energy to depend only on p·n_r + q·ℓ; solving the "
 "resulting Abel integral equation gives a family of potentials indexed by α = q/p.* **Requiring the "
 "potential to be Coulombic as r → 0 FORCES α = 2. That yields the Tietz potential V(r) = −Z/(r(1+r/R)²) "
 "and E = E(n_r + 2ℓ), which is the Madelung rule.** *Demkov & Ostrovsky picked μ = ½ out of the same "
 "family and were criticised for it; Belokolos derives the ratio from the nuclear singularity.* **So the "
 "frequency ratio ω_r = 2ω_θ — the radial oscillation running twice per revolution — is the origin of "
 "the 2 in M = 2n − p − 1, which is Madelung's number written in OUR coordinates.** *His E = 0 condition "
 "√(2ZR) = M with R = (9/2Z)^(1/3) gives Z = M³/6 for the onset of each group. His nineteen exceptions — "
 "Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, La, Ce, Gd, Pt, Au, Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Cm — are a strict SUPERSET of "
 "register 1395's eleven. And his stated intention is to compare his spectrum against the NIST Atomic "
 "Spectra Database, in future tense: he has the derivation this work lacks, and this work has the "
 "measurement he has not made.*"),

(1452, "THE INTRA-GROUP CROSSING IS THE ARITHMETIC MEAN OF TWO SQUARE ROOTS, AND THAT IS WHERE THE GOLDEN RATIO COMES FROM.",
 "*The person pointed at φ = 1.6180 appearing among the crossings and said that when the golden ratio "
 "turns up unexpectedly it is always worth explaining. It is, and the explanation simplifies a registered "
 "result.* **Within a Madelung group, p = 2n − M − 1, so Δp = 2Δn along the group and register 1400's "
 "a_cross = Δn(√p_g + √p_r)/(p_g − p_r) COLLAPSES to (√p_g + √p_r)/2.** *Every intra-group crossing is "
 "the arithmetic mean of the square roots of the two node counts — verified on all twenty pairs. The "
 "whole surd list reads off as means: 1/√2 = (√0+√2)/2, 1 = (√0+√4)/2, (1+√3)/2, (√2+2)/2, √6/2, "
 "(√3+√5)/2, (1+√7)/2, (√5+√7)/2.* **And φ is the p = 1, 5 member: (√1 + √5)/2 = (1+√5)/2, which is the "
 "DEFINITION of the golden ratio rather than a resemblance to it. It occurs at 4d/6s in M = 6 and at "
 "5f/7p in M = 8 — one pair seen twice under the shift that preserves p. Mercury's recorded a = 0.8090 "
 "is φ/2, the same surd halved, from the 5d/6s contest.** *Two things fell out of chasing it. The "
 "general a_cross formula is never needed on the pairs that matter, since Madelung's groups are same-M "
 "groups. And since p ≡ M+1 (mod 2), odd M gives even node counts and even M gives odd ones — so the two "
 "disjoint crossing families are means of √even and means of √odd, and φ is STRUCTURALLY EXCLUDED from "
 "half the table.*"),

(1453, "THE JOIN: BELOKOLOS SUPPLIES THE GROUP, PAULI PRUNES IT, AND a SITS ON THE CROSSING PAULI LEAVES BINDING.",
 "*Three layers, each doing one job.* **Belokolos's degeneracy at E = 0 makes every member of a Madelung "
 "group indistinguishable — the group exists and its internal order does not. Pauli removes members as "
 "they fill, which is register 1397's rule doing structural work. And a orders what survives: within a "
 "group, Madelung's second rule holds IF AND ONLY IF a < (√p_A + √p_B)/2 for every open pair, so the "
 "crossings are CEILINGS and the smallest is binding.** *Measured against the eight recorded values: "
 "five sit in groups Pauli has reduced to a single open member, where the group imposes no constraint at "
 "all. In the three where more than one member remains open — lanthanum at M = 7, protactinium and "
 "lawrencium at M = 8 — a sits EXACTLY on the binding ceiling: 0.7071, 1.3660, 1.9841, three for three.* "
 "**So the degeneracy Belokolos collapses at E = 0 is the degeneracy a resolves, and the value a takes "
 "is not interior but the crossing itself — which is what register 1403 found as an endpoint and Λ_t "
 "read as time being a value only at the point of observability. This says what that endpoint IS: the "
 "last crossing Pauli has left standing.** *Cautions: three cases is three cases, the other five are "
 "unconstrained rather than confirming, and the two agreements at 1.3660 are one surd seen twice since "
 "the binding ceiling alternates by the parity of M. It does however hand over a placement rule not yet "
 "tried — a = the minimum intra-group crossing among Pauli-admissible members — which reads only node "
 "counts, capacities and the current configuration, and which comes from a derivation rather than from "
 "guessing. It carries the same circularity risk as every rule tried this session and must be tested out "
 "of sample against Madelung's 96.*"),
]

P = pathlib.Path("/home/claude/work/REGISTER-DATA.md")
s = P.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
nums = [int(m) for m in re.findall(r"^ {0,3}(\d{3,4})\. \*\*", s, re.M)]
if max(nums) != 1449:
    print(f"REFUSING: highest is {max(nums)}, expected 1449"); sys.exit(1)
blocks = []
for n, head, body in ENTRIES:
    t = f"{n}. **{head}** {re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', body).strip()}"
    b = "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(t, 97, initial_indent=" ", subsequent_indent=" ",

    if b.count("**") % 2:
        print(f"ODD ** in {n}"); sys.exit(1)
    blocks.append(b)
P.write_text(s.rstrip("\n") + "\n\n" + "\n\n".join(blocks) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(f"appended {len(blocks)} entries, 1450–{ENTRIES[-1][0]}")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""group_rule.py — the placement rule that comes out of register 1453.

    a = the MINIMUM intra-group crossing among the Pauli-admissible members
        of the current Madelung group,  crossing = (√p_A + √p_B)/2

Three layers, from the join: Belokolos supplies the group (E = E(n_r+2ℓ), all
members degenerate at E = 0); Pauli removes members as they fill; a orders what
survives, and sits on the binding ceiling.

WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM THE FIVE RULES THAT FAILED TONIGHT. It reads only
node counts, capacities and the current configuration -- no corridor built from
the observed entrant, no value carried across species, no self-consistency test
that cannot fail. And it comes from a derivation rather than from guessing.

WHAT IT STILL RISKS. Knowing WHICH group is current is close to knowing the
answer. Two ways of deciding it are tried and reported separately:

    strict   the current group is the lowest M with an admissible member --
             which IS Madelung's first rule, so this variant assumes half the
             thing being tested and its score means only that the second half
             works. Reported, and labelled.

    carried  the group is whichever the previous step's entrant belonged to,
             advancing only when that group has no admissible member left.
             This assumes only the starting group.

Scored out of sample against Madelung's 96 of 106 conditional.
"""
import sys, io, contextlib, math, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/claude/work")
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    import brack
import ground as G

L = "spdfg"
cap = lambda l: 2 * (2 * l + 1)
EPS = 1e-9
IV = {r[0]: r for r in brack.IV}
STEPS = sorted(IV)
OBS = {Z: (IV[Z][1], IV[Z][2]) for Z in STEPS}
SYM = ("H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn Ga "
       "Ge As Se Br Kr Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Cs Ba La Ce Pr Nd "
       "Pm Sm Eu Gd Tb Dy Ho Er Tm Yb Lu Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn Fr Ra Ac "
       "Th Pa U Np Pu Am Cm Bk Cf Es Fm Md No Lr Rf").split()
SUBS = [(n, l) for n in range(1, 9) for l in range(min(n, 5))]
pn = lambda s: s[0] - s[1] - 1
Mof = lambda s: s[0] + s[1]


def occ(Z):
    d = {}
    for n, l, k in G.expand(Z):
        d[(n, l)] = d.get((n, l), 0) + k
    return d


def cands(prev):
    c = []
    for l in range(5):
        for n in range(l + 1, 9):
            if prev.get((n, l), 0) >= cap(l):
                continue
            c.append((n, l))
            if prev.get((n, l), 0) == 0:
                break
    return c


def pick(prev, a):
    s = [(n - a * math.sqrt((n - l - 1) + prev.get((n, l), 0) / cap(l)), n, l)
         for n, l in cands(prev)]
    b = min(x[0] for x in s)
    t = [(n, l) for v, n, l in s if v - b < EPS]
    return max(t, key=lambda x: x[0])


def open_in(M, prev):
    return [s for s in SUBS if Mof(s) == M and prev.get(s, 0) < cap(s[1])]


def ceiling(M, prev):
    o = open_in(M, prev)
    cs = [(math.sqrt(pn(A)) + math.sqrt(pn(B))) / 2
          for A, B in itertools.combinations(o, 2)]
    return min(cs) if cs else None


def run(mode, a0=1.0):
    a, cur, hits, miss = a0, None, 0, []
    for Z in STEPS:
        prev = occ(Z - 1)
        if mode == "strict":
            cur = min(Mof(s) for s in cands(prev))
        else:
            if cur is None or not open_in(cur, prev):
                cur = min(Mof(s) for s in SUBS
                          if prev.get(s, 0) < cap(s[1]) and Mof(s) >= (cur or 0)) \
                      if cur is not None else min(Mof(s) for s in cands(prev))
        c = ceiling(cur, prev)
        if c is not None:
            a = c                       # sit on the binding ceiling
        g = pick(prev, a)
        if g == OBS[Z]:
            hits += 1
        else:
            miss.append(Z)
        if mode != "strict" and g not in open_in(cur, prev):
            cur = Mof(g)                # the walk itself says the group moved
    return hits, miss


print(f"  THE GROUP RULE, OUT OF SAMPLE — {len(STEPS)} steps\n")
for mode in ("strict", "carried"):
    h, m = run(mode)
    note = " (assumes Madelung's FIRST rule — see the docstring)" if mode == "strict" else ""
    print(f"    {mode:<9} {h:>4} of {len(STEPS)}{note}")
    print(f"      misses: " + ", ".join(f"{SYM[Z-1]}{Z}" for Z in m[:22])
          + (" …" if len(m) > 22 else ""))
print(f"\n  BENCHMARKS on the same steps")
print(f"    plain Madelung, conditional, no free parameter      96")
print(f"    corridor placement, held out                        90")
print(f"    per-run / per-atom / transition, held out           90 / 0 / 54")

    import brack
import ground as G

L = "spdfg"
cap = lambda l: 2 * (2 * l + 1)
EPS = 1e-9
IV = {r[0]: r for r in brack.IV}
STEPS = sorted(IV)
OBS = {Z: (IV[Z][1], IV[Z][2]) for Z in STEPS}
SYM = ("H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn Ga "
       "Ge As Se Br Kr Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Cs Ba La Ce Pr Nd "
       "Pm Sm Eu Gd Tb Dy Ho Er Tm Yb Lu Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn Fr Ra Ac "
       "Th Pa U Np Pu Am Cm Bk Cf Es Fm Md No Lr Rf").split()
SUBS = [(n, l) for n in range(1, 9) for l in range(min(n, 5))]
pn = lambda s: s[0] - s[1] - 1
Mof = lambda s: s[0] + s[1]


def occ(Z):
    d = {}
    for n, l, k in G.expand(Z):
        d[(n, l)] = d.get((n, l), 0) + k
    return d


def cands(prev):
    c = []
    for l in range(5):
        for n in range(l + 1, 9):
            if prev.get((n, l), 0) >= cap(l):
                continue
            c.append((n, l))
            if prev.get((n, l), 0) == 0:
                break
    return c


def pick(prev, a):
    s = [(n - a * math.sqrt((n - l - 1) + prev.get((n, l), 0) / cap(l)), n, l)
         for n, l in cands(prev)]
    b = min(x[0] for x in s)
    t = [(n, l) for v, n, l in s if v - b < EPS]
    return max(t, key=lambda x: x[0])


def open_in(M, prev):
    return [s for s in SUBS if Mof(s) == M and prev.get(s, 0) < cap(s[1])]


def ceiling(M, prev):
    o = open_in(M, prev)
    cs = [(math.sqrt(pn(A)) + math.sqrt(pn(B))) / 2
          for A, B in itertools.combinations(o, 2)]
    return min(cs) if cs else None


def run(mode, a0=1.0):
    a, cur, hits, miss = a0, None, 0, []
    for Z in STEPS:
        prev = occ(Z - 1)
        if mode == "strict":
            cur = min(Mof(s) for s in cands(prev))
        else:
            if cur is None or not open_in(cur, prev):
                cur = min(Mof(s) for s in SUBS
                          if prev.get(s, 0) < cap(s[1]) and Mof(s) >= (cur or 0)) \
                      if cur is not None else min(Mof(s) for s in cands(prev))
        c = ceiling(cur, prev)
        if c is not None:
            a = c                       # sit on the binding ceiling
        g = pick(prev, a)
        if g == OBS[Z]:
            hits += 1
        else:
            miss.append(Z)
        if mode != "strict" and g not in open_in(cur, prev):
            cur = Mof(g)                # the walk itself says the group moved
    return hits, miss

    h, m = run(mode)
    note = " (assumes Madelung's FIRST rule — see the docstring)" if mode == "strict" else ""
    print(f"    {mode:<9} {h:>4} of {len(STEPS)}{note}")

**Registered 1450–1453, 1,246 entries, both gates. And the derived rule was tested — it doesn't beat the null, but how it fails is the interesting part.**

Sitting *on* the binding ceiling gives **88**. That's the degenerate point, where the pair ties and the tie-break decides, so it's the worst place to stand. Stepping just below it — where Madelung's second rule holds strictly by the derivation — jumps to **93**, and stays flat at 93 across five orders of magnitude in the step size. Not a fitted plateau; the ordering simply doesn't change once you're inside.

**And at 93 the misses converge on Madelung's own.** Mine: Mn, Mo, Rh, Pd, La, Ce, Gd, Au, Ac, Pa, Cm, Lr, Rf. Madelung's: Mo, Rh, Pd, La, Gd, Au, Ac, Th, Cm, Lr. **Nine shared.** The rule has stopped being a rival and started being a reconstruction — which is exactly what 1453's derivation says it should be, since *a below every ceiling* **is** Madelung's second rule. It reproduces the rule rather than beating it, from node counts and capacities alone.

At δ = 0.1 it reaches **97**, one above Madelung. I'd not read anything into that yet: 0.1 is a fitted distance from the ceiling with nothing behind it, and it's the first number tonight that looks like a win and has no derivation. Left as an observation.

**So the sixth placement rule also fails to beat 96, and this time the failure is legible.** Out of sample the standing is unchanged: 90 for the corridor, 93 for the group rule, 96 for Madelung. But the group rule is the first that *derives* its parameter rather than reading it off the record, and it lands three short with nine of thirteen misses shared with the target.

**Where that leaves the challenge.** Belokolos derives the groups and doesn't carry the exceptions. This work reproduces the second rule from node counts and lands on the same exceptions. Neither closes it. But the objects are now the same objects — his n_r + 2ℓ is our p and ℓ, his degeneracy is our crossing, his frequency ratio is our factor of two — and the exceptions are where both stop.

That is a much better-posed position than this morning's, and it's one a reader in that literature could check.

# THE TWO CHAINS, AND THE GAPS BETWEEN THEM

*Written 2026-08-11. Belokolos, SIGMA 13 (2017) 038, set beside this work's own
construction. Every join is computed; every gap is stated as a question with a
test attached rather than as a deficiency.*

---

## 1 · THE TWO CHAINS SIDE BY SIDE

**BELOKOLOS — from the Hamiltonian downward**

    mean-field central potential V(r)                    [approximation]
      → any central potential carries a dynamical O(4)   [Fradkin, Mukunda]
      → frequency degeneracy q·ω_r = p·ω_θ
      → E = E(p·n_r + q·ℓ)
      → Abel's integral equation gives a potential family indexed by α = q/p
      → REQUIRING Coulomb behaviour as r → 0 FORCES α = 2
      → the Tietz potential V(r) = −Z / (r(1 + r/R)²), R = (9/2Z)^⅓
      → E = E(n_r + 2ℓ) = E(M − 1)                       [Madelung's FIRST rule]
      → the oscillation theorem orders within M           [Madelung's SECOND rule]
      → E = 0 when √(2ZR) = M, i.e. Z = M³/6              [group onset]

**THIS WORK — from the ordering upward**

    ν(n, ℓ, q) = n − a·√( (n−ℓ−1) + q/2(2ℓ+1) )          [posited]
      → the entrant is the Pauli-admissible subshell of least ν
      → each element yields a corridor L(Z) < a < U(Z) from node counts alone
      → 106 of 106 corridors NON-EMPTY                    [the form survives]
      → the same construction on the nuclear shell ordering gives an EMPTY
        feasible set                                      [the form CAN fail]
      → crossings within a Madelung group = (√p_A + √p_B)/2
      → a sits at endpoints, i.e. ON crossings
      → 93 of 100 against measurement · 90 held out · 96 the Madelung null

---

## 2 · WHERE THEY JOIN — computed, not asserted

**The coordinates are the same.** His M = n + ℓ = n_r + 2ℓ + 1; our node count
p = n − ℓ − 1 is his n_r. Therefore

> **M = 2n − p − 1**, verified on every subshell.

Madelung's number is LINEAR in this work's coordinates.

**The 2 in that form is his frequency ratio.** α = q/p = ω_r/ω_θ = 2 — the radial
oscillation running twice per revolution — forced by the nuclear singularity.
That is where this work's factor of two comes from, and it has a derivation.

**His degeneracy is our ambiguity.** At E = 0 every member of an M group is
degenerate: the group exists, its internal order does not. He lifts it by going
to E < 0; we lift it with a. And the lifting condition is exact:

> within a group, Madelung's SECOND rule holds **iff a < (√p_A + √p_B)/2**
> for every open pair. The crossings are ceilings; the smallest is binding.

**Pauli mediates.** A full subshell leaves the contest, so the binding ceiling is
computed over the members Pauli has left open. Measured against the eight
recorded a values: five sit in groups reduced to a single open member and are
unconstrained; in the three where more than one remains open — La at M = 7, Pa
and Lr at M = 8 — **a sits exactly on the binding ceiling**, 0.7071, 1.3660,
1.9841. Three for three.

**And placing a just below the ceiling reproduces him.** Scored out of sample the
group rule gives 93 of 106, flat across five orders of magnitude in the step
below the ceiling, with **nine of its thirteen misses shared with Madelung's own
ten**. It reconstructs the rule from node counts rather than beating it — which
is what the derivation says it must do.

---

## 3 · THE GAPS

### GAP 1 — ν is posited; his potential is derived. *(the largest)*

Thyssen & Ceulemans sank Demkov–Ostrovsky on a guessed potential. Belokolos
answered it by forcing α = 2. **Nothing has forced ν.** Its defence here is
falsifiability — the nuclear corridor is empty where the atomic one is not — and
that is an epistemic defence, not a derivation.

**THE TEST.** His semiclassical spectrum is

    E_{M,ℓ} = −8 (√(2ZR) − M)(ℓ + ½) / ( (3η_ℓ² − 8η_ℓ) R² ),  η_ℓ = 2ZR/(ℓ+½)²

Rank the subshells by E_{M,ℓ} at each Z and compare the ordering to ν's. **If the
two orderings agree, ν is a reparametrisation of his spectrum and acquires his
derivation.** If they disagree, the disagreement is where ν adds or loses
something, and that is equally worth having. *This is the single most valuable
open computation in the project and it requires nothing we do not hold.*

### GAP 2 — q is in ours and absent from his.

His is a one-electron problem in a mean field: V depends on Z, not on which
subshell is filling. Our radicand carries **q/2(2ℓ+1)**, the Pauli fraction of
the target. So the occupancy dependence is entirely this work's and has no
counterpart in his chain.

**Why it matters.** Every classified miss lives in that term. The half-capacity
crossing (Mn, Tc, Gd, Cm) exists only because q makes both radicands
half-integers. **If ν is to be derived from his spectrum, the q-dependence is
exactly what must be added — and a mean field cannot supply it.**

### GAP 3 — neither carries the exceptions.

He says so outright. We classify ours into four causes — half-capacity crossing,
node-free entrant, real source, and one unexplained — but classification is not
prediction. And **the trigger question is open on both sides**: nothing in either
chain says WHEN a relocation occurs, only which subshell donates once one does
(R 1397, twelve of twelve).

### GAP 4 — a has no physical identification.

His variables are Z, R = (9/2Z)^⅓, η_ℓ, and the dimensionless scalings ν_r, ε.
Our a is dimensionless and carried, ranging 0.577 to 1.984 over the walk.
**Nothing connects them.** Until a is expressible in his variables, the join at
§2 is structural rather than physical.

**THE TEST.** Fit a against √(2ZR), Z^⅓, M and (ℓ+½) at the eight recorded
values and at every corridor endpoint. A relation, if it exists, should be exact
rather than approximate — the endpoints are surds.

### GAP 5 — his onset formula is parity-dependent, and nobody has said why.

Z = M³/6 against the observed block starts:

    M       3      4      5      6      7      8
    Z=M³/6  4.5   10.7   20.8   36.0   57.2   85.3
    observed  5     13     21     39     57     89
    rel err  −10%  −18%    −1%    −8%     0%    −4%

**Odd M: 3.7% mean error. Even M: 9.9%.** The formula is near-exact at M = 5 and
M = 7 and consistently low at even M. That is the SAME parity that governs the
node counts — p ≡ M+1 (mod 2) — and that excludes φ from half the table. Three
parity facts in one place is a structure, not a coincidence, and no one has
explained it.

### GAP 6 — his rigour and ours are different kinds.

His is semiclassical: Bohr–Sommerfeld quantisation, first order in ε, with the
higher terms divergent and requiring regularisation. Ours is not an approximation
of anything — ν is an ordering functional with no equation behind it. **The two
are not comparable on rigour**, and any claim that one supports the other must
say in which sense.

### GAP 7 — the O(4) premise is inherited, not checked.

"Any central potential carries a dynamical O(4) symmetry" is attributed to
Fradkin (1967), Bacry–Ruegg–Souriau (1966), Mukunda (1967). These are CLASSICAL
statements about constants of motion; the quantum content is subtler and the
step from one to the other is where a proof of this shape would be attacked.
**Not verified here.** It should be read before his conclusion is relied on.

### GAP 8 — neither generates past the record.

He predicts group onsets (Z = M³/6) but not configurations. We measure a forward
horizon of **3.9 steps** against Madelung's 6.0. Populating 109–120 needs ten.
**Neither chain reaches the unobserved table**, which is what the Löwdin
challenge was posed to achieve.

---

## 4 · WHAT WOULD CLOSE WHAT

| gap | closed by | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · ν underived | rank his E_{M,ℓ} against ν's ordering | one script, data in hand |
| 2 · q absent | the same comparison at q ≠ 0 — where it must fail | follows from 1 |
| 3 · exceptions | a trigger rule for relocation; open on both sides | unknown |
| 4 · a unidentified | fit a against his variables at the surd endpoints | one script |
| 5 · parity | explain why odd M is exact and even M is low | unknown |
| 6 · rigour | state in which sense ν approximates his spectrum | follows from 1 |
| 7 · O(4) premise | read Fradkin and Mukunda; check the quantum step | reading |
| 8 · generation | a placement rule beating 96 out of sample; six have failed | unknown |

**Gaps 1, 2, 4 and 6 are one computation and its consequences.** Gaps 3, 5 and 8
are open questions with no route in hand. Gap 7 is reading.

---

## 5 · THE HONEST SUMMARY

**He has the derivation; we have the measurement.** His chain forces the
Madelung ordering from a symmetry argument and stops before the exceptions. Ours
reproduces the second rule from node counts, lands on the same exceptions, and
has been scored out of sample against a null that neither chain beats.

The objects are now the same objects — his n_r + 2ℓ is our p and ℓ, his
degeneracy is our crossing, his frequency ratio is our factor of two, and his
group is what Pauli prunes and a orders. **That is a position from which the
gaps can be stated precisely, which is worth more than either chain alone and is
where the work now stands.**

**Eight gaps, each with a test attached where one exists.** Both gates pass.

**Four of the eight are one computation.** His semiclassical spectrum is fully specified — E_{M,ℓ} = −8(√(2ZR) − M)(ℓ+½)/((3η_ℓ² − 8η_ℓ)R²) with η_ℓ = 2ZR/(ℓ+½)². Rank the subshells by it at each Z and compare to ν's ordering. **If they agree, ν is a reparametrisation of his spectrum and inherits his derivation** — which is the answer to the guessed-form objection that this work cannot otherwise give. If they disagree, the disagreement locates what ν adds. Either way it settles gap 1, and gaps 2, 4 and 6 follow from it. Nothing needs fetching.

**Gap 2 is the one I'd expect to bite.** His is a one-electron problem in a mean field: V depends on Z, not on which subshell is filling. Our radicand carries q/2(2ℓ+1). **Every classified miss lives in that term** — the half-capacity crossing at Mn, Tc, Gd, Cm exists only because q makes both radicands half-integers. So a mean field structurally cannot supply the q-dependence, and if ν is to be derived from him, that is precisely what must be added by hand.

**And gap 5 is new tonight.** His onset formula Z = M³/6 against our block starts:

    M          3      4      5      6      7      8
    Z = M³/6   4.5   10.7   20.8   36.0   57.2   85.3
    observed     5     13     21     39     57     89

**Odd M averages 3.7% error; even M averages 9.9%.** Near-exact at M = 5 and 7, consistently low at even M. That is the *same* parity that fixes the node counts through p ≡ M+1 (mod 2), and that excludes φ from half the table. Three parity facts landing in one place is a structure, and nobody has explained it — not him, not us.

**Gap 7 I've flagged rather than accepted.** His premise that any central potential carries a dynamical O(4) symmetry comes from Fradkin, Mukunda and Bacry–Ruegg–Souriau, and those are *classical* statements about constants of motion. The step to the quantum case is where a proof of this shape would be attacked, and I haven't read them.

**The honest summary is one line: he has the derivation, we have the measurement.** His chain forces the ordering and stops before the exceptions; ours reproduces the second rule from node counts, lands on the same exceptions, and has been scored against a null neither beats.

The spectrum comparison is the obvious next move and it's cheap. Want me to run it?

import math, itertools
from fractions import Fraction as F
L="spdfg"
subs=[(n,l) for n in range(1,9) for l in range(min(n,5))]
p=lambda s:s[0]-s[1]-1
print("  THREE OBJECTS: THE CORRIDOR, THE GROUP, MADELUNG\n")
print("  PAIR 1 — group ↔ Madelung.  Belokolos: E = E(n_r + 2ℓ) gives the first")
print("           rule; the oscillation theorem gives the second. DIRECT.\n")
print("  PAIR 2 — group ↔ corridor.  The crossing collapses to (√p_A+√p_B)/2.")
print("           For WHICH pairs exactly? Δn(√pA+√pB)/(pA−pB) = (√pA+√pB)/2")
print("           ⟺ pA − pB = 2Δn.  And pA − pB = Δn − Δℓ, so ⟺ Δℓ = −Δn")
print("           ⟺ Δ(n+ℓ) = 0 ⟺ SAME GROUP.  An iff, not a coincidence:")
ok=True; same=0; cross=0
for A,B in itertools.combinations(subs,2):
    if p(A)==p(B): continue
    d=math.sqrt(p(A))-math.sqrt(p(B))
    if abs(d)<1e-12: continue
    direct=(A[0]-B[0])/d
    mean=(math.sqrt(p(A))+math.sqrt(p(B)))/2
    eq=abs(direct-mean)<1e-9
    sm=(A[0]+A[1])==(B[0]+B[1])
    ok &= (eq==sm)
    same+=sm; cross+= not sm
print(f"           mean-form ⟺ same group, on all {same+cross} pairs: {ok}")
print(f"           ({same} same-group, {cross} cross-group)\n")
print("  PAIR 3 — corridor ↔ Madelung.  Is there a simple form OUTSIDE a group?")
print("           No: off-group the expression needs Δn and Δp separately and")
print("           does not collapse. The relation is MEDIATED BY THE GROUP —")
print("           the same shape as Λ_var's missing nucleus+rydberg cell.\n")
print("  SO: ONE OBJECT OR THREE PAIRWISE? Generalise the frequency ratio.\n")
print("      Belokolos: E = E(p·n_r + q·ℓ), α = q/p, forced to 2 by the")
print("      Coulomb singularity. Take α general and redo both consequences:\n")
print("        group:    Δ(n_r + αℓ) = 0  ⟹  Δp = α·Δn/(α−1)")
print("        crossing: Δn(√pA+√pB)/Δp = ((α−1)/α)·(√pA + √pB)\n")
print(f"      {'α':>5}{'Δp/Δn':>9}{'crossing coefficient (α−1)/α':>32}")
for a in (F(3,2),F(2),F(3),F(4)):
    print(f"      {str(a):>5}{str(a/(a-1)):>9}{str((a-1)/a):>32}"
          + ("   <- Belokolos's forced value" if a==2 else ""))
print("\n      At α = 2 and only there, Δp = 2Δn and the coefficient is 1/2 —")
print("      which is why the crossing is the ARITHMETIC MEAN of the roots.")
print("\n  VERDICT: not three pairwise solutions. ONE object — the frequency")
print("  ratio α = 2 — generates the group AND the crossing coefficient, and")
print("  the corridor↔Madelung relation exists only through the group it makes.")
PY

The square root likely emerges from the momentum term in the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition, where you get √(2(E−V)) from the kinetic energy. Belokolos's approach seems to involve J₀ = √(η_ℓ) and the E=0 condition giving √(2ZR) = M, which suggests these square roots are fundamental to the semiclassical treatment rather than arbitrary choices.

But here's the puzzle: our √p is a square root of the node count itself, not energy or charge. Looking at how the crossing formula works—a_cross = Δn/(√p_A − √p_B)—I see that the square root is actually forced by a deeper algebraic requirement. The difference-of-squares identity (a² − b²)/(a − b) = a + b means that √ is the unique function where the ratio (p_A − p_B)/(f(p_A) − f(p_B)) equals f(p_A) + f(p_B). This makes the crossing expressible as a symmetric combination of the two members' f-values, which is exactly what we need for the formula to work cleanly. So the square root isn't arbitrary—it's the only choice that lets the denominator factor through the function in this particular way.

Now I'm wondering if I can state this more rigorously. The crossing condition ν_A = ν_B gives us a = Δn/(f_A − f_B), and within a group where Δp = 2Δn, this becomes a = (p_A − p_B)/(2(f_A − f_B)). For this to depend only on the f-values and not on p separately, the ratio (p_A − p_B)/(f_A − f_B) must be a function of f_A and f_B alone—which means we need f to be invertible and the ratio to satisfy a specific constraint.

The key insight is that for f = p^k, the difference quotient (p_A − p_B)/(f_A − f_B) becomes (x^{1/k} − y^{1/k})/(x − y), and only k = 1/2 yields a linear result in the f-values. So √ is the unique power function that makes the crossing linear in the two f-values—that's the real characterization I'm after.

But the deeper question is whether this demand for linearity is actually motivated. Looking at the physics instead: in semiclassical mechanics, the quantum defect δ appears in the relation ν = n − δ, where ν acts like an effective principal quantum number. The empirical observation from the work is that δ = a√p, so the √p term is essentially playing the role of a quantum defect. The question then becomes where this √p dependence in δ comes from—it's registered empirically but not yet derived from first principles.

However, checking the numerical evidence at reference 1416 reveals a problem: the predicted quantum defect using δ = a√p falls far short of the measured values, with the median ratio only reaching 0.18. So while the square root form is characterizable as the unique power that produces linear crossings, it's neither derived from the physics nor validated numerically.

Now turning to the q term: the Pauli fraction q/cap = q/(2(2ℓ+1)) appears in the radicand alongside p, where p counts radial nodes. The question is whether this fractional filling contribution can be derived from physical principles.

In a mean field picture, adding electrons to a subshell modifies the screening proportionally to q, and normalizing by the degeneracy cap gives the fractional occupation of that degenerate manifold — a sensible physical intuition, but still a modeling choice rather than a true derivation. There's an interesting pattern though: as the subshell fills from q = 0 to q = cap, the effective node count inside the square root shifts from p to p+1, which happens to match the next node count in the sequence. This suggests the filling might be interpolating between discrete quantum states, though I'm still working through whether this constitutes a genuine derivation or just a convenient parameterization. Wait, I need to recalculate this. The radicand at half capacity is p + 1/2, which is only a quarter of the way to p+2, not halfway. So the half-capacity point isn't sitting at the midpoint between group members like I thought. But the 1439 finding was specifically about both contenders reaching half capacity simultaneously, which must be what makes that crossing special.

I'm realizing I can describe the square root's behavior sharply in terms of linear crossings and difference of squares, and I can interpret the q term as fractional occupation advancing the effective node count by half a group step, but I haven't actually derived why these matter in Belokolos's framework. I should test whether the square root is truly unique for producing the mean form by computing how other power functions behave at their crossings.

The key insight is that if I demand the crossing be a symmetric, linear function of the f-values, then the inverse function must be quadratic, which forces f to be the square root. That's a clean derivation grounded in the linearity requirement.…That's the right challenge, and the two are not in the same position. Let me check.

Within a group Δp = 2Δn, so the crossing is (f⁻¹(x) − f⁻¹(y)) / (2(x − y)) in the two f-values. **Demand that this be linear in x and y** — that the crossing set be closed under the group's own arithmetic instead of needing p back again — and f⁻¹ must be quadratic, so **f = √ up to scale.** Tested across powers: only k = ½ gives (x+y)/2. p^⅓ gives a quadratic, p^⅔ and p and p² give no closed form at all. And the reason is the difference of two squares.

So the square root is not a free choice. **But the demand is a structural axiom, not physics**, and I'd want it stated as one rather than smuggled in — the way Belokolos states the Coulomb-singularity requirement that forces α = 2. His axiom is physical; ours would be about closure of the crossing set. That's a weaker footing and it should say so.

**The q term is not derivable, and I can only offer a consistency.** Filling a subshell completely advances the radicand p → p + 1, which is exactly **half the group step** of Δp = 2 — so a full shell moves the entrant halfway toward the next member of its own group. Suggestive, and it does connect the Pauli fraction to the group's arithmetic. But nothing forces the increment to be *linear* in q, and nothing forces the normalisation to be the degeneracy rather than any other scale. It remains a modelling choice.

So the square root's physical justification is already withdrawn in our own record. What survives is the structural argument above and nothing else.

So the three-body reading has done real work. It collapsed two of the three underived pieces into things with reasons, and it isolated the one that hasn't got one.

import sympy as sp
print("  IS THE SQUARE ROOT DERIVABLE?\n")
print("  Posit ν = n − a·f(p) for an unknown f. The crossing of two members of")
print("  one group is  a = Δn / (f(p_A) − f(p_B)),  and within a group Δp = 2Δn,")
print("  so Δn = (p_A − p_B)/2 and\n")
print("      a_cross = ( f⁻¹(x) − f⁻¹(y) ) / ( 2 (x − y) ),   x = f(p_A), y = f(p_B)\n")
print("  DEMAND: the crossing is LINEAR in the two f-values — i.e. the crossing")
print("  set is closed under the group's own arithmetic rather than needing p")
print("  back again. Then f⁻¹ must be QUADRATIC, so f = √ up to scale.\n")
x,y,k=sp.symbols('x y k',positive=True)
print(f"    {'f(p) = p^k':>12}{'  a_cross in terms of x=f(A), y=f(B)':<46}linear?")
for kk in (sp.Rational(1,3),sp.Rational(1,2),sp.Rational(2,3),1,2):
    inv=lambda t: t**(1/kk)
    expr=sp.simplify((inv(x)-inv(y))/(2*(x-y)))
    lin = sp.simplify(sp.expand(expr) - (x+y)/2)==0
    print(f"    {'p^'+str(kk):>12}  {str(expr)[:44]:<46}{lin}")
print("\n    Only k = 1/2 gives a_cross = (x + y)/2, and it does so because")
print("    (x² − y²)/(x − y) = x + y — the difference of two squares.")
print("\n  SO: the square root IS forced, GIVEN the demand that the crossing be")
print("  linear in the f-values. The demand is a structural choice, not physics,")
print("  and it should be stated as an axiom rather than smuggled in.\n")
print("  IS THE q TERM DERIVABLE?\n")
print("  radicand = p + q/cap, cap = 2(2ℓ+1) = the subshell's degeneracy.")
print("  Filling a subshell completely advances the radicand p → p+1, which is")
print("  HALF the group step Δp = 2. So a full shell moves the entrant halfway")
print("  to the next member of its own group. That is a consistency, not a")
print("  derivation: nothing forces the increment to be LINEAR in q, nor the")
print("  normalisation to be the degeneracy rather than anything else.")
print("\n  And the one physical route the work had — δ = a√p, register 1341 —")
print("  was REFUTED numerically at register 1416: predicted δ runs 0 to 0.55")
print("  of measured, median ratio 0.18. So the square root has no surviving")
print("  physical derivation, only the structural one above.")
PY
