There's no Farkas certificate here, and register 1493's reading of the +16/−9 as an infeasibility signature is wrong. That's the third hypothesis of mine today that the data has refused, and it was declared before the sampling, which is the only reason I can say so cleanly.

**But the correlation is the real finding, and it explains the eight failures.** The two NEC counts move together at **r = +0.905** in this rule family. Any edit that pulls NEC ≥ 2 down pulls NEC ≥ 3 down with it, and the target needs them moved in **opposite** directions — sixteen down, nine up. That is why eight separate attacks left +16 and −9 untouched: they were all moving along the correlated direction, and the residual lies across it.

So the eight attacks weren't weak. They were **aimed along the grain**.

**And that turns the next move into something specific.** Not a ninth search of the same kind, but a search that can move the two counts *independently* — which means finding rules whose removed boxes straddle the NEC = 2 boundary asymmetrically, since those are the only ones that separate the two marginals. `vi_best` already sits in the rare 0.9% region, so it found such a rule; what's needed is more of that one kind, not more rules in general.

The ninth attempt, this time attacking across the grain, only shifted the distance from 79 to 78 and improved X ≥ 2 (from +2 to +1), but left the NEC pair untouched. The +16/−9 remains completely fixed — even restricting the search to NEC-asymmetric rules can't budge it. This most targeted attack still fails on the same pair as all the others, so I've now tried eight attacks along the grain and one across, with no success on that stubborn pair.

My sampling data showed that opposite-sign errors do occur in about 20 of 2210 cases, so they're achievable in principle. But the sampling never got close to (0,0), and the targeted search can't move this pair at all. The evidence is pointing toward (+16, −9) being a fixed point under this rule family, at least near the exact-cells constraint — which is stronger evidence for infeasibility than I had before, though I need to be careful not to overstate it given what the sampling revealed.…

The existence of Hadamard states of the free scalar ﬁeld in certain curved spacetimes was proved in · [8] by deforming Minkowski spacetime into another globally hyperbolic spacetime.

#### 3.2 Existence of a local Reeh-Schlieder state for higher spin field theories

We can now use the analysis of the previous section to prove our main result. The line of reasoning can be summarized as follows: Since every globally hyperbolic spacetime (M', g') is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R} \times \Sigma$ , $\Sigma$ being a three-dimensional Cauchy surface, it is always possible to apply proposition 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 by fixing (M,g) as an ultrastatic spacetime which is in turn diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R} \times \Sigma$ . In the latter case it was proven in [Stro00] that, for a scalar or a Proca field, every quasifree and continuous state which is ground or KMS with respect to the timelike Killing vector field in M has the Reeh-Schlieder property. 

Furthermore, if $(\mathfrak{H}_{\omega'}, \pi_{\omega'}, \Omega_{\omega'})$ is the GNS triplet associated to $\omega'$ , $\Omega_{\omega'}$ is both cyclic and separating for $\pi_{\omega'}(W_m(\mathfrak{O}, g'|_{\mathfrak{O}}))''$ .

Proof. In proposition 2.2 it was proven that a Proca field can be described as a locally covariant quantum field theory which, furthermore, satisfies the time-slice axiom. Hence we can apply the procedure depicted in the previous section by deforming the chosen globally hyperbolic spacetime (M',g') into an ultrastatic one, (M,g). On the latter the Weyl algebra for a massive spin 1 field, $\mathcal{W}_m(M,g)$ , admits a ground state with respect to the timelike Killing field [Fur99]. On account of [SaVe00] we also know that such a state is of Hadamard form and, on account of [Stro00] that it has the Reeh-Schlieder property. 

Hence, proposition 3.2 guarantees the existence of a \*-isomorphism $\alpha: \mathcal{W}_m(M',g') \to \mathcal{W}_m(M,g)$ whereas proposition 3.3 asserts that $\omega' = \alpha^* \omega$ has the sought properties. Furthermore, the very same deformation argument (see [SaVe01]) entails also that $\omega'$ enjoys the Hadamard property.

Microlocal analysis of quantum fields on curved spacetimes: Analytic wavefront sets and Reeh-Schlieder theorems ... We show in this article that the Reeh-Schlieder property holds for states of quantum fields on real analytic spacetimes if they satisfy an analytic microlocal spectrum condition. This result holds in the setting of general quantum field theory, i.e. without assuming the quantum field to obey a specific equation of motion. Moreover, quasifree states of the Klein-Gordon field are further investigated in this work and the (analytic) microlocal spectrum condition is shown to be equivalent to simpler conditions.

content.text:
It is shown that ground- and KMS-states on certain static spacetimes and adiabatic vacuum states on Robertson-Walker spaces are Hadamard states. Finally, the problem of constructing Hadamard states on arbitrary curved spacetimes is solved in principle.

#### Zusammenfassung

Es werden quasifreie Zustände eines quantisierten linearen Klein-Gordon-Feldes auf global hyperbolischen Raumzeit-Mannigfaltigkeiten betrachtet. Unter Verwendung von Methoden aus der Theorie der Pseudodifferentialoperatoren und Wellenfrontenmengen auf Mannigfaltigkeiten wird ein Kriterium entwickelt, das es ermöglicht, die Hadamard-Eigenschaft von Zuständen nachzuweisen. Es wird gezeigt, daß Grund- und KMS-Zustände auf gewissen statischen Raumzeiten und adiabatische Vakuumzustände auf Robertson-Walker-Raumzeiten Hadamard-Zustände sind. Zu guter Letzt wird ein Konstruktionsverfahren für Hadamard-Zustände auf beliebigen gekrümmten Raumzeiten angegeben.

$$(p,\xi) \sim (q,\zeta) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \qquad \exists \text{ lightlike geodesic } c\colon I \to M \text{ and } t,t' \in I\colon \\ c(t) = p, \ c(t') = q, \ \dot{c}(t) = \xi^{\sharp}, \ \dot{c}(t') = \zeta^{\sharp}. \tag{1.7}$$

Note that, unlike the criterion given in [KW1991], this is a local condition, which Sahlmann and Verch generalized to sections in general vector bundles [SV2001]. It includes Hadamard states of the Dirac field in the sense of [Köh1995, Kra2000, Hol2001], which have been used, for instance, for a mathematical rigorous description of the chiral anomaly [BS2016]. In addition, [SVW2002] proposed an even more elegant characterization of the Hadamard property in terms of Hilbert space valued distributions $\varphi \mapsto \Phi_{\tau}[\varphi]\Omega_{\tau} \in \mathscr{H}_{\tau}$ , involving the GNS-representation induced by $\tau$ . Also for non-quasifree states, one can formulate (1.6) as a constraint on the whole n-point-function,



which is compatible with the special case of quasifree states [San2010]. Moreover, in analytic spacetimes, this generalized Hadamard condition can be sharpened to a condition on the analytic wave front set, thereby implying the Reeh-Schlieder-property [SVW2002]. Likewise, for non-globally hyperbolic spacetimes, there is a formulation of the Hadamard condition via restriction to globally hyperbolic subregions. Hadamard states have therefore been studied in connection with the Casimir effect and on anti-de Sitter spacetime (see [DNP2014, DFM2018] and references therein). By using the weaker concept of Sobolev wave front sets, a definition of adiabatic states on globally hyperbolic spacetimes similar to (1.6) is given in [JS2002], thus implying that Hadamard states are adiabatic.

However, most importantly for the purpose of this work, the Hadamard condition in the form (1.6) allows us to employ the techniques of microlocal analysis provided by Duistermaat and Hörmander [DH1972].

content.title: [0801.4676] On the Reeh-Schlieder Property in Curved Spacetime
content.text:
We attempt to prove the existence of Reeh-Schlieder states on curved spacetimes in the framework of locally covariant quantum field theory using the idea of spacetime deformation and assuming the existence of a Reeh-Schlieder state on a diffeomorphic (but not isometric) spacetime. We find that physically interesting states with a weak form of the Reeh-Schlieder property always exist and indicate their usefulness. Algebraic states satisfying the full Reeh-Schlieder property also exist, but are not guaranteed to be of physical interest.

View a PDF of the paper titled On the Reeh-Schlieder Property in Curved Spacetime, by Ko Sanders (University of York and 1 other authors View PDF · Abstract: We attempt to prove the existence of Reeh-Schlieder states on curved spacetimes in the framework of locally covariant quantum field theory using the idea of spacetime deformation and assuming the existence of a Reeh-Schlieder state on a diffeomorphic (but not isometric) spacetime.

content.thinking:
The Sanders paper directly undermines the first claim by showing that Reeh-Schlieder states can only be constructed on diffeomorphic but non-isometric spacetimes, and even then only in a weakened form—not the strong version the claim requires.

The Strohmaier-Verch-Wollenberg result is even more damaging: they prove that on real analytic spacetimes with an analytic microlocal spectrum condition, the full Reeh-Schlieder property holds without any Killing vector field at all, and this works for general quantum field theories without assuming any specific equation of motion.

So Gemini's assertion that Reeh-Schlieder strictly requires a continuous isometry group with a null Killing vector is demonstrably false—both papers show the property can hold under much weaker conditions.

I'm also noticing the logical gap at step (c) where Gemini claims modular flow being geometric determines cyclicity, which it doesn't.

For claim 2, the core error is conflating "image confined to a coadjoint orbit" with "continuous stabilizer in Diff(S²)"—Mackey's argument requires the stabilizer, not just the image dimension, so a map from S² onto a 2D orbit could have a trivial stabilizer.

Both verdicts rest on unverified arguments, though they might still be correct. Let me think through what would actually establish them.…

**You were right to flag them. Both verdicts fail on their reasoning, and one premise is false against the literature.**

**Claim 1 says Reeh–Schlieder strictly requires a null Killing vector field. It doesn't.**

Strohmaier, Verch and Wollenberg (2002) prove the property on **real analytic spacetimes** from an **analytic microlocal spectrum condition**, in general QFT and without assuming any equation of motion — **no isometry anywhere in the hypotheses**. And Sanders (arXiv 0801.4676) constructs Reeh–Schlieder states by deformation from a spacetime that is **diffeomorphic but explicitly not isometric**, concluding that states with the full property exist. Strohmaier (2000) *is* the Killing-field result — ground and KMS states on **stationary** spacetimes — but that's a sufficient condition asserted as necessary.

**And the argument fails independently at its last step.** *"The modular group does not act geometrically, as a result the cut algebra fails to generate a dense subspace"* — that doesn't follow. Cyclicity is a density statement about an algebra acting on a vector; geometric modular flow is separate. Borchers–Wiesbrock **derive** the geometric action **from** standardness, not the reverse.

**But Sanders supplies a better gap than the claimed one:** full Reeh–Schlieder states exist and *"are not guaranteed to be of physical interest."* So the existence of *some* cyclic state doesn't make **the ANE-vacuum** one — which is exactly what question (A) asks. **The verdict may well be right; the reason given isn't the reason.**

**Claim 2's premises hold and its conclusion doesn't follow.** Θ = 0 and σ = 0 is register 1039's own result. sl(2,ℝ)-dual as 3D Minkowski with hyperboloid and light-cone orbits is standard. That Θ = σ = 0 forces the Casimir constant **across** the cut is plausible and unchecked — constancy *along* the generators follows from Lie-dragging; across y it doesn't.

**And even granting all three: Mackey's second step is empty when the stabiliser is finite, not when the image fills three dimensions.** A map from S² onto a two-dimensional orbit can have trivial stabiliser — generic maps to a surface carry folds and cusps and no continuous symmetry. *Non-generic as a map into ℝ³* and *has a continuous stabiliser* are different statements, and only the second decides (B).

What would settle it is **axisymmetry or another continuous isometry of the cut data** — which Kerr has and a generic NEH need not. So the verdict is probably right **for Kerr** and unestablished for non-expanding horizons.

 * Reeh–Schlieder holds without Isometries: As established by Strohmaier, Verch, and Wollenberg (2002), the Reeh–Schlieder property for a local algebra follows from an analytic microlocal spectrum condition (a strong Hadamard-type condition) on real analytic spacetimes. Cyclicity and separability (standardness) are the inputs to modular theory. A state \Omega can be cyclic for \mathcal{A}(H_{>S}) without the associated modular group \Delta^{it} implementing a geometric transformation on the null surface.

The core issue for Question (A) lies in the definition and existence of an Average-Null-Energy (ANE) vacuum on a generic non-expanding horizon (NEH):
 * Ill-defined ANE Operator: The average null energy operator,

The previous argument incorrectly equated a target-space dimension restriction with non-genericity of the map itself.

 * Genericity in C^\infty(S, \mathcal{O}): Considered as a smooth map between two 2-dimensional manifolds (S \cong S^2 and the orbit \mathcal{O}), a generic map j \in C^\infty(S, \mathcal{O}) is Whitney generic. It exhibits standard 2D singularities (smooth fold lines and cusp points).

**(B) — closed.** The revision is right and it corrects the error I identified: restricting the target from the three-dimensional dual to a two-dimensional coadjoint orbit does *not* make the map non-generic. Considered as a map **between two 2-manifolds**, it's Whitney generic — fold lines, cusp points, **trivial stabiliser in Diff(S)**. So Mackey's second step is empty and **the d = 4 block dissolves for a generic horizon**. Kerr's rotational Killing field forces U(1)-invariance and a continuous stabiliser, so: **no for Kerr, yes for an NEH without a continuous spatial symmetry.**

**(A) — the new obstruction is register 1022's own statement**, reached independently: the ANE operator depends on the affine parameter, and an NEH supplies no canonical one. That's 1020's ℓ → a(y)ℓ with u → u/a(y) + b(y), and the convergence is worth noting.

**But the inference to non-existence doesn't survive the same method 1020 used.** Working the rescaling through the operator rather than asserting its effect:

    ℓ → a(y)ℓ    gives   dṽ = dv/a
    T_ab a tensor        T_ṽṽ = a² T_vv
    q_ab transverse      √q unchanged

    ∫dṽ T_ṽṽ = a(y) ∫dv T_vv        hence   P_λ  ↦  P_{λ·a}

**The operator is relabelled, not destroyed.** Since a(y) > 0, λ ↦ λ·a is a **bijection** of the non-negative smearings, so the *family* of smeared ANE operators maps onto itself. Faulkner and Speranza define Ω as the simultaneous ground state of **all** of them — and a condition quantified over an invariant family is invariant. **So the ANE vacuum, if it exists, doesn't depend on the parametrisation.**

And the surface-gravity point aims at the wrong object: κ non-constant across the cut affects the **boost**, hence the modular flow — not the null **translations** the ANE operators generate. That's register 1021's own distinction between a canonical map *between* cuts and a canonical scaling *along* them.

**So (A) stands open**, with its sharpest form still Sanders's: full Reeh–Schlieder states exist on spacetimes without isometries but *are not guaranteed to be of physical interest*, and whether the ANE vacuum is one of them is what remains.

And degenerate ground states typically aren't cyclic, which would undermine the entire construction.…

content.text:
**It's not the vacuum of the theory. It's a state defined by a condition on the horizon only:**

**P_λ|Ω⟩ = 0 for every non-negative smearing λ**

where P_λ integrates the average null energy along each generator and weights it across the cut. Since the ANEC makes each P_λ **positive**, annihilating it means sitting at its minimum. So in words: **a state with zero net energy flux across every generator of the horizon.** Nothing crosses. It's well-defined as a simultaneous condition because ANE operators on *different* generators commute — one state can minimise all of them at once.

Faulkner and Speranza are explicit that it **may not coincide with a global minimal energy state.**

**And its role is total.** P_λ|Ω⟩ = 0 is Borchers' third condition. Ω cyclic and separating is the fourth — the assumed one. And Δ and J come from the pair *(algebra, Ω)*, so **the modular flow M.C2 is about is this state's**. Change the state and M.C2 changes.

Which means **M.C2 is not a property of the horizon alone. It's a property of the horizon together with this state** — and nothing in the register said so until now.

**And the sharpest threat to (A) was in their own paper three pages before they assume cyclicity:**

# Gravitational algebras and the generalized second law

Thomas Faulkner\*1 and Antony J. Speranza $^{\dagger 1}$ 

<sup>1</sup>Department of Physics, University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, Urbana IL 61801, USA

May 1, 2024

#### Abstract

We derive the generalized second law (GSL) for arbitrary cuts of Killing horizons from the perspective of crossed-product gravitational algebras, making use of a recent proposal by one of us for the construction of local gravitational algebras. This construction relies on the existence of a state whose modular flow is geometric on the horizon. In both free and interacting quantum field theories, such states are guaranteed to exist by the properties of half-sided translations on the horizon.

## 8 Implications

A central result of this paper is that once corner edge modes are included, the half-sided null translation/boost symmetries become unitarily implemented as gravitational half-sided modular inclusions on a one-parameter family of Type II<sub>\infty</sub> factors $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathscr{H}_{>u}}$ . Generalized entropy then becomes amenable to the methods of Tomita–Takesaki theory. In this section we exploit this structure as a calculational framework to derive several important aspects of perturbative quantum gravity purely from the bulk. The main technical step, as we've seen, is to rewrite $\bar{S}_{\text{gen}}(u)$ as (minus) an Araki relative entropy on $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathscr{H}_{>u}}$ , so that its null derivatives are controlled by the null translation generator associated with the gravitational half-sided modular inclusion algebra.

We give a simplified proof of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC). Our proof is based on an explicit formula for the shape derivative of the relative entropy, with respect to an entangling cut. It allows bypassing the analytic continuation arguments of a previous proof by Ceyhan and Faulkner and can be used e.g., for defining entropy current fluctuations.

Among other things, it is the basis of the generalized second law for dynamical apparent black hole horizons [17, Sec. VII]. In [10], a heuristic argument in favor of the QNEC was given.

It's compelling and it's worth saying where it holds and where it doesn't, because the history is more interesting than the received version — and one piece of it does bear on the question.

**What's solid:** Greek astronomy really was done as geometry of positions, and the constellations carried the myths — Ptolemy's *Almagest* is the culmination. **Trigonometry genuinely comes out of it**: Hipparchus's chord table exists to compute where things will be, so triangulation and trajectory really are astronomical children.

**What's not:** algebra isn't Greek in origin. The word is Arabic, from al-Khwārizmī's *al-jabr* (c. 820 CE), and its deeper roots are Babylonian — and **the Babylonians are the better fit for your point anyway**, since their astronomy was arithmetical rather than geometric and genuinely bound up with divination. Diophantus is the Greek algebraic figure, and he's late and unmythological. Greek mathematics at its peak was aggressively *not* narrative — Euclid is the opposite of storytelling.

**But here's the piece that does bear on M.C2, and it isn't a metaphor.**

Ptolemy's system worked and was wrong, and it was wrong in a specific way: **it had a free parameter it couldn't fix.** The equant point, the deferent radii — these were fitted to save the phenomena, and nothing in the system determined them. Copernicus's actual complaint was aesthetic-structural: the model contained arbitrariness where it should have contained necessity.

**That is exactly a(y).** The corner boost is a function nothing in the non-expanding horizon's definition determines, and register 1022's phrasing — *"a canonical scaling of the affine parameter that a non-expanding horizon does not supply and something else must"* — is formally the same complaint. The system is consistent, reproduces its phenomena, and carries an undetermined parameter at its heart.

And the resolution, historically, wasn't a better fit. **It was a change of frame that made the parameter no longer arise** — heliocentrism didn't compute the equant, it dissolved the need for one. Which is precisely what today's session found: the Killing field doesn't *determine* a(y); its presence means the question never comes up.

So the useful transfer isn't the storytelling. It's the diagnostic: **an undetermined parameter at the centre of a working system is usually a sign the frame is wrong, not that the parameter is hard to compute.** M.C2 has spent 400 registers trying to compute a(y). Every route today said the same thing — nothing determines it — and the one structure that resolves it does so by removing the question.

Worth registering as a methodological note rather than a physics one, I think. Shall I?

Your instinct about the storytelling was doing real work, even though the history needed correcting: the transferable thing wasn't the narrative form but **the shape of a system that works and contains an arbitrariness it can't justify.** That's what Ptolemy had, what ν had, and what M.C2 has.

**Four appear. Counting them properly collapses three.**

    a(y)   the relative boost        a positive function on the cut
    b(y)   the null translation      a real function on the cut
    λ(y)   the ANE smearing          a non-negative function on the cut
    u      which cut                 a real parameter along the horizon

**b(y) is invisible.** P_λ integrates T_vv over the **whole affine line** on each generator, and a full-line integral is translation-invariant — so under v → v + b(y) the inner integral is unchanged and **b drops out entirely**. It only moves where you call v = 0, and the ANE operator never asks.

**a(y) and λ(y) are one freedom, not two.** Register 1498 gave P_λ ↦ P_{λ·a} under ℓ → a(y)ℓ, and that action is **transitive** on strictly positive smearings: given any λ₁ and λ₂, set a = λ₂/λ₁, which is smooth and positive. **So choosing the boost *is* choosing the smearing.**

**And u is free by design** — the source's *arbitrary cuts*, the very thing that makes the inclusion a one-parameter family.

**So M.C2 carries one undetermined parameter: the pair (a, λ) counted once — and it's a choice of observable, not something the horizon fails to supply.**

**Which shifts the equant diagnosis I registered an hour ago.** Registers 1485–1490 asked what *determines* a(y) and found nothing — **correctly, because a(y) isn't the kind of thing that gets determined.** It labels which member of an invariant family you're looking at. Ptolemy's equant was a number the model *needed* and couldn't supply. a(y) is a coordinate on a structure that's already complete.

Two limits flagged in the entry: the b result is exact given convergence of the full-line integral, which is the ANEC's own hypothesis; and the transitivity holds on the **strictly positive** stratum, since smearings that vanish on part of the cut aren't in one orbit.

**Four appear. Counting them properly collapses three.**

    a(y)   the relative boost        a positive function on the cut
    b(y)   the null translation      a real function on the cut
    λ(y)   the ANE smearing          a non-negative function on the cut
    u      which cut                 a real parameter along the horizon

**b(y) is invisible.** P_λ integrates T_vv over the **whole affine line** on each generator, and a full-line integral is translation-invariant — so under v → v + b(y) the inner integral is unchanged and **b drops out entirely**. It only moves where you call v = 0, and the ANE operator never asks.

**a(y) and λ(y) are one freedom, not two.** Register 1498 gave P_λ ↦ P_{λ·a} under ℓ → a(y)ℓ, and that action is **transitive** on strictly positive smearings: given any λ₁ and λ₂, set a = λ₂/λ₁, which is smooth and positive. **So choosing the boost *is* choosing the smearing.**

**And u is free by design** — the source's *arbitrary cuts*, the very thing that makes the inclusion a one-parameter family.

**So M.C2 carries one undetermined parameter: the pair (a, λ) counted once — and it's a choice of observable, not something the horizon fails to supply.**

**Which shifts the equant diagnosis I registered an hour ago.** Registers 1485–1490 asked what *determines* a(y) and found nothing — **correctly, because a(y) isn't the kind of thing that gets determined.** It labels which member of an invariant family you're looking at. Ptolemy's equant was a number the model *needed* and couldn't supply. a(y) is a coordinate on a structure that's already complete.

Two limits flagged in the entry: the b result is exact given convergence of the full-line integral, which is the ANEC's own hypothesis; and the transitivity holds on the **strictly positive** stratum, since smearings that vanish on part of the cut aren't in one orbit.

Registers to 1505, both gates, checkpointed.

content.text:
## Asymptotic Limit of Null Hypersurfaces

## Luca Ciambelli

Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, 31 Caroline St. N., Waterloo ON, Canada, N2L 2Y5

E-mail: ciambelli.luca@gmail.com

ABSTRACT: We study null hypersurfaces approaching null infinity in asymptotically flat spacetimes within the Bondi-Sachs gauge. The null Raychaudhuri constraint is shown to asymptote to the Bondi mass-loss formula, interpreted as a stress tensor conservation law. This stress tensor, the null Brown-York tensor, yields a Carrollian stress tensor at null infinity from the bulk. Furthermore, we establish that the canonical phase space on finite-distance null hypersurfaces asymptotes to the Ashtekar-Streubel phase space. This connection between finite-distance null physics and null infinity unveils promising insights.

# Contents

| 1 | Introduction                    |                                 | 2         |
|---|---------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------|


Recent work has begun exploring the construction of a flat-space stress tensor analogous to the AdS/CFT one [34, 35]. However, these studies consider a timelike hypersurface in the bulk, the stretched horizon, that asymptotes to null infinity. The key novelty of the present work lies in the direct consideration of a family of null hypersurfaces within the bulk, providing a more direct and profound connection between bulk physics on null hypersurfaces and the null conformal boundary. In a similar vein, our procedure allows us to relate the finite-distance gravitational phase space and dynamics discussed in [9, 10, 36–41] to null infinity. Indeed, in this work we will demonstrate that this phase space smoothly and precisely asymptotes to the Ashtekar-Streubel phase space [42], opening the door to a wide range of future investigations, which we summarize in the Conclusions. We regard the present work as an initial exploration, setting the stage and vocabulary for future works.

Adopting Ashtekar's asymptotic quantization procedure [3], the Bondi free data of the NSF equations is promoted to a quantum operator that obeys commutation relations at null infinity. It then follows from the field equations that the null surfaces themselves become operators that obey non-trivial commutation relations [2]. Furthermore, since it is possible to identify points of the space-time as intersections of null surfaces, it can also be shown that the space-time points themselves become quantum operators.

As shown by Ashtekar, it is possible to define a Hilbert space at null infinity but doing so imposes severe restrictions on the free data of the associated phase space since one leaves out almost all physically relevant spaces [3]. content.title: BMS-like symmetries in cosmology
content.text:
For asymptotically flat spacetimes describing isolated systems in vacuum general relativity, it is well-known that the asymptotic symmetries at null infinity are given by the infinite-dimensional Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) group [1–3], which is a semi-direct product of the infinite-dimensional group of supertranslations and the Lorentz group. The supertranslations are essentially "angle-dependent" translations which are not exact symmetries of flat Minkowski spacetime, but only arise in the asymptotic regime at null infinity and are intimately tied to the presence of gravitational radiation. This "infinite enhancement" of the Poincaré group of symmetries to BMS symmetries in the presence of gravitational radiation is related to many non-trivial phenomena at null infinity. For example, the gravitational memory effect — a permanent displacement of test bodies after the passage of a gravitational wave — can be related to the non-trivial supertranslations at null infinity [4–9]. 

Using this procedure Kehagias and Riotto obtained the BMS algebra as the asymptotic symmetry algebra even for FLRW spacetimes. However, general diffeomorphisms of FLRW spacetimes cannot be written as the scale factor times a diffeomorphism of the Minkowski spacetime; one also needs to transform the scale factor (see Remark 4.1). Thus, the symmetry algebra obtained by Kehagias and Riotto does not arise from diffeomorphisms of the FLRW spacetime and should not be considered as the asymptotic symmetry algebra in FLRW spacetimes.

The goal of this paper is to reanalyze the asymptotic symmetries at null infinity in FLRW spacetimes using the covariant formalism of a conformal completion à la Penrose. It is well-known that for decelerating FLRW spacetimes the conformal completion has a smooth null boundary $\mathscr{I}$ denoting null infinity [32, 33].

**Searching for the witness rather than for M.C2 found a twenty-year programme — and the register has been citing it as an obstacle.**

**Dappiaggi, Moretti and Pinamonti**, *Hadamard States from Light-like Hypersurfaces* (SpringerBriefs in Mathematical Physics 25, 2017), consolidating CMP 2009 on cosmological horizons, JMP 2009 on distinguished cosmological states, and ATMP 2011 on the Unruh state.

Their **bulk-to-boundary correspondence** encodes bulk observables on the conformal **null boundary** and identifies a **distinguished state** there whose bulk counterpart is automatically Hadamard — proved for a class of spacetimes explicitly *"not necessarily homogeneous or isotropous."*

**And a later generalisation goes exactly where M.C2 needs.** *Asymptotic (conformal) Killing horizons* — null hypersurfaces tangent to a vector field satisfying the Killing equation **only in a limiting sense** — with the construction described by its authors as theory-agnostic and using no Einstein equations. It reproduces DMP for asymptotic Killing horizons and yields a larger group in the conformal case.

**And M.C2's own check has cited Dappiaggi–Moretti–Pinamonti all along** — filed as an example of positivity being *"a selection criterion assumed by everyone who needs it."* The register held the reference for four hundred entries as evidence of the difficulty, when the same programme is the construction of the witness. **The reframing didn't find a new source; it re-read one already in hand.**

**Two things to check against it, in order, and I've put both in the queue:**

1. **Is the distinguished boundary state annihilated by the smeared ANE operators?** Hadamard is not that condition. This is the substantive question and nothing found so far answers it.
2. **Does it have Reeh–Schlieder for the exterior algebra?** Cyclicity for the *full* algebra is automatic in GNS; for the subalgebra it isn't.

Registers to 1508, both gates, checkpointed. That's a pathway with named authors, a named book, and two specific unanswered questions — rather than an open grade.

Phys. 1 June 2009; 50 (6): 062304. https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3122770 ... In a recent paper, we proved that a large class of spacetimes, not necessarily homogeneous or isotropous and relevant at a cosmological level, possesses a preferred codimension 1 submanifold, i.e., the past cosmological horizon, on which it is possible to encode the information of a scalar field theory living in the bulk. Such bulk-to-boundary reconstruction procedure entails the identification of a preferred quasifree algebraic state for the bulk theory, enjoying remarkable properties concerning invariance under isometries (if any) of the bulk and energy positivity and reducing to well-known vacua in standard situations.

 "*Taking the first ordered check from register 1508 — is the distinguished boundary state annihilated "

 "EVERY Bondi coordinate frame, u being the affine parameter of the null geodesics forming the boundary, "
 "which he calls a remnant of the spectral condition inherited from Minkowski spacetime. The cluster "
 "property holds under u-displacements for every pure u-invariant state with positive generator. And "
 "THERE IS A UNIQUE ALGEBRAIC PURE QUASIFREE STATE INVARIANT UNDER u-DISPLACEMENTS HAVING POSITIVE "
 "SELF-ADJOINT GENERATOR.** *And the non-symmetric case is explicit in the 2009 paper: a large class of "
 "spacetimes NOT NECESSARILY HOMOGENEOUS OR ISOTROPOUS possesses a preferred past cosmological horizon "
 "carrying a preferred quasifree state with 'invariance under isometries IF ANY of the bulk and energy "
 "positivity'. The parenthesis is theirs, and it says the construction runs when there are none.* "
 "**MATCHED AGAINST THE FOUR: condition one, positivity, is SUPPLIED and in every frame. Condition two, "
 "the inclusion, was already held as causal at register 1506. Condition three, invariance of the state, "
 "is SUPPLIED and comes with a UNIQUENESS theorem rather than merely a construction. Condition four, "
 "standardness for the cut algebra, is NOT supplied and is the remaining gap.** *Two things I have not "
 "established and will not assert. That the self-adjoint generator of u-translations IS the smeared ANE "
 "operator: for a free field the affine translation generator is the integrated null energy so they "
 "should coincide, but that is inference and the general smearing is a SUPERTRANSLATION rather than a "

content.text:
# Galilean Reeh-Schlieder Obstruction

Leonardo A. Pachón<sup>1</sup>

guane Enterprises, R+D+I Unit, Medellín 050010, Colombia

(Dated: 30 April 2026)

We prove that the standard Galilean Haag-Kastler axioms, augmented by Bargmann mass superselection, are inconsistent with the Reeh-Schlieder property: no such net admits a vacuum that is cyclic and separating for every local field algebra. Two ingredients combine: Galilean Schrödinger fields annihilate the Fock vacuum, and Bargmann mass superselection forbids the Hermitian-combination evasion that keeps relativistic axioms consistent. The result extends beyond the Fock-representation hypothesis: any Galilean Haag-Kastler net whose canonical fields carry definite Bargmann mass charges and admit time-zero restrictions on a field-algebra-stable common dense domain is incompatible with Reeh-Schlieder. 

The bounded-below mass spectrum and the vacuum-at-spectral-minimum, usually imposed as separate axioms, are derived consequences—of positive-energy boost positivity and a Bose-CCR algebraic descent, respectively. The Tomita-Takesaki modular flow is consequently unavailable on Galilean local field algebras. We identify the Reeh-Schlieder property as the precise structural ingredient distinguishing relativistic from Galilean algebraic quantum field theory: relativistic AQFT has it as a theorem, Galilean AQFT cannot.

#### I. INTRODUCTION

The structural distinction between relativistic and non-relativistic quantum field theory has been recognized since Lévy-Leblond's 1967 axiomatization<sup>1</sup>: Galilean QFTs are "less constrained" than relativistic ones, and the rigidity-style theorems that pin down relativistic QFT—CPT, spin-statistics, Haag's theorem—fail in the Galilean setting.

content.text:
Bisognano–Wichmann turns it into a boost energy statement for wedges, and the Casini–Huerta–Myers formula gives a stress-tensor version for bounded regions of conformal field theories. Local unitaries can only reach states of nonnegative modular energy. Negative modular sectors require nonunitary or postselected outcomes, giving a preparation cost bound that complements vacuum embezzlement in type III local algebras.

# I. INTRODUCTION

Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a bounded open region of Minkowski space. In the Haag–Kastler framework a quantum field theory assigns to it a von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O})$ acting on the vacuum Hilbert space [1, 2]. The Reeh–Schlieder theorem states that [3]

$$\overline{\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O})\Omega} = \mathcal{H}.\tag{1}$$

Every vector in the Hilbert space can be approximated by acting on the vacuum inside $\mathcal{O}$ alone.

This is not a statement about efficient preparation. 

The theorem gives no bound on ||A||, no bound on the energy of $A\Omega$ , and no constructive way to find A. The gap matters because local algebras in QFT are type III factors, which support state-conversion phenomena absent from finite tensor-product systems. Relativistic quantum fields can act as universal entanglement embezzlers, drawing entanglement from the vacuum while disturbing a reference state arbitrarily little [4, 5].

The natural next question is not whether local state preparation is possible. Reeh–Schlieder already answers that. The question is how expensive the local operator must be.

We ask one basic question. If $A \in \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O})$ prepares $\xi = A\Omega$ , how large must ||A|| be? Modular theory supplies a canonical lower bound, controlled by the signed expectation of the vacuum modular Hamiltonian of $\mathcal{O}$ in the target state. 

In geometries where this Hamiltonian is explicit, the bound becomes a quantitative statement about boost energy in wedges and about a weighted stress-tensor integral

The action of the modular and conjugation operators for the pair $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{W},\Omega)$ is, respectively,

$$J_{\mathcal{W}} = \Theta.U(R(\pi), 0),$$

#### 3.1 Anti-locality and the Reeh-Schlieder theorem

Let $\mathfrak{R}$ be some subalgebra of $\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}))$ . We say that a vector $\psi \in \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H})$ is *cyclic* for $\mathfrak{R}$ just in case $[\mathfrak{R}\psi] = \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H})$ , where $[\mathfrak{R}\psi]$ denotes the closed linear span of $\{A\psi : A \in \mathfrak{R}\}$ . Of course, every vector in $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H})$ , including the vacuum vector $\Omega$ , is cyclic for the global algebra $\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}))$ of all bounded operators on $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H})$ . The Reeh-Schlieder theorem, however, tells us that the vacuum vector $\Omega$ is cyclic for any *local* algebra $\mathfrak{R}(G)$ .

The first version of the Reeh-Schlieder theorem I will present is a restricted version of the theorem—due to Segal and Goodman—applicable only to the free Bose field model. 

But since H and $H^{-1}$ are anti-local, the two integrals in (22) will not generally vanish. Therefore, the vacuum state is not a product state across $\mathfrak{R}(G_1)$ and $\mathfrak{R}(G_2)$ .

**Check two has a route, and it's a bijection.**

**Guido, Longo and Wiesbrock** establish a **bijection** between isomorphism classes of standard half-sided modular inclusions and **strongly additive local conformal nets on the circle**. Longo and Tanimoto put it in the form this thread needs: an HSMI of two **half-line algebras** from the strongly additive chiral component of a 2D CFT *completely remembers the structure of QFT on the lightray*. And for such a net, **the vacuum is cyclic and separating by locality and Reeh–Schlieder**.

**So for a chiral net on the lightray, condition four is a theorem, not a hypothesis.**

**And the null surface supplies that structure** — quantising on a null hypersurface yields a CFT associated with **each null ray**, a consequence of the **ultralocal** nature of null physics.

    null surface     ultralocal → one chiral theory per generator
    per generator    chiral net on the lightray
    chiral net       Ω cyclic and separating for half-line algebras  ← Reeh–Schlieder
    all generators   the cut algebra is the product over the cut
    hence            condition (iv)  ... IF the product step holds

**And the product step is where I stop, because it isn't a detail.** Cyclicity of a product vector for a product of algebras is fine for finite or countable products. **The generators of a horizon form a continuum**, and continuous tensor products of type III factors are exactly where this kind of argument needs care or fails. Nothing found today addresses it.

**So the honest position:** every piece of M.C2's conditional hypothesis now has a named source, and the one remaining question is whether per-generator Reeh–Schlieder survives the **continuous** product over the cut.

That's operator algebras, not gravity — **the fourth time today this object has handed its remaining difficulty to a different field.** Which is itself the pattern worth noticing: each narrowing has moved the problem further from physics and closer to structure.

content.text:
**The cut.** Ashtekar's NEH conditions require **H ≅ S × ℝ**, generators along the ℝ. A **cut** is a cross-section — one copy of S at fixed affine parameter. In d = 4, **S ≅ S²**: compact, two-dimensional, no boundary.

So *the product over the cut* is indexed by the points **y ∈ S**, one per generator, with measure √q d²y. A continuum, and in four dimensions a two-dimensional compact one.

**The word has been doing two jobs today, and I should have separated them.** *The cut* as the cross-section S, and *the cut u* as **which** cross-section — M.C2's u₁ < u₂ is the second, and the product is over the first.

**And asking made me check the register, which states the structure more precisely than I did an hour ago.**

**M.C1, verified:** the presymplectic potential carries **no transverse derivative**, so the symplectic form is **block diagonal in y**, with

    {φ(u,y), φ(u′,y′)} = (1/4√q(y)) sgn(u−u′) δ^(d−2)(y−y′)

M.ledger calls this **the transverse direct integral** — not a tensor product. And that distinction decides the question: **cyclicity does pass through a direct integral** given a measurable field of cyclic vectors; through a **continuous tensor product** it does not pass automatically.

cd /home/claude/work && python3 - <<'PY'
import re, pathlib, sys, textwrap
W=pathlib.Path("/home/claude/work")
E=(1512,"THE SUDOKU METHOD APPLIED TO THE SAMPLE RETURNS THAT THE SAMPLE IS DEGENERATE, AND THE NARRATION CONTRADICTED THE COMPUTATION.",
 "*The person proposed sampling the cut across all relative groups and then applying the sudoku method to "
 "the result. Six groups tabulated against five attributes — compact cut, exact Killing field, "
 "asymptotic Killing field, state exists, Reeh–Schlieder holds — with Rindler, the bifurcate Killing "
 "horizon, null infinity and the de Sitter cosmological horizon fully known, and the non-expanding "
 "horizon the open row.* **ONE THING THE SAMPLE SETTLES DECISIVELY: THE CONTINUOUS-PRODUCT PASSAGE IS "
 "NOT AN OBSTRUCTION IN PRINCIPLE. In the Rindler case the transverse continuum is non-compact ℝ^(d−2) "
 "and Reeh–Schlieder for the wedge is a THEOREM, so cyclicity does survive a continuous product of "
 "chiral half-line algebras. Register 1510's worry that it might fail structurally is answered.** *Then "
 "the sudoku question — can the missing cell be filled by implication from the others — and the answer "
 "is that the sample is DEGENERATE. Every known row has Reeh–Schlieder holding. There is NOT ONE "
 "NEGATIVE EXAMPLE, so every implication whose antecedent fires is automatically satisfied and three "
 "vacuous ones were duly found. A constraint network whose target column is CONSTANT carries no "
 "information: the check cannot fail.* **THAT IS THE SAME ANSWER `sudoku_index.py` GAVE THIS MORNING IN "
 "THE SAME SHAPE — E = 648 of a maximum 648, redundancy zero, every pairwise envelope vacuous. The "
 "instrument returns 'nothing to work with', not 'the answer is unknown'.** *And a fault to record "
 "against myself: the search FOUND three implications and I printed NONE in the very next line. The "
 "narration contradicted the computation, which is precisely what `contingency.py` exists to catch, "
 "committed in the sentence after the result.* **WHAT WOULD MAKE THE SAMPLE INFORMATIVE IS A NEGATIVE "
 "ROW — a setting where Reeh–Schlieder for half-line algebras FAILS. Without one the table can only say "
 "it has worked everywhere anyone looked, which is induction rather than propagation. The Galilean "
 "obstruction found earlier is a genuine negative, but it is non-relativistic, and whether it belongs in "
 "this table is the question to settle before it is used.**")
P=W/"REGISTER-DATA.md"; s=P.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
H=re.compile(r"^ {0,3}((?:\d{3,4}, )*\d{3,4})\. ",re.M)
top=max(int(x) for m in H.finditer(s) for x in re.findall(r"\d{3,4}",m.group(1)))
if top!=1511: sys.exit(f"REFUSING: top is {top}")
n,h,b=E
t=f"{n}. **{h}** {re.sub(r'\s+',' ',b).strip()}"
k="\n".join(textwrap.wrap(t,97,initial_indent=" ",subsequent_indent=" ",
            break_long_words=False,break_on_hyphens=False))
bo=it=0
for x in re.findall(r"\*{1,2}",k):
    if x=="**": bo^=1
    else: it^=1
assert not bo and not it
P.write_text(s.rstrip("\n")+"\n\n"+k+"\n",encoding="utf-8"); print("appended 1512")
PY

**The assumption inverts, and testing it against the register's own criterion gives something better than the assumption would have.**

**M.C2 has two equivalent forms, and they have different arity.**

**Borchers triple form** — four conditions:

    P ≥ 0                            translations alone           UNARY
    T(x) M T(x)† ⊆ M                 translations and algebra     PAIRWISE
    T(x) Ω = Ω                       translations and vector      PAIRWISE
    Ω standard for M                 algebra and vector           PAIRWISE

**Not one condition closes on all three.** That form is a **2-body** system.

**Wiesbrock form** — N ⊂ M with Ω standard for both, and σ_t(N) ⊆ N where σ_t is the modular group of (M, Ω). That second condition is **irreducibly ternary**: the flow is *built from* (M, Ω) and *acts on* N. Remove any one and there's no statement.

**And the two forms are equivalent** — Borchers 1992, Wiesbrock 1993, which register 1481 recorded without noticing what the equivalence *says*: **a genuine ternary condition decomposes into unary and pairwise ones.**

**So M.C2 isn't a three-body remnant. It's the converse case** — an instance where the reduction register 489 says is generally unavailable actually **succeeds**, with a named theorem exhibiting it. 489's "the three-body shortfall is exactly one level... pairs, plus one thing pairs cannot carry" — Borchers–Wiesbrock is a case where **that one thing is carried**.

Both are correct, and the difference is exactly this: **M.C2's ternary form admits a pairwise presentation; the three-body problem's does not.**

That's the real link between the two threads — not inheritance, but contrast. And it's the kind the method values: the same measurement, opposite answers, and the difference localised.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""helly_index.py — the three-axis index, built in algebra.

THE COMMON LANGUAGE, DECLARED BEFORE ANYTHING IS COMPUTED.

Each of the three objects is a SYSTEM OF LINEAR INEQUALITIES in an unknown
vector x of dimension d:

    Loewdin      L(Z) < a < U(Z)  for Z = 3..108      d = 1, unknown a
    three-body   a K_3 constraint network             d = 2 (the nuclear
                 (nuclear: 4*beta + alpha sign        instance: alpha, beta)
                 conditions, six pairs)
    M.C2         the four Borchers conditions         d = ? (to be read off)

For such systems there is ONE algebraic quantity that governs whether low-order
consistency implies global consistency: the HELLY NUMBER.

    HELLY'S THEOREM. For a finite family of CONVEX sets in R^d, if every d+1 of
    them have a common point, then all of them do.

So the Helly number h = d+1 is exactly the "defect order" the register has been
circling: the smallest k such that k-wise consistency DOES imply global
consistency. Below h, consistency propagates nothing; at h, it propagates
everything.

    R 489's "the three-body shortfall is exactly one level" and
    Kraft-Pratt-Seidenberg's "cancellation conditions of every order" and
    Freuder's k-consistency

are then three names for h, read in three literatures.

THE PREDICTION, ON THE RECORD BEFORE THE RUN (R 1120):

    Loewdin has ONE unknown, so h = 2. If the corridor system is globally
    infeasible, Helly forces a PAIR of corridors to be disjoint — the failure
    must already be visible at order 2, and cannot hide at higher order.

    If that is right, Loewdin and the three-body problem do NOT share a defect
    order after all: Loewdin's is 2 and the three-body's is 3, and register
    1515's "same mechanism" is right about the KIND and wrong about the LEVEL.

I expect to find disjoint pairs. If none exist, Helly is contradicted and the
error is mine, not the theorem's.
"""
import sys, io, contextlib, itertools
from fractions import Fraction as F

sys.path.insert(0, "/home/claude/work")
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    import brack

IV = {r[0]: r for r in brack.IV}
STEPS = sorted(IV)
BIG = 1e8

print("  THE THREE-AXIS INDEX, IN ALGEBRA\n")
print("  Axis 1 · the UNKNOWN SPACE, dimension d")
print("  Axis 2 · the HELLY NUMBER h = d + 1, the order at which consistency")
print("           becomes global")
print("  Axis 3 · whether the system is globally FEASIBLE\n")

# ---- LOEWDIN: d = 1 ------------------------------------------------------
print("  LOEWDIN — d = 1, the single unknown a\n")
cor = {Z: (IV[Z][4], IV[Z][5]) for Z in STEPS
       if -BIG < IV[Z][4] < BIG and IV[Z][5] < BIG}
print(f"    corridors with finite bounds: {len(cor)} of {len(STEPS)}")
lo = max(c[0] for c in cor.values())
hi = min(c[1] for c in cor.values())
print(f"    global intersection: ({lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f})   "
      f"{'NON-EMPTY' if lo < hi else 'EMPTY'}")

pairs = [(A, B) for A, B in itertools.combinations(sorted(cor), 2)
         if max(cor[A][0], cor[B][0]) >= min(cor[A][1], cor[B][1])]
print(f"\n    HELLY AT h = 2: disjoint PAIRS of corridors: {len(pairs)}")
if pairs:
    print(f"    the first six: {pairs[:6]}")
    A, B = pairs[0]
    print(f"    e.g. Z={A} ({cor[A][0]:.4f}, {cor[A][1]:.4f})  vs  "
          f"Z={B} ({cor[B][0]:.4f}, {cor[B][1]:.4f})")
print(f"\n    ** Helly in d=1 says global emptiness REQUIRES a disjoint pair.")
print(f"       Global is {'EMPTY' if lo >= hi else 'NON-EMPTY'} and disjoint pairs "
      f"number {len(pairs)}: consistent = "
      f"{(lo >= hi) == (len(pairs) > 0)} **")

# ---- THREE-BODY / NUCLEAR: d = 2 ----------------------------------------
print("\n  THE THREE-BODY INSTANCE (nuclear shell model) — d = 2, unknowns (alpha, beta)\n")
LEV = {"2s1/2": (2, 0, +1), "1d3/2": (1, 2, -1), "2d5/2": (2, 2, +1),
       "2p3/2": (2, 1, +1), "1f5/2": (1, 3, -1), "2f7/2": (2, 3, +1),
       "3p3/2": (3, 1, +1), "2f5/2": (2, 3, -1), "3s1/2": (3, 0, +1),
       "2d3/2": (2, 2, -1), "1g7/2": (1, 4, -1), "1h9/2": (1, 5, -1)}
lsv = lambda s: F(LEV[s][1], 2) if LEV[s][2] > 0 else F(-(LEV[s][1] + 1), 2)
cen = lambda s: F(LEV[s][1] * (LEV[s][1] + 1))
PAIRS = [("2s1/2", "1d3/2"), ("2p3/2", "1f5/2"), ("3p3/2", "2f5/2"),
         ("2d3/2", "3s1/2"), ("1g7/2", "2d5/2"), ("1h9/2", "2f7/2")]
SIGN = [+1, +1, +1, -1, -1, -1]
vecs = []
for (a, b), s in zip(PAIRS, SIGN):
    vecs.append((s * (cen(b) - cen(a)), s * (lsv(b) - lsv(a))))
print(f"    six constraint vectors (coefficient of beta, of alpha), signed:")
for (a, b), v in zip(PAIRS, vecs):
    print(f"      {a:>7} vs {b:<7}  ({v[0]}, {v[1]})   "
          f"ratio {v[0]/v[1] if v[1] else '—'}")
rat = {v[0] / v[1] for v in vecs if v[1]}
print(f"\n    distinct ratios: {rat}   rank of the 6x2 matrix: "
      f"{1 if len(rat) == 1 else 2}")
print(f"    ** all six are positive multiples of one direction — RANK ONE.")
print(f"       Three demand it positive and three negative, so the feasible set")
print(f"       is EMPTY, and the certificate needs only TWO of the six. **")
half = [i for i in range(6) if vecs[i][0] > 0]
print(f"\n    HELLY AT h = 3 (d = 2): but the emptiness is witnessed by a PAIR,")
print(f"       one from each sign class — so the EFFECTIVE dimension is 1, not 2,")
print(f"       because the six vectors span a LINE.")

# ---- M.C2 ----------------------------------------------------------------
print("\n  M.C2 — the four Borchers conditions\n")
print("    Not a system of inequalities in a finite-dimensional unknown: the")
print("    unknowns are an ALGEBRA, a UNITARY GROUP and a VECTOR. So d is not")
print("    a number here, and Helly does not apply directly.")
print("    What stands in its place is register 1514's finding: the ternary")
print("    condition DECOMPOSES into unary and pairwise ones, which is the")
print("    same conclusion Helly would deliver if it applied — consistency at")
print("    low order gives global consistency.")

print("\n" + "=" * 72)
print("  THE INDEX, ASSEMBLED\n")
print(f"    {'object':<16}{'d':<5}{'h = d+1':<10}{'feasible':<12}"
      f"{'failure visible at order':<26}")
rows = [("Loewdin", 1, 2, "NO", "2 — a disjoint PAIR"),
        ("three-body", 2, 3, "NO", "2 — the six span a LINE, so effective d = 1"),
        ("M.C2", "—", "—", "conditional", "decomposes; no defect")]
for a, b, c, dd, e in rows:
    print(f"    {a:<16}{str(b):<5}{str(c):<10}{dd:<12}{e:<26}")

**Built in algebra, and the common quantity has a name: the Helly number.**

Each object becomes a **system of linear inequalities** in an unknown of dimension d, and **h = d + 1** governs whether low-order consistency implies global consistency. Register 489's *"the shortfall is exactly one level"*, Kraft–Pratt–Seidenberg's cancellation conditions, and Freuder's k-consistency are **three names for h in three literatures**.

**Löwdin has one unknown, so h = 2** — and the prediction was that global emptiness must show as a **disjoint pair**. Computed:

    73 corridors with finite bounds
    global intersection EMPTY at (1.9841, 1.0000)
    DISJOINT PAIRS: 183      first: Z=13 (0, 1.3660) vs Z=88 (1.3938, 5.0952)

Helly satisfied exactly.

**And the nuclear three-body instance collapses to the same number.** Nominally two unknowns, h = 3 — but the six constraint vectors are (6, −3/2), (10, −5/2), (10, −5/2), (6, −3/2), (14, −7/2), (18, −9/2), **every one at ratio exactly −4**. Rank one. The six span a **line**, so effective d = 1, effective h = 2, and **the certificate needs only two of the six** — one from each sign class.

**So the shared mechanism is exact, and it isn't "all orders":**

> **Both objects have effective dimension one, and both fail at Helly order two, witnessed by a pair.**

That's sharper than register 1515, which said Löwdin needs cancellation conditions of every order — the general Kraft–Pratt–Seidenberg statement, which **doesn't apply to a one-parameter system**. Marked and corrected.

**And M.C2 supplies the third axis by *not* being of this kind.** Its unknowns are an algebra, a unitary group and a vector — not a finite-dimensional vector — so Helly doesn't apply, and what stands in its place is the Borchers–Wiesbrock decomposition, **which is the conclusion Helly would deliver if it did apply.** The control confirms the measure by returning no defect.

**No. It forecloses a family rather than supplying a mechanism — and that turns out to be worth more.**

A Helly certificate at order two says **two constraints already conflict**. That's a *proof* the one-parameter form cannot work: complete, localised, and a foreclosure rather than a construction. There's no cleverer choice of the single parameter, because disjoint pairs can't be reconciled by any value of one number. **The only remedy is to raise the dimension** — which in both cases means letting the parameter vary with the cell.

**But it does return a number, and the number is small.**

    all 106 corridors      73 fully bounded · 7 lower only · 26 upper only · 0 unbounded
    max PAIRWISE DISJOINT  3    B 5 (−∞, 0.7071) · La 57 (0.7071, 1.7071) · Lr 103 (1.9841, 2.4409)
    min STABBING POINTS    3    0.7071 · 1.7071 · 2.4409
    Gallai duality         holds exactly — both numbers certified, not heuristic

**Three distinct values of a suffice for the entire table.** The walk's **fourteen** resets are an artefact of processing Z in order; the minimum is **three**, forced by boron, lanthanum and lawrencium.

That's new. Register 1434's fourteen emptyings and 1466's ten trajectory values both describe a **greedy left-to-right walk**. Nobody had asked for the minimum, and it's smaller by a factor of three to five.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""binary_mechanism.py — the mechanism as a BINARY RELATION, one graph per object.

THE PERSON'S PROPOSAL. The Helly object is a translator between languages, and
the whole of the mechanism may only be visible in binary — as a two-place
relation rather than as anything higher.

THE TEST, DECLARED BEFORE THE RUN. For each object build ONE GRAPH:

    vertices = the constraints
    edge Z—W  iff  constraints Z and W CANNOT BE SATISFIED TOGETHER

Call it the CONFLICT GRAPH. If the person is right, every verdict this session
has produced should be readable off that graph alone, with no reference to the
original object — and the graph invariants should be the SAME invariants in
every case.

WHAT WOULD REFUTE IT. If any verdict needs information not present in the
pairwise conflict relation — a genuine three-place obstruction — then the
mechanism is not binary and this returns nothing.

Recorded before computing: I expect the Loewdin and nuclear verdicts to be
readable, because both certificates found this session were PAIRS. I do not know
what the graphs look like, and in particular I do not know whether they are of
the same family.
"""
import sys, io, contextlib, itertools
from fractions import Fraction as F

sys.path.insert(0, "/home/claude/work")
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    import brack

BIG = 1e8
IV = {r[0]: r for r in brack.IV}
STEPS = sorted(IV)


def maxclique(V, adj):
    """exact, by expansion — these graphs are small enough."""
    best = []

    def go(cur, cand):
        nonlocal best
        if not cand:
            if len(cur) > len(best):
                best = list(cur)
            return
        if len(cur) + len(cand) <= len(best):
            return
        for i, v in enumerate(list(cand)):
            go(cur + [v], [w for w in cand[i + 1:] if w in adj[v]])
    go([], list(V))
    return best


def greedy_colour(V, adj):
    col = {}
    for v in sorted(V, key=lambda x: -len(adj[x])):
        used = {col[w] for w in adj[v] if w in col}
        c = 0
        while c in used:
            c += 1
        col[v] = c
    return max(col.values()) + 1 if col else 0


print("  THE MECHANISM IN BINARY — ONE CONFLICT GRAPH PER OBJECT\n")

# ---------------- LOEWDIN -------------------------------------------------
cor = {}
for Z in STEPS:
    lo, hi = IV[Z][4], IV[Z][5]
    cor[Z] = (-float('inf') if lo <= -BIG else lo,
              float('inf') if hi >= BIG else hi)
V1 = [Z for Z in STEPS]
adj1 = {Z: set() for Z in V1}
for A, B in itertools.combinations(V1, 2):
    if max(cor[A][0], cor[B][0]) >= min(cor[A][1], cor[B][1]):
        adj1[A].add(B); adj1[B].add(A)
e1 = sum(len(a) for a in adj1.values()) // 2
k1 = maxclique(V1, adj1)
print(f"  LÖWDIN")
print(f"    vertices {len(V1)}   edges {e1}   density "
      f"{2*e1/(len(V1)*(len(V1)-1)):.4f}")
print(f"    MAX CLIQUE {len(k1)}  at Z = {sorted(k1)}")
print(f"    colouring  {greedy_colour(V1, adj1)}")
iso1 = [Z for Z in V1 if not adj1[Z]]
print(f"    isolated vertices (conflict with nothing): {len(iso1)}")

# ---------------- NUCLEAR -------------------------------------------------
LEV = {"2s1/2": (2, 0, +1), "1d3/2": (1, 2, -1), "2d5/2": (2, 2, +1),
       "2p3/2": (2, 1, +1), "1f5/2": (1, 3, -1), "2f7/2": (2, 3, +1),
       "3p3/2": (3, 1, +1), "2f5/2": (2, 3, -1), "3s1/2": (3, 0, +1),
       "2d3/2": (2, 2, -1), "1g7/2": (1, 4, -1), "1h9/2": (1, 5, -1)}
lsv = lambda s: F(LEV[s][1], 2) if LEV[s][2] > 0 else F(-(LEV[s][1] + 1), 2)
cen = lambda s: F(LEV[s][1] * (LEV[s][1] + 1))
PAIRS = [("2s1/2", "1d3/2"), ("2p3/2", "1f5/2"), ("3p3/2", "2f5/2"),
         ("2d3/2", "3s1/2"), ("1g7/2", "2d5/2"), ("1h9/2", "2f7/2")]
SIGN = [+1, +1, +1, -1, -1, -1]
vec = []
for (a, b), s in zip(PAIRS, SIGN):
    vec.append((s * (cen(b) - cen(a)), s * (lsv(b) - lsv(a))))
V2 = list(range(6))
adj2 = {i: set() for i in V2}
for i, j in itertools.combinations(V2, 2):
    # two half-planes through the origin conflict iff their normals oppose
    if vec[i][0] * vec[j][0] < 0 or (vec[i][0] * vec[j][0] == 0 and
                                     vec[i][1] * vec[j][1] < 0):
        adj2[i].add(j); adj2[j].add(i)
e2 = sum(len(a) for a in adj2.values()) // 2
k2 = maxclique(V2, adj2)
print(f"\n  NUCLEAR (three-body instance)")
print(f"    vertices {len(V2)}   edges {e2}   density "
      f"{2*e2/(len(V2)*(len(V2)-1)):.4f}")
print(f"    MAX CLIQUE {len(k2)}  at constraints {sorted(k2)}")
print(f"    degree sequence {sorted(len(adj2[v]) for v in V2)}")
bip = all(len(adj2[v]) == 3 for v in V2)
print(f"    every vertex of degree 3, six vertices: COMPLETE BIPARTITE K(3,3) "
      f"= {bip}")

# ---------------- LAMBDA --------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n  Λ  (the book's own index)")
print(f"    E(Λ) = 0, so NO two constraints conflict.")
print(f"    conflict graph: 8 vertices, ZERO EDGES — the EMPTY graph")
print(f"    MAX CLIQUE 1")

# ---------------- M.C2 ----------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n  M.C2")
print(f"    the four Borchers conditions are jointly satisfiable on a Killing")
print(f"    horizon, so no two conflict.")
print(f"    conflict graph: 4 vertices, ZERO EDGES — the EMPTY graph")
print(f"    MAX CLIQUE 1")

print("\n" + "=" * 70)
print("  THE VERDICTS, READ OFF THE GRAPHS ALONE\n")
print(f"    {'object':<14}{'vertices':>9}{'edges':>7}{'max clique':>12}  verdict")
for nm, nv, ne, kc, vd in [
        ("Λ", 8, 0, 1, "CLOSED — nothing conflicts"),
        ("M.C2", 4, 0, 1, "CONDITIONAL — nothing conflicts"),
        ("nuclear", 6, e2, len(k2), "REFUTED — a conflicting pair exists"),
        ("Löwdin", len(V1), e1, len(k1), "REFUTED — and needs "
         f"{len(k1)} parameters")]:
    print(f"    {nm:<14}{nv:>9}{ne:>7}{kc:>12}  {vd}")
print("\n  ** MAX CLIQUE = 1 MEANS CLOSED. MAX CLIQUE = k MEANS k PARAMETERS ARE")
print("     NEEDED AND ONE WILL NOT DO. Every verdict of this session is that")
print("     single integer, and every certificate is an EDGE. **")

    edge Z—W  iff  constraints Z and W CANNOT BE SATISFIED TOGETHER

every case.

pairwise conflict relation — a genuine three-place obstruction — then the
mechanism is not binary and this returns nothing.

    import brack

BIG = 1e8

def maxclique(V, adj):
    """exact, by expansion — these graphs are small enough."""
    best = []

    def go(cur, cand):
        nonlocal best
        if not cand:
            if len(cur) > len(best):
                best = list(cur)
            return
        if len(cur) + len(cand) <= len(best):
            return
        for i, v in enumerate(list(cand)):
            go(cur + [v], [w for w in cand[i + 1:] if w in adj[v]])
    go([], list(V))
    return best

    col = {}
    for v in sorted(V, key=lambda x: -len(adj[x])):

        c = 0

The audits already enforce it. ## Abstract

A comprehensive database for experimental X-ray absorption spectroscopy data is presented. This integrated and user-friendly platform combines spectrum visualization, raw data processing, spectrum matching and downloading.

## Introduction

1.



X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) (Rehr & Albers, 2000[14]) is a principal technique for material characterization, offering critical information about the local atomic chemical environment of interested species (Guo *et al.*, 2023[5]), including bond length, charge transfer, symmetry of coordination atoms and core/valence bands. XAS is particularly significant for the analysis of solid materials, especially those that are amorphous, disordered or multicomponent. Due to its broad range of applications across various scientific fields, XAS has emerged as an essential tool for research in areas such as catalytic reactions and battery materials (Gaur *et al.*, 2023[4]).

content.text: There are special difficulties involved when dealing with atoms with open outer shells (obviously this is the most common case). Computing all energies EJ for total angular momentum J would be both impossible and useless. The Dirac-Fock method circumvents this difficulty. One can evaluate directly an average energy that corresponds to the barycenter of all EJ with weight (2J + 1). There are still a few cases for which the average calculation cannot converge (when the open shells have identical symmetry). **Done, and the captures turned out not to need the URLs at all.**

**The three are joined as queue section 0** — one object, one measure, the conflict graph, with the max-clique table, the three languages, the method's boundary, and what remains on each face written in rather than left in prose.

**And B1 is unblocked.** The NIST X-ray Transition Energies database serves its queries from a CGI endpoint that fetches directly:

    physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/XrayTrans/search.pl?download=column&element=All&trans=<T>&units=eV

B1 has been marked as *needs five supplied URLs* since the queue was written. **It needs none.**

**`captures/XRAY-L3M5.tsv` is held** — 78 rows, Ca through Fm, theory and direct experimental energies with uncertainties, blend flags, reference codes. Fetched **twice by different routes** (HTML table and column download), values agree, three spot-checks verified after writing.

**And a fault worth more than the capture: requesting L3M4 returned L3M5.** The response's own `destination_url` said `trans=L3M5` against a request for `L3M4` — the parameter didn't take. Had I not read the destination back, **a file labelled L3M4 would now hold L3M5 values.** That's the lost-tail fault in another costume: a capture that succeeds while holding the wrong thing.

Standing rule now in the queue: **read the destination URL back on every fetch and confirm it matches the request before writing anything.**

Remaining and now known to be reachable: **L2M1, L2M4, L3M1, L3M4** for B1; **L1N2, L1N3** for B1b's falsifiable σ-offset test; and the **K–Kr ionisation ladders** for D2 from the ASD side.

print(f"    3p post-Kr offset (R 1391, held)  : 5.296 ± 0.108, n = 45")
if p: print(f"    4p post-Kr offset (measured now)  : {p[0]:.3f} ± {p[1]:.3f}, n = {p[2]}")
if p:
    diff=p[0]-5.296
    print(f"    difference                        : {diff:+.3f}\n")
    if diff>5: v="A COUNT — outcome one"
    elif abs(diff)<=2: v="EFFECTIVE SCREENING — outcome two"
    else: v="NEITHER as stated — between the branches"
    print(f"    ** VERDICT: {v} **")
    print(f"    sd {p[1]:.3f} against the 3p sd of 0.108 — "
          f"{'comparable, structure holds' if p[1]<0.5 else 'MUCH LARGER, outcome three'}")

**B1b ran as a real test, and it failed against the branch I favoured.**

The prediction was on the record before the fetch, with three distinguishable outcomes. I leaned toward **effective screening** — the offset landing within a unit or two of the 3p value of 5.296.

**The post-Kr 4p offset came out at 15.776** — squarely inside the range I'd named for a *count*. So my lean was wrong. But the sd was **5.259** against the 3p value's 0.108, which was my signature for the *third* outcome. Split verdict.

**Then two faults of mine, both caught on re-reading.**

I wrote that the offset *"rises steadily at r = −0.034"* — contradicting the number printed one line above, since −0.034 is no correlation and the slope was negative. And I had **ignored the blend flag the source supplies**: Rb through Xe are marked **L1N2,3**, meaning the two lines are *not resolved* there, so their difference isn't a measured splitting at all.

**Redone on the 45 unblended elements, the answer is clean and it's neither of my first two branches:**

    Z ≥ 55, unblended, Sm removed as the one 3-sd outlier
    n = 41    mean 14.420    sd 1.620
    slope −0.1129 per unit Z    r = −0.858

**The offset falls monotonically. A count cannot drift, and this drifts 5.1 units across the range.**

So the σ-offset is **not a count**. It's a screening that weakens steadily as the nucleus dominates — which is exactly the reading *you* supplied at register 1390 for the 3p ratio, now reached independently at 4p from a different pair of lines.

Registers to 1528, both gates, checkpointed. Seven captures held.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""lshell_test.py — does Lambda_xray's nine-cell closure hold at a second depth?

Lambda_xray closed at E = 0 on (Delta-n, Delta-l, jtype_hole) with nine cells,
built from K-shell lines (R 1379, 1387). The five L-shell captures are the
second depth. THE TEST: classify them on the SAME three coordinates and ask
whether they land in the SAME nine cells, or open new ones.

THE COORDINATES, from Lambda's own transition alphabet:
    Delta-n     = n_initial - n_final of the electron making the jump
    Delta-l     = l_final - l_initial
    jtype_hole  = whether the HOLE state has j = l + 1/2 or j = l - 1/2

THE FIVE LINES, decomposed. The hole is in the L shell (n = 2); the electron
falls from M (n = 3) or N (n = 4).

    line   hole    electron   Delta-n   Delta-l   jtype_hole
    L3M1   2p3/2   3s         1         -1        +  (j = l + 1/2)
    L3M4   2p3/2   3d         1         +1        +
    L3M5   2p3/2   3d         1         +1        +
    L2M1   2p1/2   3s         1         -1        -  (j = l - 1/2)
    L2M4   2p1/2   3d         1         +1        -
    L1N2   2s      4p         2         +1        0  (l = 0, no splitting)
    L1N3   2s      4p         2         +1        0

DECLARED BEFORE THE RUN. If the nine-cell closure is a property of the ALPHABET
rather than of the K shell, these land inside it. If it is a property of the K
shell, the L lines open cells the K lines never reached — and Delta-n = 2 with
a 2s hole is the obvious candidate, since no K line has an s-hole at all.

I expect NEW CELLS, because L1 is an s-hole and the K shell's only s-hole is
the 1s itself, which cannot be the FINAL state of an L-shell transition.
"""
import itertools
from collections import defaultdict

# (name, hole_n, hole_l, hole_j_type, elec_n, elec_l)
LINES = [
    ("L3M1", 2, 1, +1, 3, 0),
    ("L3M4", 2, 1, +1, 3, 2),
    ("L3M5", 2, 1, +1, 3, 2),
    ("L2M1", 2, 1, -1, 3, 0),
    ("L2M4", 2, 1, -1, 3, 2),
    ("L1N2", 2, 0,  0, 4, 1),
    ("L1N3", 2, 0,  0, 4, 1),
]
# the K-shell set that produced the nine cells: hole is 1s, electron from n>=2
KLINES = [
    ("KL2", 1, 0, 0, 2, 1), ("KL3", 1, 0, 0, 2, 1),
    ("KM2", 1, 0, 0, 3, 1), ("KM3", 1, 0, 0, 3, 1),
    ("KN2", 1, 0, 0, 4, 1), ("KN3", 1, 0, 0, 4, 1),
]


def cell(hn, hl, hj, en, el):
    return (en - hn, hl - el, hj)


print("  DOES THE NINE-CELL CLOSURE HOLD AT L-SHELL DEPTH?\n")
print("  Coordinates: (Delta-n, Delta-l, jtype_hole), Lambda_xray's own.\n")
print(f"    {'line':<7}{'hole':<8}{'electron':<10}{'Dn':>4}{'Dl':>5}{'jtype':>7}   cell")
kc = set()
for nm, hn, hl, hj, en, el in KLINES:
    c = cell(hn, hl, hj, en, el); kc.add(c)
    print(f"    {nm:<7}{f'{hn}{chr(115+0)}':<8}{f'{en}{chr(115)}pdf'[0]:<10}"
          f"{c[0]:>4}{c[1]:>5}{c[2]:>7}   {c}")
print()
lc = defaultdict(list)
L = "spdfg"
for nm, hn, hl, hj, en, el in LINES:
    c = cell(hn, hl, hj, en, el)
    lc[c].append(nm)
    print(f"    {nm:<7}{f'{hn}{L[hl]}':<8}{f'{en}{L[el]}':<10}"
          f"{c[0]:>4}{c[1]:>5}{c[2]:>7}   {c}")

print(f"\n  K-shell cells reached : {len(kc)}   {sorted(kc)}")
print(f"  L-shell cells reached : {len(lc)}   {sorted(lc)}")
new = set(lc) - kc
print(f"\n  ** CELLS THE L-SHELL OPENS THAT THE K-SHELL NEVER REACHED: {len(new)} **")
for c in sorted(new):
    print(f"      {c}   from {', '.join(lc[c])}")
shared = set(lc) & kc
print(f"\n  cells shared with the K shell: {len(shared)}  {sorted(shared)}")

print("\n  AND THE COLLAPSE — how many distinct lines per cell:\n")
for c in sorted(lc):
    print(f"      {c}  <- {len(lc[c])} line(s): {', '.join(lc[c])}")
print(f"\n    seven L lines collapse to {len(lc)} cells, a {7/len(lc):.2f}:1 reduction")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""xray_cells.py — does Lambda_xray's cell membership predict MEASURED behaviour?

CORRECTION TO MY FIRST FRAMING. Lambda_xray is 33 dipole-allowed inner-shell
lines through the N shell collapsing to 9 cells on (Delta-n, Delta-l,
jtype_hole), E = 0, and the artefact states it was BUILT WITH NO NEW DATA —
from Lambda's own alphabet, EM.map's dipole rule and T.a12's j triangle. So the
five L-shell captures were ALREADY inside the 33. They do not open cells.

What they do is supply MEASUREMENT to a structure that was predicted. That makes
the real test sharper than the one I first wrote:

    DOES CELL MEMBERSHIP PREDICT HOW A LINE BEHAVES?

Two of the captured pairs share a cell and one pair does not:

    L3M4, L3M5   share (1, -1, +)    hole 2p3/2, electron 3d
    L1N2, L1N3   share (2, -1,  0)   hole 2s,    electron 4p
    L3M4, L2M4   DIFFER in jtype only: (1,-1,+) against (1,-1,-)
    L3M1, L3M4   DIFFER in Delta-l only: (1,+1,+) against (1,-1,+)

THE TEST. Fit Moseley's law E = A(Z - s)^2 to each line separately and compare
the exponent and the screening. If the cell is doing work, SAME-CELL lines
should agree more closely than DIFFERENT-CELL lines.

DECLARED BEFORE THE RUN. The null is that all seven lines behave alike because
they are all inner-shell transitions in the same atom — in which case same-cell
and different-cell pairs agree equally well and the cell predicts nothing. That
null is live and I do not know the answer.
"""
import math, itertools
from collections import defaultdict

CELL = {"L3M1": (1, +1, +1), "L3M4": (1, -1, +1), "L3M5": (1, -1, +1),
        "L2M1": (1, +1, -1), "L2M4": (1, -1, -1),
        "L1N2": (2, -1, 0), "L1N3": (2, -1, 0)}
SYM = ("H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn "
       "Ga Ge As Se Br Kr Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Cs Ba La Ce "
       "Pr Nd Pm Sm Eu Gd Tb Dy Ho Er Tm Yb Lu Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn "
       "Fr Ra Ac Th Pa U Np Pu Am Cm Bk Cf Es Fm").split()
Z = {s: i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(SYM)}
BLEND = set("Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Ru Rh Pd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Ba".split())


def load(n):
    d = {}
    for l in open(f"/home/claude/work/captures/XRAY-{n}.tsv"):
        if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip():
            continue
        f = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        # theory is field 2 for the five L-shell files, field 2 for L1N*
        try:
            v = float(f[2])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        d[f[0]] = v
    return d


D = {n: load(n) for n in CELL}


def fit(d, lo=30, hi=92):
    """E = A (Z - s)^p ; fit log E against log(Z - s) over a grid of s."""
    best = None
    for s10 in range(0, 300):
        s = s10 / 10
        xs, ys = [], []
        for e, v in d.items():
            z = Z.get(e)
            if z is None or not (lo <= z <= hi) or z - s <= 1 or e in BLEND:
                continue
            xs.append(math.log(z - s)); ys.append(math.log(v))
        if len(xs) < 8:
            continue
        n = len(xs); mx = sum(xs) / n; my = sum(ys) / n
        sxx = sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in xs)
        p = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sxx
        a = my - p * mx
        ss = sum((y - (a + p * x)) ** 2 for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
        tot = sum((y - my) ** 2 for y in ys)
        r2 = 1 - ss / tot
        if best is None or r2 > best[0]:
            best = (r2, p, s, n)
    return best


print("  MOSELEY FIT PER LINE — exponent p and screening s, Z = 30–92, unblended\n")
print(f"    {'line':<7}{'cell':<14}{'p':>8}{'s':>8}{'R^2':>10}{'n':>5}")
F = {}
for nm in ("L3M1", "L3M4", "L3M5", "L2M1", "L2M4", "L1N2", "L1N3"):
    r2, p, s, n = fit(D[nm])
    F[nm] = (p, s, r2)
    print(f"    {nm:<7}{str(CELL[nm]):<14}{p:>8.4f}{s:>8.2f}{r2:>10.6f}{n:>5}")

print("\n  SAME-CELL AGAINST DIFFERENT-CELL — the declared test\n")
pairs = list(itertools.combinations(CELL, 2))
same = [(a, b) for a, b in pairs if CELL[a] == CELL[b]]
diff = [(a, b) for a, b in pairs if CELL[a] != CELL[b]]


def gap(a, b):
    return abs(F[a][0] - F[b][0]), abs(F[a][1] - F[b][1])


print(f"    {'pair':<16}{'same cell':<12}{'|dp|':>10}{'|ds|':>10}")
for a, b in same:
    dp, ds = gap(a, b)
    print(f"    {a}/{b:<9}{'YES':<12}{dp:>10.4f}{ds:>10.2f}")
for a, b in sorted(diff, key=lambda x: gap(*x)[0])[:6]:
    dp, ds = gap(a, b)
    print(f"    {a}/{b:<9}{'no':<12}{dp:>10.4f}{ds:>10.2f}")

sp = [gap(a, b)[0] for a, b in same]
dpv = [gap(a, b)[0] for a, b in diff]
ss = [gap(a, b)[1] for a, b in same]
dsv = [gap(a, b)[1] for a, b in diff]
print(f"\n    mean |delta p|   same-cell {sum(sp)/len(sp):.4f}   "
      f"different-cell {sum(dpv)/len(dpv):.4f}")
print(f"    mean |delta s|   same-cell {sum(ss)/len(ss):.3f}   "
      f"different-cell {sum(dsv)/len(dsv):.3f}")
better = sum(1 for d in dpv if d > max(sp))
print(f"\n    different-cell pairs whose exponent gap EXCEEDS every same-cell gap: "
      f"{better} of {len(dpv)}")
