1. Introduction
A key property of atomic nuclei is their finite size, which cannot be precisely calculated from first principles. It must
be measured. Knowledge of the size of protons and neutrons and how they distribute within nuclei not only enriches
our basic understanding of nuclear structure, but also serves as input to a host of fundamental atomic and nuclear
applications. On the atomic physics side, confronting experiment and theory in light, simple atomic systems require
reliable values of root-mean-square (RMS) nuclear charge radii (see e.g. [1] and references therein). In heavier simple
systems, which are highly charged ions, experiment and theory approach a precision where finite size effects becomes
appreciable (e.g., [2–6]). In the realm of nuclear physics, refined studies of beta decay are based on accurately determined
electroweak moments [7–11]. Particular attention is paid to mirror nuclei, characterized by an interchanged number of
protons and neutrons. Exploring the radii of mirror nuclei provides insight into isospin effects in nuclei [12, 13], the
extent of the neutron skin [14], the equation of state of nucleonic matter [15], and the size of neutron stars [16].
This work serves two purposes, first to provide an up-to-date, transparent, critical evaluation of reference radii in
the Z = 3 − 32 range where mirror nuclei are relevant. Second, to predict unknown radii of mirror nuclei, including
examples of their applications. The structure is as follows; in Section 2 I reevaluate the radii of the relevant stable nuclei
from a combined analysis of muonic atom x-ray spectroscopy and electron scattering experiments. In Section 3 I update
the radii of the neon isotopic chain based on a recent high-precision measurement with coupled ions [17]. In Section 4 I
update the radii of pairs of mirror nuclei and demonstrate that, as predicted in [14], their difference is proportional to the
isospin asymmetry. Using the fit results I predict the unknown radii of 73 proton-bound mirror partners. In Section 5
I give two examples of useful applications of the predicted radii to fundamental physics. The first example focuses on
the Na isotopic chain, where the predicted radius of 21Na facilitates a precise benchmark of many-body atomic theory
calculations. In the second example, I demonstrate how to precisely predict the charge and weak radii of every nucleus
that participates in the determination of the magnitude of the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix element
Vud. A summary is given in Section 6.

proton-rich isotopes taking part in the mirror fit.

4. The mirror shift fit
Extensive ab initio calculations suggest that the differences in radii between mirror nuclei (mirror shifts) are proportional to the isospin asymmetry I = (N − Z)/A, at least up to I ≈ 0.2 [14]. The experimental situation is not
as healthy. In contrast with isotope shifts, which can be measured directly via optical spectroscopy, mirror shifts are
difficult to measure with high fractional precision. To obtain them, one has to take the difference between the absolute
radii of the mirror pair, contending with large experimental and theoretical uncertainties, which are emphasized in the
previous sections. Nevertheless, with the reference radii given in Tab. 2, δr2from the literature (the references are
given in Tab. 5), and the re-calibrated neon differential radii given in Tab. 3, we have all the ingredients to test the
linear theoretical prediction experimentally. The relevant data is given in Tab. 4. I excluded the pair 21Na-21Ne, as
its uncertainty is too large to be of use. The pairs with Cl isotopes were not included as their radii were determined
from electron scattering experiments, the interpretation of which depends on the nuclear model. The result of a simple
one-parameter fit to the weighted mirror shifts is shown in Figure 5. It has a reduced Chi-square of 11.5/11 = 1.04
indicating that such a fit is not inconsistent with the data. The resulting mirror shift parametrization is

6. Summary
In this work I reanalyzed the absolute root-mean-square charge radii of stable nuclei up to Z = 32 using the
conventional ‘Barret moment’ recipe for combined analysis of muonic x rays and electron scattering. I showed that even
within this simplified framework, there is a notably large missing uncertainty contribution to the reference radii from my
knowledge of the charge distribution. A shortcoming of this method which is emphasized by this work is that the Barret
recipe prevents us from benefiting from possible cancellations between the elastic and inelastic part of the two-photon
exchange, as is seen in light systems where a perturbative expansion is suitable [53].
The reference radii were combined with isotopic differences, stemming from measured electronic isotope shifts and
atomic theory calculations, to obtain those of isotopic chains. In some cases, large uncertainties in the theory have not
been taken into account, which is remedied here. More emphasis is placed on the neon chain, which was calibrated using
a novel measurement in coupled high-charged ions [17]. The physics discussed in this work would greatly benefit from
extending such measurements to more even-even pairs, notably of O, Si, Ar, and Ca.
Having constructed the database, I focus on 12 pairs of mirror nuclei with reasonably measured radii. Their difference
is found to be proportional to the isospin asymmetry, which confirms the calculations of [14], at least for the nuclei with
18 < A and I < 0.12. From the fitted proportionality constant and its uncertainty, the radii of 73 previously unknown
mirror partners are predicted.
Two examples of applications benefiting from these new and or improved radii are given. First, I use the predicted
radius of 21Na with the calculated field shift factor of a relevant transition to determine its mass shift factor. This factor
is used to recalibrate the radii of the chain spanning 20Na to 31Na, also giving the radii of their mirror partners, such
as 20F. The factor also compares favorably with atomic many-body calculations [48], setting a stringent benchmark for
the next generation of calculation methods [34].
The second example deals with radii of isotriplet nuclei as sandbox for isospin symmetry breaking studies. Assuming
that symmetry breaking is negligible as compared with the relevant uncertainties. In this case, I can combine the fit
result with the relation from [7] to obtain a simple equation for determining unknown radii of T = 1, Tz = 0 nuclei from
the mostly well known radii of those with T = 1, Tz = 1. This completes a model-independent, high-precision extraction
12
of the charge radii of all nuclei involved in the testing of the unitarity of the CKM matrix. Relaxing the assumption of
zero isospin symmetry breaking effects enables to test it. Without the mirror fit, this could only be done with the A = 38
triplet. Here, four more cases are considered. I find a general agreement except for with the A = 26 case. This calls for
refined isotope shift measurements in the Aluminum chain, more atomic factor calculations of the relevant transitions,
and a direct measurement of the radioactive 26Al radius with muonic atoms and microgram targets. Extending recent
measurements from neutron- to proton-rich Si would be beneficial as well. Finally, I extract the weak radii of all nuclei
involved in the test of the unitarity of the CKM matrix. Half of these weak radii were previously unknown, and the rest
have improved by an order of magnitude.

**The prediction held, and the paper says something about the table I captured an hour ago.**

**Register 1556 predicted this wouldn't reach Z = 97.** Its scope is **Z = 3 to 32** — it stops at germanium. A1's measurement bound stands unaltered.

**But its reference [25] is Angeli & Marinova 2013.** It states that compilation gives **no uncertainty** in the V₂(Z) charge-distribution factor; that the missing σ_CD is **up to four times larger** than the quoted totals; that from phosphorus onward it **dominates**; and that *"even larger missing uncertainties are expected for the heavier nuclei"* — **which is exactly where A1's anchors sit.** It also finds r(¹²C) **6σ** and r(¹⁸Ne) **5σ** from that table's values.

So the held table is the best available for the actinides and is **under active correction below them, by an author who expects the problem to worsen with Z**. The uncertainty columns are **lower bounds**, and the capture file now says so.

**And the paper carries a one-parameter law of the register's own shape.** The mirror shift **Δ = 1.382(34) × I**, fitted on twelve points, used to predict **seventy-three** unknown radii, at reduced χ² = 1.04. Register 1517 showed a one-parameter form is refuted the moment two constraints conflict. Here none do — **the same test, opposite verdict.** The mirror shift *is* representable in one parameter where ν was not.

**One thing flagged rather than asserted.** The paper says its slope *agrees* with theory's 1.574 ± 0.021. On the numbers as printed:

    fit     [1.348, 1.416]        theory  [1.553, 1.595]
    separation 4.7σ, gap 0.137 fm — the intervals do not overlap

The ± may be a **spread across calculations** rather than an uncertainty — the figure caption reads as the latter, the text as the former. **I don't resolve it.**

And Fishburn's warning applies to the seventy-three predictions exactly as to the corridor: validated only over 18 < A and I < 0.12, which the author states — alongside his own worst point at 2.3σ and three possible causes, none picked. That's the habit the register enforces, met in someone else's paper.

**It's a calibration failure, not a measurement one — and that's a sharper answer than "nobody has done it."**

**Three of the four methods need tens of milligrams.** Angeli & Marinova state it plainly: Kα X-ray isotope shift *"can be performed only on stable isotopes since the experimental method requires several tens of milligrams of target,"* and the same holds for muonic atoms and electron scattering. **Only optical isotope shift works on traces** — *"negligible quantities… inclusive single ones, with lifetimes down to 1 ms."*

**And OIS gives differences only.** Their equation (1) is the trap:

    R²(A) = R²(A′) + δ⟨r²⟩

It needs an absolute anchor **R(A′)**. Optical spectroscopy could measure δ⟨r²⟩ for Bk and Cf tomorrow — but **neither element has any isotope with a measured absolute radius**, so the chain has nothing to attach to. The shift is measurable; the result would be **uncalibrated**.

**And the wall is a staircase starting at 96, not a cliff at 97:**

    Z ≤ 95   both measured — americium is the last
    Z = 96   δ⟨r²⟩ survives; the absolute R is CALCULATED from a 3-parameter fit
    Z ≥ 97   neither

**The physical cost is computable:**

    20 mg ²⁴⁹Cf      3.0 GBq
    20 mg ²⁴⁹Bk    1,176 GBq   (330-day half-life)
    20 mg ²³⁸U         250 Bq   ← the anchor of the same table

Seven orders of magnitude, on material produced in **milligrams per year**, in a target that decays while you use it.

**And one route may move the wall.** Ohayon cites **Heines et al., *"Muonic x-ray spectroscopy on implanted targets"*, NIM B 541 (2023) 173**, and proposes measuring ²⁶Al with a **microgram-scale target**. That's a **20,000× reduction** — a 1 µg ²⁴⁹Cf target is 1.5 × 10⁵ Bq rather than 3.0 × 10⁹.

If microgram muonic spectroscopy works on implanted targets, **the single constraint blocking Z ≥ 97 stops binding**, and A1's two missing anchors become obtainable. That's now flagged in the queue as worth watching — it would turn a domain statement back into a fetchable item.

content.text:
**It's a calibration failure, not a measurement one — and that's a sharper answer than "nobody has done it."**

**Three of the four methods need tens of milligrams.** Angeli & Marinova state it plainly: Kα X-ray isotope shift *"can be performed only on stable isotopes since the experimental method requires several tens of milligrams of target,"* and the same holds for muonic atoms and electron scattering. **Only optical isotope shift works on traces** — *"negligible quantities… inclusive single ones, with lifetimes down to 1 ms."*

**And OIS gives differences only.** Their equation (1) is the trap:

    R²(A) = R²(A′) + δ⟨r²⟩

It needs an absolute anchor **R(A′)**. Optical spectroscopy could measure δ⟨r²⟩ for Bk and Cf tomorrow — but **neither element has any isotope with a measured absolute radius**, so the chain has nothing to attach to. The shift is measurable; the result would be **uncalibrated**.

**And the wall is a staircase starting at 96, not a cliff at 97:**

    Z ≤ 95   both measured — americium is the last
    Z = 96   δ⟨r²⟩ survives; the absolute R is CALCULATED from a 3-parameter fit
    Z ≥ 97   neither

**The physical cost is computable:**

    20 mg ²⁴⁹Cf      3.0 GBq
    20 mg ²⁴⁹Bk    1,176 GBq   (330-day half-life)
    20 mg ²³⁸U         250 Bq   ← the anchor of the same table

Seven orders of magnitude, on material produced in **milligrams per year**, in a target that decays while you use it.

**And one route may move the wall.** Ohayon cites **Heines et al., *"Muonic x-ray spectroscopy on implanted targets"*, NIM B 541 (2023) 173**, and proposes measuring ²⁶Al with a **microgram-scale target**. That's a **20,000× reduction** — a 1 µg ²⁴⁹Cf target is 1.5 × 10⁵ Bq rather than 3.0 × 10⁹.

If microgram muonic spectroscopy works on implanted targets, **the single constraint blocking Z ≥ 97 stops binding**, and A1's two missing anchors become obtainable. That's now flagged in the queue as worth watching — it would turn a domain statement back into a fetchable item.

Registers to 1559, both gates, checkpointed.

**The formula, validated before use:**

    R0 = (0.9071 + 1.105/A^(2/3) − 0.548/A^(4/3)) × A^(1/3)

A least-squares fit along the line of stability, used by the authors for Re, Po, Rn, Fr, Ra and Cm. **It reproduces their listed Cm-244 to 0.0000 fm** — so the implementation is right.

**Then tested where a test exists.** Against the four *measured* actinides it runs systematically **low**: +0.0335 fm at Th, +0.0597 at U, +0.0550 at Pu, +0.0694 at Am. And it has a defect that matters here — **it is a function of A alone**, giving Bk-249 and Cf-249 the identical radius, which is useless for an element-specific anchor.

**So the residual was regressed on Z:** −0.4995 + 0.00597·Z, r = +0.873, scatter 0.0090 fm. That recovers **0.0060 fm per proton** and separates the elements.

    Bk-249   5.9600 ± 0.0090 fm        Cf-249   5.9660 ± 0.0090 fm
    Bk-250   5.9674 ± 0.0090           Cf-250   5.9734 ± 0.0090
                                       Cf-251   5.9807 ± 0.0090

**And the quantity A1 actually consumes is the difference, which is far better determined.** The per-neutron δ⟨r²⟩ slope across **eighteen adjacent pairs in five elements** is **0.0874 ± 0.0213 fm²** — element means running 0.1014 at thorium down to 0.0710 at americium.

    Bk 249→250   0.0874 ± 0.0213 fm²
    Cf 249→250   0.0874 ± 0.0213
    Cf 249→251   0.1747 ± 0.0301

**The two carry different confidence and the file says so.** The absolute radii rest on a **four-point trend with two free parameters** — indicative only. The differences rest on **eighteen pairs across five elements** and are usable with their stated error.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""predict_radii.py — what Bk and Cf charge radii should look like when observed.

THE MATERIAL, all established and all held:

  (1) Angeli & Marinova's own reference-radius formula, given because SOME
      elements in their own table have no experimental R:

          R0 = (r0 + r1/A^(2/3) + r2/A^(4/3)) * A^(1/3)
          r0 = 0.9071(13) fm   r1 = 1.105(25) fm   r2 = -0.548(34) fm

      "which are the results of a least-squares fit to radii along the line
      of stability". They used it for Re, Po, Rn, Fr, Ra and Cm.

  (2) The measured actinide radii captured at R 1557 — U, Pu, Am — and the
      calculated one for Cm.

  (3) The measured delta<r^2> values, which give the isotopic slope.

THE DISCIPLINE. The formula is not applied to Bk and Cf until it has been
tested where a test is possible:
  TEST A  reproduce Cm, where the formula was ACTUALLY USED. If this fails,
          my implementation is wrong.
  TEST B  predict Am, U and Pu, which are MEASURED. This gives the formula's

print("  EASIER quantity, and the held actinides constrain it directly.\n")

**We didn't need it. Running A1's test for the first time shows why.**

**On the four measured pairs the proportionality already holds:**

    U  233/238   ratio 4.60        r = +0.916
    Pu 239/244         3.29        mean 4.13, spread 12%
    Am 241/243         4.23
    Cm 245/248         4.42

**The predicted pairs come out at 6.86 and 6.30 — far outside.** And the reason is the finding: **the column A1 uses is the *theoretical* KL3 energy**, and Deslattes et al. computed those with an **assumed nuclear charge radius**. For Bk and Cf, whose radii have never been measured, the theoretical isotope shift **already encodes a radius assumption**. Testing my extrapolation against it isn't a test of the field shift — it's my extrapolation against theirs, and the factor of 1.6 says only that we disagree.

**The experimental column is no escape:**

    U   4.99      Cm    2.41
    Pu −14.67     Bk  181.92
    Am −14.08

Two negative, one absurd. The KL3 experimental uncertainties are **0.2–15 eV** against shifts of **0.6–2.2 eV** — on most pairs the signal sits at or below the measurement error. That's presumably why A1 was built on the theory column to begin with.

**So A1's test is circular where it's precise and buried where it's independent.** The four measured anchors establish everything the six can, on values that don't depend on the radius being tested. Adding the predicted pairs moves the slope 13.5% and the correlation by 0.007 — **it contaminates rather than sharpens.**

**The honest answer: Z = 97 wasn't needed.** The work wasn't wasted — registers 1555–1560 turned an item carried as *blocked* into a domain statement with a named physical cause, a route that might lift it, and a labelled prediction. But **it did not do what it was begun for**, and the prediction file now says so in its header: kept as a record of the method, not as A1 input.

**Three uses survive, and one of them is new.**

**1 · The sign — which is what register 1381 actually claimed.** *The lighter isotope lies higher.* This is robust where the magnitude isn't: a bigger nucleus binds the 1s electron less, so the transition energy falls, and the radius rises with A universally. **An assumed radius cannot flip a sign.** Tested across every multi-isotope element in the capture, it holds on **five of six**.

*(And I misread my own table again — wrote "holds on every element" one line after printing that californium fails. It's five.)*

**2 · The failure is informative, and it's the new use.** Californium doesn't reverse — it **ties**. Cf-249 and Cf-250 carry the *identical* theoretical value, 115031.1 eV, where one neutron should give ~0.5 eV against a quoted precision of 0.1. It reads zero because Deslattes et al. **had no measured radius for californium** and used one assumed value for both mass numbers.

> **Where the theory column stops varying with A, it is announcing that it has no radius to vary.**

A1 can be run as a **detector** of exactly that — across the whole X-ray capture, not just the actinides. It finds cells with missing inputs, and it found its own.

**3 · A1 measures the electronic field-shift factor.**

    F = 4.13 ± 0.51 eV/fm²   KL3 transition, Z = 92–96

From the four anchors whose δ⟨r²⟩ come from optical and Kα work **independent** of the theoretical X-ray column. A measured quantity, extracted from material already held — and it needs four anchors, not six.

**4 · What A1 is not for:** validating a predicted radius. Circular on theory, buried in noise on experiment. That's now in both the queue and the prediction file's header.

So the item that looked like it needed unobtainable data turns out to yield a measured constant and a diagnostic tool from what was already on the shelf.

Registers to 1563, both gates, checkpointed.

import re
print("  PR3 — CAN A GLYPH SOLVE IT? TESTED.\n")
print("  The problem: `n*` opens a markdown italic span that never closes.")
print("  The current fix is `n\\*`, an ESCAPE — which is fragile, because a")
print("  later edit that drops the backslash silently reopens the fault.\n")
print("  ** A GLYPH THAT IS NOT THE MARKDOWN CHARACTER CANNOT BE MISREAD AT")
print("     ALL. And the right one already exists and is SEMANTICALLY CORRECT: **\n")
cands=[("*","U+002A","ASTERISK","the markdown emphasis character — the problem"),
       ("∗","U+2217","ASTERISK OPERATOR","the MATHEMATICAL asterisk. Unicode's own\n"
        "                        description is 'used in mathematics'"),
       ("⋆","U+22C6","STAR OPERATOR","a different math operator, means convolution"),
       ("★","U+2605","BLACK STAR","decorative, not mathematical"),
       ("′","U+2032","PRIME","already means something else — derivative")]
print(f"    {'glyph':<7}{'code':<9}{'name':<20}note")
for g,c,n,note in cands: print(f"    {g:<7}{c:<9}{n:<20}{note}")
print("\n  TESTING U+2217 AGAINST THE PARITY CHECK:\n")
tests=[("n* is the effective quantum number","raw asterisk"),
       (r"n\* is the effective quantum number","escaped"),
       ("n∗ is the effective quantum number","U+2217 glyph")]
for t,lab in tests:
    b=it=0
    for x in re.findall(r"\*{1,2}",t):
        if x=="**": b^=1
        else: it^=1
    hits=len(re.findall(r"(?<!\\)\*",t))
    print(f"    {lab:<12}  markdown asterisks found: {hits}   "
          f"italic parity: {'BROKEN' if it else 'clean'}")
print("\n  ** U+2217 CARRIES ZERO MARKDOWN ASTERISKS. The parity check cannot")
print("     see it, because there is nothing to see. **\n")
print("  AND IT SURVIVES THE ROUND-TRIP AND THE AUDIT UNCHANGED, because both")
print("  operate on the character stream and U+2217 is simply a letter to them.")
print("\n  THE CASE FOR THE GLYPH OVER THE ESCAPE:\n")
for l in ["· the escape is INVISIBLE in rendered output but PRESENT in source, so",
          "  the two representations differ and an editor sees a backslash that",
          "  the reader does not;",
          "· the glyph is IDENTICAL in both — what you type is what renders;",
          "· an escape can be lost by a careless edit and the fault returns",
          "  silently; a glyph cannot degrade into a markdown character;",
          "· and it is SEMANTICALLY RIGHT. n∗ with the asterisk operator is what",
          "  the notation actually means — the mathematical star, not a footnote",
          "  marker and not an emphasis delimiter.",
          "",
          "** ONE COST, STATED: anyone grepping for 'n\\*' will miss 'n∗'. Any",
          "   script that searches for the notation must search for the glyph. **"]:
    print(f"    {l}")

import re
r=open("REGISTER-DATA.md",encoding="utf-8").read()
H=re.compile(r"^ {0,3}((?:\d{3,4}, )*\d{3,4})\. ",re.M)
ms=list(H.finditer(r))
ESC=[673,904,943,1275,1300,1302]
print("  THE ESCAPE DOES NOT FIX THE PARITY CHECK. Testing the six entries")
print("  the queue calls 'escaped correctly':\n")
print(f"    {'entry':<8}{'has n\\\\*':<10}{'italic parity':<16}")
for i,m in enumerate(ms):
    e=ms[i+1].start() if i+1<len(ms) else len(r)
    t=r[m.end():e]; n=int(re.findall(r"\d{3,4}",m.group(1))[0])
    if n not in ESC: continue
    b=it=0
    for x in re.findall(r"\*{1,2}",t):
        if x=="**": b^=1
        else: it^=1
    print(f"    {n:<8}{'yes':<10}{'UNBALANCED' if it else 'clean':<16}")
print("\n  ** FOUR OF THE SIX 'CORRECTLY ESCAPED' ENTRIES STILL READ AS")
print("     UNBALANCED, because the parity counter sees the asterisk whether")
print("     or not a backslash precedes it. **\n")
print("  ** SO THE ESCAPE FIXES RENDERING AND NOT THE AUDIT. The glyph fixes")
print("     BOTH, because there is no asterisk left to count. That settles it")
print("     on evidence rather than preference — and it means PR5's audit 26")
print("     would have kept firing on escaped entries forever. **")

**All three decisions taken. PR3's glyph works, and it exposed something.**

**PR1 — held, and your criterion is met.** The front matter is *generated*, counts headings (1,357) where there are numbers (1,386), gap 29. **No computation, audit, or round-trip consumes it.** One paragraph of REGISTER.md. Book-time.

**PR2 — kept, on your reasoning.** Re-verified: none of the five has an entry, each appears exactly once, in the note about them. They stand as a visible gap in the record.

**PR3 — solved with U+2217 ∗, the ASTERISK OPERATOR.** Unicode's *mathematical* asterisk, which is what n∗ actually means.

    37 replaced (14 escaped, 23 raw) — 0 notation asterisks remain
    unbalanced italics: 25 → 14
    verified against backup: files identical once normalised,
    14 characters shorter, headings unchanged, both gates pass

**And the decisive finding: the escape never worked.** Four of the six entries the queue called *"escaped correctly"* — 904, 943, 1275, 1302 — **still read as unbalanced**, because the parity counter sees the asterisk whether or not a backslash precedes it. The escape fixed *rendering*, not the *audit*. **PR5's audit 26 would have fired on correctly-escaped entries forever.** The glyph leaves nothing to count.

Your instinct was better than the queue's plan.

---

**PR4 needs your call, because the fourteen split into two patterns wanting opposite fixes:**

    OPENS, never closes    789, 791, 846
      **…FAILS.** *Fitting α_d and α_q…   ← the italic prose section, unclosed

    CLOSES, never opened   604, 668, 747, 770, 808, 822, 1003, 1263
      …not a cleanup.*                     ← a closing mark with no opener

    mid-text strays        277, 313, 435
      **Computable* defined by…            ← one asterisk short of **bold**

**Deleting the stray is safe** — the span never closed, so no reader ever saw the emphasis. **Adding a partner invents emphasis you didn't write.** But for the eight that *close* without opening, deletion loses an italic section that was probably intended.

My read: **delete for the three mid-text strays, add the opener for the eight closers, add the closer for the three openers.** But that's editorial judgement on your prose, so I've stopped rather than swept.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""register_review.py — is every entry self-explanatory where it needs to be?

M's instruction: a full register review and audit. Read it all, check that it
is self-explanatory where it needs to be, see whether gaps can be filled from
the mathematics itself, then assess a new list of open problems.

THE TEST, DECLARED BEFORE THE RUN. An entry is SELF-CONTAINED when a reader
who has not read the rest of the register can tell what it claims and how it
was checked. The failure modes are mechanical enough to find:

  A  BARE BACK-REFERENCE   "as 1391 found" with no restatement of WHAT it found
  B  UNSOURCED FIGURE      a number with no method, script, or citation
  C  DANGLING PRONOUN      opens with "It" / "That" / "This" and no antecedent
  D  ORPHAN OBJECT         names an object never defined anywhere
  E  UNRESOLVED PROMISE    "will be tested" / "next session" never followed up
  F  NAKED CLAIM           a verdict word with no supporting number

None of these is fatal alone. A back-reference is fine if the entry restates
what it refers to. What matters is entries carrying SEVERAL at once, and
entries whose central claim is unreachable without another entry in hand.

This script FINDS candidates. It does not judge them — the reading does.
"""
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

SRC = "/home/claude/work/REGISTER-DATA.md"
raw = open(SRC, encoding="utf-8").read()
H = re.compile(r"^ {0,3}((?:\d{3,4}, )*\d{3,4})\. ", re.M)
ms = list(H.finditer(raw))

ENT = {}
ORDER = []
for i, m in enumerate(ms):
    e = ms[i + 1].start() if i + 1 < len(ms) else len(raw)
    body = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", raw[m.end():e]).strip()
    for num in re.findall(r"\d{3,4}", m.group(1)):
        ENT[int(num)] = body
    ORDER.append(int(re.findall(r"\d{3,4}", m.group(1))[0]))

print(f"  REGISTER REVIEW — {len(ms)} headings, {len(ENT)} numbers\n")

# ---- A. back-references, and whether they are restated -------------------
REF = re.compile(r"\b(?:register|registers|R)\s+(\d{3,4})", re.I)
bare = []
for n in ORDER:
    b = ENT[n]
    refs = set(int(x) for x in REF.findall(b))
    if not refs:
        continue
    # a reference is RESTATED if the sentence containing it also carries a
    # number, a quoted phrase, or a colon-introduced restatement
    for r in refs:
        seg = ""
        for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?]) ", b):
            if re.search(rf"\b(?:register|registers|R)\s+{r}\b", s, re.I):
                seg = s
                break
        has = bool(re.search(r"\d|'|\"|—|:", seg))
        if not has:
            bare.append((n, r, seg[:90]))

print("  A · BARE BACK-REFERENCES — cite an entry without restating it\n")
print(f"    found: {len(bare)}")
for n, r, s in bare[:10]:
    print(f"      {n} → {r}:  …{s}…")

# ---- C. dangling openers -------------------------------------------------
OPEN = re.compile(r"^\*{0,2}(It|That|This|These|Those|They|Both|Neither|Such)\b")
dang = [n for n in ORDER if OPEN.match(ENT[n].lstrip("*"))]
print(f"\n  C · ENTRIES OPENING ON A PRONOUN WITH NO ANTECEDENT\n")
print(f"    found: {len(dang)}  {dang[:14]}")

# ---- E. unresolved promises ---------------------------------------------
PROM = re.compile(r"\b(will be (?:tested|checked|run|built|written|done)|"
                  r"next session|to be (?:done|tested|checked)|remains to|"
                  r"not yet (?:run|built|tested|written)|owed)\b", re.I)
prom = [(n, PROM.search(ENT[n]).group(0)) for n in ORDER if PROM.search(ENT[n])]
print(f"\n  E · UNRESOLVED PROMISES\n")
print(f"    found: {len(prom)}")
for n, p in prom[:12]:
    print(f"      {n}: '{p}'")

# ---- D. orphan objects ---------------------------------------------------
OBJ = re.compile(r"\b([A-Z][a-z]?\.[a-z][a-z0-9]+)\b")
named = Counter()
for n in ORDER:
    for o in set(OBJ.findall(ENT[n])):
        named[o] += 1
try:
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, "/home/claude/work")
    import io, contextlib
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
        import mathreg
    defined = set(mathreg.REG)
except Exception:
    defined = set()
orphan = {o: c for o, c in named.items() if o not in defined}
print(f"\n  D · OBJECTS NAMED IN THE REGISTER BUT NOT IN mathreg.py\n")
print(f"    objects named   : {len(named)}")
print(f"    defined in reg  : {len(defined)}")
print(f"    ORPHANS         : {len(orphan)}")
for o, c in sorted(orphan.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:14]:
    print(f"      {o:<18}{c:>4} mention(s)")

**Fourteen, not thirteen — and reading them changes the count twice more.**

**Six are false positives, and three say the opposite of what was counted.** Register 1393's *"a precedent search, run late and owed earlier"* records a search that **was run** — it found Nilsson 1955. Register 1450's *"owed since the work began"* likewise, finding Scerri's consensus. Register 1011's *"had to be checked"* is past tense. **My pattern read the word without reading the tense**, so three *discharged* debts were counted as outstanding. The other three aren't promises at all — a general principle, a warning, and my own entry describing the count.

**One is discharged now.** Register 1489 flagged an echo *to be tested*: SL(2,ℝ) appearing once as the stabiliser of a global diffeomorphism orbit and once as the ultralocal corner factor. Tested under register 1398's own rule — **the coordinates are not the same.** One acts on maps from the cut into a dual space, global and singular; the other on the affine line of a single generator, one copy per point. One obstructs, one frees. **SL(2,ℝ) is the group that acts on an affine line, so it turns up wherever an affine line does.** And its one possible consequence is foreclosed anyway: 1498 established the corner map is Whitney generic with a trivial stabiliser.

**Six remain real — and only two were tracked.**

    433   Cowan & Andrew 1965 as precedent            one search
    534   the 105 cells' delimiter counts             ← R 1538 may have unblocked this
    630   twenty rows to reconcile a disclosed gap    ← same endpoint
    730   precedent search, high-ℓ noble-gas defects  owed BEFORE any novelty claim
    1296  THE BOOK AND FIVE COMPENDIA NEED THE LÖWDIN WORK (R 1249–1295)
    1475  the space index, defined through observability

**They appear nowhere in the queue** — carried in the register alone, which is precisely the failure the queue exists to prevent. Now section 0-c.

**Two things worth flagging.** 534 says *"no levels URL surfaced"* — and register 1538 found the reason: `energy1.pl` wants **`spectrum`** singular. **That may now be reachable**, and 630 needs the same endpoint. And **1296 is the largest owed item in the register** — forty-seven entries of Löwdin work that has never reached an artefact.

*In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin set a challenge: derive the n+ℓ filling rule from the
Schrödinger equation. It has stood since. This chapter states the challenge, what
the method delivered, and how the method itself did the work.*

### The problem, and the wrong target

Löwdin asked for the n+ℓ rule. **The rule is not what atoms obey.**

Read from the observed ground configurations of all 108 neutrals, the sequence in
which subshells OPEN is

> 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s **5d 4f** 6p 7s **6d 5f** 7p

**Madelung's rule inverts 5d/4f and 6d/5f.** Lanthanum opens 5d at Z = 57 and 4f
does not appear until cerium; actinium opens 6d at Z = 89 and 5f not until
protactinium. *Seventeen of nineteen openings agree; two do not.*

**So deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at two elements.**
The target is the ORDER, and n+ℓ is a name for it that is 89% accurate.

> **ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**
>
> **The incoming electron occupies the subshell of least ν among those with
> q < 2(2ℓ+1).**

**Both Pauli quantities appear.** The capacity 2(2ℓ+1) governs admissibility AND
sits inside the radicand. *The radicand is the count of states below: complete
lower shells of the same ℓ, plus the fraction of the current one already filled.*

**And the occupancy enters only through Pauli.** With the fraction q/2(2ℓ+1) in the
radicand the scatter in a within a subshell falls from 0.187 to 0.041 at 3p, 0.119
to 0.028 at 4p, 0.088 to 0.018 at 5p, 0.059 to 0.021 at 6p, 0.086 to 0.047 at 5d.
**Raw occupancy makes every one worse.** *The law needs no new coordinate.*

### The three bodies, and the pair that has no variable

A Rydberg atom is three bodies — a nucleus, a core of Nₑ−1 electrons, and one
outer electron — and the equation's shape follows from how they are indexed.

**Λ_var** places every variable of the problem on (body, role). **E = 0.**

| body | input | intermediate | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **nucleus** | Z | · | · |
| **core** | Nₑ | ℓ_core, n_out | · |
| **core + rydberg** | · | p, n₀, T | · |
| **nucleus + core** | c | u | · |
| **rydberg** | ℓ | · | δ |
| **nucleus + rydberg** | **—** | **—** | **—** |

> **No variable in the index relates the Rydberg electron to the nucleus
> directly.** Every quantity that connects them — the effective charge c, the
> collapse variable u — is a nucleus–core quantity that the Rydberg electron then
> reads.

**That is the screening statement appearing as a fact about the coordinates**, and
it is a claim about the index and not about the interaction: *the nucleus does
attract the outer electron, and strongly. What the index says is that no
COORDINATE of this problem carries that attraction unmediated.*

**And the channel equation has exactly that shape.** δ = √p · f(u) is a
core–rydberg factor times a nucleus–core factor, **with no third factor because
the index holds no third pair.**

### What the ladders can and cannot reach

Because **Z = Nₑ + c − 1**, only two of the three electronic quantities are
independent. **A ladder fixing one varies the other two, and no ladder can vary Z
alone.**
…
the trajectory was mine.*

**And the one microscope caught the largest thing.** ℓ(ℓ+1) had been recorded four
separate times — as the gate, the collapse switch, the barrier and Seaton's ratio —
before it appeared a fifth and sixth time in the angular factor 1/(2ℓ+1) and the
entry point √(ℓ(ℓ+1)/2). **One object, six appearances, and each had been given a
different discipline's name.**

---

*A Rydberg atom is three bodies: a nucleus, a core of Nₑ−1 electrons, and one
outer electron. The method's contribution is not a solution to the general
three-body problem but a statement about which pairs exist.*


# APPENDICES

# The Löwdin challenge

> **DRAFT — UNFINISHED, AND DELIBERATELY SO.**
> This chapter records where the work stands, not where it will end. It
> supersedes §34 of *The Method 1.6*, which was written before register 1460
> deactivated ν as a law and still presents ν as the solution. Everything
> below is registered; the register numbers are given so any claim can be
> checked against its own computation. Written at register 1569.

---

## 1 · The challenge, and its standing

In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin asked for a derivation of the n+ℓ filling rule from
the Schrödinger equation. It has stood since.

**It is open by consensus, and we did not establish that ourselves — we found
it out late.** Scerri, *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A* **378**, 20190300 (2020):
numerous authors claim to have met the challenge, and the generally held
opinion is that none has succeeded as Löwdin intended it (R 1450). *A
precedent search was owed from the beginning of this work and was run near
its end. That order was the wrong way round and the register says so.*

## 2 · The wrong target, and this is the chapter's firmest result

**The n+ℓ rule is not what atoms obey.**

Read from the observed ground configurations of all 108 neutrals, the sequence
in which subshells OPEN is

> 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s **5d 4f** 6p 7s **6d 5f** 7p

**Madelung's rule inverts 5d/4f and 6d/5f.** Lanthanum opens 5d at Z = 57 and
4f does not appear until cerium; actinium opens 6d at Z = 89 and 5f not until
protactinium. Seventeen of nineteen openings agree; two do not.

**So deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at two
elements.** The target is the ORDER. n+ℓ is a name for that order which is
about 89% accurate, and a derivation of the name is not a derivation of the
thing.

*This survives everything that follows. It does not depend on ν, on the
corridor, or on any fitted quantity.*

## 3 · ν, and its deactivation

The work's central construction was

> **ν(n, ℓ, q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**
>
> the incoming electron occupies the subshell of least ν among those with
> q < 2(2ℓ+1).

**Both Pauli quantities appear**: the capacity 2(2ℓ+1) governs admissibility
and also sits inside the radicand, which counts the states below — complete
lower shells of the same ℓ, plus the fraction of the current one already
filled. **The occupancy enters only through Pauli**, and with the fraction in
the radicand the scatter in a within a subshell falls from 0.187 to 0.041 at
3p, 0.119 to 0.028 at 4p, 0.088 to 0.018 at 5p. Raw occupancy makes every one
worse.

**ν IS DEACTIVATED AS A LAW AND RETAINED AS A FORM (R 1460).** Three findings
forced this and each is independent of the others.

**(a) The score was fitted.** `scorer.py` placed a using each step's own
corridor — and a corridor is built by `brack.py` FROM the observed entrant at
that step. The answer was setting the parameter that produced the answer.
**Held out, the walk scores 90 against plain Madelung's 96** (R 1445). *A
construction that loses to the rule it was built to explain has not explained
it.*

**(b) The physical reading is structurally impossible, not merely wrong.**
The connection δ = a√p would give ν a derivation. It cannot: **δ is bounded as
n → ∞ and a√p diverges** (R 1457–1458). The held series are flat to five per
cent where √p demands a factor of six. And the Tietz potential has no Coulomb
tail, so no defect can be derived from it even in principle. *There is no
route from the walk to δ.*

**(c) It was already known.** Register 1303 had established the impossibility
before register 1341 reopened the question. **The register caught its own
repetition**, which is what it is for.

**What ν retains: it ORDERS, and does not MEASURE.** As an ordering functional
it is intact. As an effective quantum number it is refuted. *The corridor —
the instrument built to test ν — survives entirely, and is the more useful
object.*

## 4 · What the form still recovers

**Five of Madelung's ten exceptions**, using principled placement: the
geometric mean of the binding ceilings of the current and next groups. *No
parameter is fitted at this step.* Against Madelung's own 96, the fitted form
reached 99 and the held-out form 90 — but the five exceptions are recovered by
a rule stated in advance, and that is a different kind of result from a score.

**Where it fails, it fails in a nameable place.** The corridor's feasible set
is empty exactly where two constraints conflict, and those places are
enumerable rather than mysterious.

## 5 · The corridor is additive representability, and this was known in 1959

The corridor construction — a system of linear inequalities in one unknown,
one per step, feasible iff a placement exists — **is an instance of additive
representability of a ranked order.** The literature is Kraft–Pratt–Seidenberg
(1959), Scott (1964), and Krantz–Luce–Suppes–Tversky (1971). **Empty feasible
sets correspond exactly to cancellation conditions.**

**Fishburn's warning is on the record and is a standing caution**: low-order
feasibility does not imply global representability. A corridor that is
feasible at every order tested may still fail at an order not tested.

## 6 · The measure: Helly, and three names for one number

**The index forecloses a family rather than supplying a mechanism, and it
returns the number three** (R 1517).

Each object here is a system of linear inequalities in d unknowns, and the
Helly number is h = d + 1. **Register 489's "one level short", Freuder's
k-consistency, and the KPS cancellation conditions are THREE NAMES FOR h.**

| object | d | h | feasible | fails at order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ | tree | 2 | **yes**, E = 0 | — |
| Löwdin | 1 | 2 | **no** | 2 — 183 disjoint pairs, minimum 3 values |
| nuclear shell | 1 effective | 2 | **no** | 2 — K(3,3), certificate one edge |
| M.C2 | ternary, decomposes | — | conditional | no defect |

**The binary mechanism is a conflict graph** (R 1521): vertices are
constraints, an edge joins two that cannot hold together, and **the maximum
clique IS the verdict.** Λ has clique 1 and closes. M.C2 has clique 1 and is
conditional. The nuclear corridor has clique 2 and is refuted. **Löwdin has
clique 3** — and the three values that cannot be reconciled are at boron 5,
lanthanum 57 and lawrencium 103.

**And three languages describe the same thing** (R 1518): geometry
(Helly, Radon, Gallai), logic (k-consistency), statistics (centrepoint,
fractional Helly). *Use the language that is NON-DEGENERATE for the object.*
For Löwdin, d = 1 and the geometry face is the live one.

## 7 · Belokolos, and what a global form with exceptions is not

Belokolos (2017) derives Madelung's first rule by requiring Coulomb behaviour
at the origin, which forces the frequency ratio α = 2. **That answers the
"guessed potential" objection** and is properly attributed.

**It does not answer Löwdin.** A global form with exceptions is not a solution
for all circumstances, and his ranking is 87 of 106 (R 1520). *The distinction
matters and is not a criticism of the paper: it answers a different question,
well.*

## 8 · What is actually open

**The challenge is not met here and the chapter says so plainly.**

- **The order is the target, not n+ℓ.** Settled, and independent of everything
  else in this chapter.
- **ν orders and does not measure.** Settled.
- **The corridor is additive representability.** Settled, with Fishburn's
  caution standing.
- **The clique-3 obstruction at B/La/Lr.** Measured. *Why those three and not
  others is not explained.*
- **P1 — what the corridor is an instrument OF.** Open. The question is no
  longer "what is a" but what class of problem the corridor measures.
- **P3 — why are the onsets exact?** K(x) = (1/6)x(x² + 2 − 3μ(x)) reproduces
  all eight Klechkovski–Hakala onsets exactly. **Nobody here knows why.**
- **P4 — a seventh placement rule for a is NOT to be attempted.** Six have
  failed. This is recorded as a prohibition, not a gap.

---

*The honest summary: the method established what the target is, refuted its own
candidate law by three independent routes, identified its instrument as a
known construction from 1959, and measured the obstruction. It did not derive
the filling order from the Schrödinger equation. Löwdin's challenge stands.*

4f does not appear until cerium; actinium opens 6d at Z = 89 and 5f not until
protactinium. Seventeen of nineteen openings agree; two do not.

**So deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at two
elements.** The target is the ORDER. n+ℓ is a name for that order which is
about 89% accurate, and a derivation of the name is not a derivation of the
thing.

*This survives everything that follows. It does not depend on ν, on the
corridor, or on any fitted quantity.*

## 3 · ν, and its deactivation

The work's central construction was

> **ν(n, ℓ, q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**
>
> the incoming electron occupies the subshell of least ν among those with
> q < 2(2ℓ+1).

**Both Pauli quantities appear**: the capacity 2(2ℓ+1) governs admissibility
and also sits inside the radicand, which counts the states below — complete
lower shells of the same ℓ, plus the fraction of the current one already
filled. **The occupancy enters only through Pauli**, and with the fraction in
the radicand the scatter in a within a subshell falls from 0.187 to 0.041 at
3p, 0.119 to 0.028 at 4p, 0.088 to 0.018 at 5p. Raw occupancy makes every one
worse.

**ν IS DEACTIVATED AS A LAW AND RETAINED AS A FORM (R 1460).** Three findings
forced this and each is independent of the others.

**(a) The score was fitted.** `scorer.py` placed a using each step's own
corridor — and a corridor is built by `brack.py` FROM the observed entrant at
that step. The answer was setting the parameter that produced the answer.
**Held out, the walk scores 90 against plain Madelung's 96** (R 1445). *A
construction that loses to the rule it was built to explain has not explained
it.*

**(b) The physical reading is structurally impossible, not merely wrong.**
The connection δ = a√p would give ν a derivation. It cannot: **δ is bounded as
n → ∞ and a√p diverges** (R 1457–1458). The held series are flat to five per
cent where √p demands a factor of six. And the Tietz potential has no Coulomb
tail, so no defect can be derived from it even in principle. *There is no
route from the walk to δ.*

**(c) It was already known.** Register 1303 had established the impossibility
before register 1341 reopened the question. **The register caught its own
repetition**, which is what it is for.

**What ν retains: it ORDERS, and does not MEASURE.** As an ordering functional
it is intact. As an effective quantum number it is refuted. *The corridor —
the instrument built to test ν — survives entirely, and is the more useful
object.*

## 4 · What the form still recovers

**Five of Madelung's ten exceptions**, using principled placement: the
geometric mean of the binding ceilings of the current and next groups. *No
parameter is fitted at this step.* Against Madelung's own 96, the fitted form
reached 99 and the held-out form 90 — but the five exceptions are recovered by
a rule stated in advance, and that is a different kind of result from a score.

**Where it fails, it fails in a nameable place.** The corridor's feasible set
is empty exactly where two constraints conflict, and those places are
enumerable rather than mysterious.

## 5 · The corridor is additive representability, and this was known in 1959

The corridor construction — a system of linear inequalities in one unknown,
one per step, feasible iff a placement exists — **is an instance of additive
representability of a ranked order.** The literature is Kraft–Pratt–Seidenberg
(1959), Scott (1964), and Krantz–Luce–Suppes–Tversky (1971). **Empty feasible
sets correspond exactly to cancellation conditions.**

**Fishburn's warning is on the record and is a standing caution**: low-order
feasibility does not imply global representability. A corridor that is
feasible at every order tested may still fail at an order not tested.

## 6 · The measure: Helly, and three names for one number

**The index forecloses a family rather than supplying a mechanism, and it
returns the number three** (R 1517).

Each object here is a system of linear inequalities in d unknowns, and the
Helly number is h = d + 1. **Register 489's "one level short", Freuder's
k-consistency, and the KPS cancellation conditions are THREE NAMES FOR h.**

| object | d | h | feasible | fails at order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ | tree | 2 | **yes**, E = 0 | — |
| Löwdin | 1 | 2 | **no** | 2 — 183 disjoint pairs, minimum 3 values |
| nuclear shell | 1 effective | 2 | **no** | 2 — K(3,3), certificate one edge |
| M.C2 | ternary, decomposes | — | conditional | no defect |

**The binary mechanism is a conflict graph** (R 1521): vertices are
constraints, an edge joins two that cannot hold together, and **the maximum
clique IS the verdict.** Λ has clique 1 and closes. M.C2 has clique 1 and is
conditional. The nuclear corridor has clique 2 and is refuted. **Löwdin has
clique 3** — and the three values that cannot be reconciled are at boron 5,
lanthanum 57 and lawrencium 103.

**And three languages describe the same thing** (R 1518): geometry
(Helly, Radon, Gallai), logic (k-consistency), statistics (centrepoint,
fractional Helly). *Use the language that is NON-DEGENERATE for the object.*
For Löwdin, d = 1 and the geometry face is the live one.

## 7 · Belokolos, and what a global form with exceptions is not

Belokolos (2017) derives Madelung's first rule by requiring Coulomb behaviour
at the origin, which forces the frequency ratio α = 2. **That answers the
"guessed potential" objection** and is properly attributed.

**It does not answer Löwdin.** A global form with exceptions is not a solution
for all circumstances, and his ranking is 87 of 106 (R 1520). *The distinction
matters and is not a criticism of the paper: it answers a different question,
well.*

## 8 · What is actually open

**The challenge is not met here and the chapter says so plainly.**

- **The order is the target, not n+ℓ.** Settled, and independent of everything
  else in this chapter.
- **ν orders and does not measure.** Settled.
- **The corridor is additive representability.** Settled, with Fishburn's
  caution standing.
- **The clique-3 obstruction at B/La/Lr.** Measured. *Why those three and not
  others is not explained.*
- **P1 — what the corridor is an instrument OF.** Open. The question is no
  longer "what is a" but what class of problem the corridor measures.
- **P3 — why are the onsets exact?** K(x) = (1/6)x(x² + 2 − 3μ(x)) reproduces
  all eight Klechkovski–Hakala onsets exactly. **Nobody here knows why.**
- **P4 — a seventh placement rule for a is NOT to be attempted.** Six have
  failed. This is recorded as a prohibition, not a gap.

---

*The honest summary: the method established what the target is, refuted its own
candidate law by three independent routes, identified its instrument as a
known construction from 1959, and measured the obstruction. It did not derive
the filling order from the Schrödinger equation. Löwdin's challenge stands.*

# The three-body problem, and which pairs exist

> **DRAFT — UNFINISHED, AND DELIBERATELY SO.**
> This chapter records where the work stands. The material currently sits as a
> four-line coda to §34 of *The Method 1.6*; it is larger than that and is
> given its own chapter here. Every claim carries its register number.
> Written at register 1569.

---

## 1 · What is and is not claimed

**The method offers no solution to the general three-body problem.** It offers
a statement about **which pairs of bodies the problem's own coordinates
carry** — and that statement turns out to have consequences.

A Rydberg atom is three bodies: a nucleus, a core of Nₑ − 1 electrons, and one
outer electron. *The claim below is about the INDEX of that problem, not about
the interaction.*

## 2 · The pair that has no variable

**Λ_var** places every variable of the problem on (body, role), and **closes
with E = 0**.

| body | input | intermediate | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **nucleus** | Z | · | · |
| **core** | Nₑ | ℓ_core, n_out | · |
| **core + rydberg** | · | p, n₀, T | · |
| **nucleus + core** | c | u | · |
| **rydberg** | ℓ | · | δ |
| **nucleus + rydberg** | **—** | **—** | **—** |

> **No variable in the index relates the Rydberg electron to the nucleus
> directly.** Every quantity connecting them — the effective charge c, the
> collapse variable u — is a nucleus–core quantity that the Rydberg electron
> then reads.

**This is the screening statement appearing as a fact about coordinates**, and
it must be read carefully. *The nucleus does attract the outer electron, and
strongly. What the index says is that no COORDINATE of this problem carries
that attraction unmediated.*

**And the channel equation has exactly that shape.** δ = √p · f(u) is a
core–rydberg factor times a nucleus–core factor, **with no third factor
because the index holds no third pair.**

## 3 · The constraint the ladders inherit

Because **Z = Nₑ + c − 1**, only two of the three electronic quantities are
independent. **A ladder fixing one varies the other two, and no ladder can
vary Z alone.**

*This is why the isoelectronic, isonuclear and isoionic ladders are three
views of a two-dimensional space rather than three independent axes — a fact
about the coordinates, not about the experiments.*

## 4 · Two Helly orders, one problem

**The two-state three-body structure is one problem at two Helly numbers,
differing by N − 1** (R 1520).

The known-mass and unknown-mass cases are the same object measured at
different orders. **Certificates transfer UPWARD only**: an infeasibility
proved at low order holds at high order, but feasibility at low order proves
nothing above it. *This is Fishburn's warning again, in the three-body
setting.*

**The envelope IS the feasible set, of dimension N − 1.**

## 5 · The shared mechanism

The three-body structure, the Löwdin corridor and M.C2 were joined as **one
object under one measure** (R 1515–1521). Each is a system of linear
inequalities; each has a Helly number; each has a conflict graph whose maximum
clique is its verdict.

    Λ              clique 1    closed
    M.C2           clique 1    conditional
    nuclear        clique 2    refuted
    Löwdin         clique 3    obstructed

**Where the geometry degenerates, use another face.** The nuclear corridor is
rank-one, so the geometric face is degenerate and the statistical face —
fractional Helly — is the live one. *The measure does not change; the language
does.*

## 6 · The nuclear corridor, and a structural emptiness

The nuclear shell model corridor is the sharpest result in this family.

**Six consecutive pairs all require the same combination 4β + α. Three demand
it positive and three demand it negative.** The feasible set is therefore
**structurally empty** — established by exact rational arithmetic, not by
numerical near-miss.

**And the refuted family is named**: Nilsson's modified oscillator,
H = HO − κℏω₀[2 l·s + μ(l² − ⟨l²⟩_N)], Nilsson (1955), where β = −κμℏω and
α = 2κℏω (R 1393). *So the corridor tested the Nilsson potential in its
spherical limit.* The transfermium orbital check found 11 of 12 pass and one
fails on parity — but that is the deformed regime, which does not test the
spherical-limit refutation either way.

## 7 · What is open

- **Why N − 1?** The gap between the two Helly orders is measured and not
  explained.
- **The nuclear correction into the artefacts.** The six-pair count and the
  4β + α identity are established but register 1370, HANDOFF and the
  Mathematical Compendium still carry the earlier undercount and the
  "coincidence" reading. **This is owed and is the concrete next step.**
- **Whether the conflict-graph measure extends past these four objects.**
  Four is not a pattern.

---

*The three-body contribution is negative in form and useful in consequence: the
index carries no nucleus–rydberg pair, so the channel equation has two factors
and not three, the three ladders span two dimensions and not three, and the
same Helly measure that reads the corridor reads this.*

**CHAPTER-LOWDIN.md** (174 lines) supersedes it, and leads with the firmest result rather than the prettiest: **the n+ℓ rule is not what atoms obey** — 5d/4f and 6d/5f invert, so deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at two elements. That survives everything else in the chapter. Then ν's deactivation with all three independent grounds, the five exceptions the *form* still recovers by principled placement, the corridor as additive representability (KPS 1959) with Fishburn's caution standing, the Helly measure and the clique of three at **B, La, Lr**, Belokolos attributed and bounded, and Scerri's consensus.

**CHAPTER-THREEBODY.md** (121 lines) — the material was a four-line coda and it's larger than that. Λ_var's empty **nucleus–rydberg** cell and why that's a claim about *coordinates*, not the interaction; the two-factor channel equation that follows; **Z = Nₑ + c − 1** forcing three ladders through two dimensions; the two Helly orders differing by N − 1 with certificates transferring **upward only**; and the nuclear corridor's structural emptiness with **Nilsson (1955)** named.

Both marked **DRAFT** in their third line, both parity-clean, and **every register citation resolves** — checked against the register, not asserted.

Neither finishes. Each closes with what's open, including P4's *prohibition* against a seventh placement rule and the nuclear six-pair correction still owed to R 1370 and the Compendium.

**u < p < ℓ−ℓ_core < Z−T**, and 288 of 120,960 orderings reach it.

two angular momenta, Z−T is one distance to one threshold. **The index says which
law runs in which variable, and fitting a law in the wrong carrier is what took
the ℓ-spread from a spurious r² 0.868 to a real 0.356.**

## Λ_const — the constants

**What it is.** Fourteen constants on (role, carrier), role order
**exponent < centre < width < scale**. **E = 0** at 2 of 576 orderings.

**What only it contributes.** *That `standing` cannot be a coordinate.* With
attributed/derived/measured/fitted on an axis the index cannot close at any
ordering; without it, it closes at once. **An index whose coordinates mix the

is offered as an answer to Löwdin's challenge**: the amplitude law remains
three fitted numbers, and the chapter `CHAPTER-LOWDIN.md` states what is and is
not derived.*

## Λ_law — the laws of the channel equation

**Seven laws on (law, carrier). E = 0.**

An arbitrary ordering gave E = 7. Across all 7! × 4! = **120,960 orderings** the
defect runs from 0 to 21, and **288 of them reach zero** — so closure is neither
forced nor accidental, and the closing orders share a reading.

**The closing carrier order is u < p < ℓ − ℓ_core < Z − T**, which is monotone in
**how LOCAL the variable is**:

| carrier | what it spans | laws on it |
|---|---|---|
| **u** | the whole atom | 2 |
| **p** | one ℓ's shells | 3 |
| **ℓ − ℓ_core** | two angular momenta | 1 |
| **Z − T** | one distance to one threshold | 1 |

The held cells form a **staircase**, which by `A.staircls` is exactly the
condition for E(ℛ) = 0. *The closure is not a coincidence of this ordering; it
is the staircase theorem.*

**What only this index contributes: THE CARRIER.** The index says which law runs
in which variable — and **fitting a law in the wrong carrier is what took the
ℓ-spread from a spurious r² of 0.868 to a real 0.356.**

**Fourteen constants on (role, carrier). E = 0 at 2 of 576 orderings**, role
order **exponent < centre < width < scale**.

small integer or half-integer — **2** for the free shells, **2** for the gate,
**−1.5** for the switch, **2.5** for the ℓ-validity, **u₀ ≈ 4**. *No scale is.*
The role axis therefore orders by **how much physics a number has absorbed**.

**And β = ⅔ is the load-bearing constant**: the only one of arity three,
appearing in the amplitude, the exponent and the validity — **and it is the one
that is attributed rather than fitted.**

fitted on an axis, the index closes at **no** ordering; remove it and it closes
at once.

> **An index whose coordinates mix the OBJECT with the OBSERVER cannot close,
> because the observer's axis has no order the object respects.**

*The same fault recurs as `origin` in Λ_var, `kind` in Λ_phys and `state` in
Λ_ladder — four independent occurrences of one mistake, which is why it is
stated here as a rule rather than as an incident.*
"""

p.write_text(s,encoding="utf-8")

 "**THE CONTENT IS NOW WHERE IT BELONGS. Λ_law and Λ_const are in COMPENDIUM-TAIL.md; the channel "

The **Theodosiou experimental column** is indexed on (Z, z, ℓ), which maps *straight* onto the index's own coordinates. All 42 rows land on admitted cells, and **twelve aren't currently measured** — Na I's s, p, d, f; Fe VIII's p, d, f; Ca I's p; Ca III's s, d; Ca X's s, d. Those are immediate.

The **ionisation ladder** is larger and weaker. 495 rows give a ground-state defect via μ = n − z√(R/IE) — but register 1546 established that's a *different quantity* from the asymptotic defect the index holds, and 1552 measured the gap closing as z rises. Usable above z ≈ 3, and only **19.4% of the ladder is measured** rather than interpolated. That leaves **60 rows**, each giving one cell at the ground ℓ only.

    + ladder z≥3      400    0.39%               9.5%

---

    Ca X   s          ok

    Ca I    p         *** off by 0.24 ***

Checking tells you where a hundred thousand computed cells can and cannot be trusted.** The index was built to be a place where every claim is registered and auditable — and the captures already in hand deliver that, at the cost of admitting the filler has holes.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sudoku3.py — three independent determinations of one cell.

THE SHAPE. A sudoku cell is constrained three ways — row, column, box — and the
puzzle is solvable because the three must agree. Where two agree and one does
not, the odd one out is LOCALISED rather than merely suspected.

The spectra index has the same shape and has never been read that way:

    A  THE FILLER      delta computed by the channel equation      COORDINATES.tsv
    B  THEODOSIOU      the ASYMPTOTIC quantum defect, measured     QDEFECT-*.tsv
    C  THE LADDER      the GROUND-STATE defect from an ionisation  LADDER-K-Kr.tsv
                       energy, mu = n - z*sqrt(R/IE)

All three are indexed on (Z, z, l) and none was fitted to either other.

WHAT MAKES IT A SUDOKU AND NOT THREE LISTS. B and C measure DIFFERENT
QUANTITIES — register 1546 established the asymptotic and ground-state defects
are not the same number, and register 1552 measured the gap closing as z rises
at slope -0.0037. So the three-way cell carries a KNOWN OFFSET between two of
its faces, and that offset is itself checkable.

    A vs B   does the filler reproduce a measured asymptotic defect?
    A vs C   does the filler reproduce a measured ground state?
    B vs C   does R 1552's offset law hold where both are present?

THE LANGUAGES (register 1518). The same disagreement can be read three ways and
the right one depends on the cell:

    geometry     is the triple feasible within tolerance?  (a Helly question)
    logic        which pair is consistent, which is not?   (k-consistency)
    statistics   is the deviation inside the spread?       (fractional)

Use the language that is NON-DEGENERATE for the cell. Where only two faces are
present, geometry at order 3 is degenerate and the pairwise logic face is live.
"""
import math, collections, sys

R = 13.605693

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face A
rows = [l.rstrip("\r\n").split("\t")
        for l in open("COORDINATES.tsv", encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")[1:]
        if l.strip()]
A = {}
for x in rows:
    try:
        A[(int(x[0]), int(x[1]), int(x[2]))] = (float(x[4]), x[5], x[8])
    except (ValueError, IndexError):
        pass

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face B
B = {}
for l in open("captures/QDEFECT-Theodosiou-1986.tsv", encoding="utf-8"):
    if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip():
        continue
    f = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    if len(f) < 8:
        continue
    try:
        B[(int(f[2]), int(f[3]), int(f[5]))] = float(f[7])
    except ValueError:
        pass

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face C
# the ground-state defect needs the OUTER ORBITAL (n, l) of the species, which
# follows from the electron count N = Z - z + 1 under the observed filling order.
ORDER = [(1,0,2),(2,0,2),(2,1,6),(3,0,2),(3,1,6),(4,0,2),(3,2,10),(4,1,6),
         (5,0,2),(4,2,10),(5,1,6),(6,0,2),(5,2,10),(4,3,14),(6,1,6),(7,0,2),
         (6,2,10),(5,3,14),(7,1,6)]

def outer(N):
    """(n, l) of the last electron under the OBSERVED opening order."""
    for n, l, cap in ORDER:
        if N <= cap:
            return n, l
        N -= cap
    return None

C = {}
for l in open("captures/LADDER-K-Kr.tsv", encoding="utf-8"):
    if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip():
        continue
    zs, cs, es, q = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    Z = int(zs); z = int(cs[1:]) + 1; ie = float(es)
    o = outer(Z - z + 1)
    if not o or ie <= 0:
        continue
    n, ll = o
    C[(Z, z, ll)] = (n - z * math.sqrt(R / ie), q, n)

print(f"  FACES:  A filler {len(A):,}   B Theodosiou {len(B)}   C ladder {len(C)}\n")

keys = sorted(set(A) & (set(B) | set(C)))
tri = sorted(set(A) & set(B) & set(C))
ab = sorted((set(A) & set(B)) - set(C))
ac = sorted((set(A) & set(C)) - set(B))

print(f"  CELLS WITH ALL THREE FACES : {len(tri)}")
print(f"  A+B only                   : {len(ab)}")
print(f"  A+C only                   : {len(ac)}")
print(f"  total multi-face cells     : {len(keys)}\n")

SYM = {1:"H",2:"He",3:"Li",4:"Be",5:"B",6:"C",7:"N",8:"O",9:"F",10:"Ne",
       11:"Na",12:"Mg",13:"Al",14:"Si",15:"P",16:"S",17:"Cl",18:"Ar",
       19:"K",20:"Ca",21:"Sc",22:"Ti",23:"V",24:"Cr",25:"Mn",26:"Fe",
       27:"Co",28:"Ni",29:"Cu",30:"Zn",31:"Ga",32:"Ge",33:"As",34:"Se",
       35:"Br",36:"Kr"}
ROM = {1:"I",2:"II",3:"III",4:"IV",5:"V",6:"VI",7:"VII",8:"VIII",9:"IX",
       10:"X",11:"XI",12:"XII",13:"XIII",14:"XIV",15:"XV",16:"XVI"}

if tri:
    print("  THE THREE-FACE CELLS — every one read three ways\n")
    print(f"    {'cell':<12}{'l':>2}{'A filler':>10}{'B asympt':>10}"
          f"{'C ground':>10}{'A-B':>8}{'B-C':>8}   verdict")
    for k in tri:
        Z, z, l = k
        a = A[k][0]; b = B[k]; c = C[k][0]
        nm = f"{SYM.get(Z,Z)} {ROM.get(z,z)}"
        dab = a - b; dbc = b - c
        v = "AGREE" if abs(dab) < 0.05 else "A OFF"
        print(f"    {nm:<12}{'spdf'[l]:>2}{a:>10.4f}{b:>10.3f}{c:>10.4f}"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sudoku3.py — three independent determinations of one cell.

THE SHAPE. A sudoku cell is constrained three ways — row, column, box — and the
puzzle is solvable because the three must agree. Where two agree and one does
not, the odd one out is LOCALISED rather than merely suspected.

The spectra index has the same shape and has never been read that way:

    A  THE FILLER      delta computed by the channel equation      COORDINATES.tsv
    B  THEODOSIOU      the ASYMPTOTIC quantum defect, measured     QDEFECT-*.tsv
    C  THE LADDER      the GROUND-STATE defect from an ionisation  LADDER-K-Kr.tsv
                       energy, mu = n - z*sqrt(R/IE)

All three are indexed on (Z, z, l) and none was fitted to either other.

WHAT MAKES IT A SUDOKU AND NOT THREE LISTS. B and C measure DIFFERENT
QUANTITIES — register 1546 established the asymptotic and ground-state defects
are not the same number, and register 1552 measured the gap closing as z rises
at slope -0.0037. So the three-way cell carries a KNOWN OFFSET between two of
its faces, and that offset is itself checkable.

    A vs B   does the filler reproduce a measured asymptotic defect?
    A vs C   does the filler reproduce a measured ground state?
    B vs C   does R 1552's offset law hold where both are present?

THE LANGUAGES (register 1518). The same disagreement can be read three ways and
the right one depends on the cell:

    geometry     is the triple feasible within tolerance?  (a Helly question)
    logic        which pair is consistent, which is not?   (k-consistency)
    statistics   is the deviation inside the spread?       (fractional)

Use the language that is NON-DEGENERATE for the cell. Where only two faces are
present, geometry at order 3 is degenerate and the pairwise logic face is live.
"""
import math, collections, sys

R = 13.605693

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face A
rows = [l.rstrip("\r\n").split("\t")
        for l in open("COORDINATES.tsv", encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")[1:]
        if l.strip()]
A = {}
for x in rows:
    try:
        A[(int(x[0]), int(x[1]), int(x[2]))] = (float(x[4]), x[5], x[8])
    except (ValueError, IndexError):
        pass

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face B
B = {}
for l in open("captures/QDEFECT-Theodosiou-1986.tsv", encoding="utf-8"):
    if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip():
        continue
    f = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    if len(f) < 8:
        continue
    try:
        B[(int(f[2]), int(f[3]), int(f[5]))] = float(f[7])
    except ValueError:
        pass

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- face C
# the ground-state defect needs the OUTER ORBITAL (n, l) of the species, which
# follows from the electron count N = Z - z + 1 under the observed filling order.
ORDER = [(1,0,2),(2,0,2),(2,1,6),(3,0,2),(3,1,6),(4,0,2),(3,2,10),(4,1,6),
         (5,0,2),(4,2,10),(5,1,6),(6,0,2),(5,2,10),(4,3,14),(6,1,6),(7,0,2),
         (6,2,10),(5,3,14),(7,1,6)]

def outer(N):
    """(n, l) of the last electron under the OBSERVED opening order."""
    for n, l, cap in ORDER:
        if N <= cap:
            return n, l
        N -= cap
    return None

C = {}
for l in open("captures/LADDER-K-Kr.tsv", encoding="utf-8"):
    if l.startswith("#") or not l.strip():
        continue
    zs, cs, es, q = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    Z = int(zs); z = int(cs[1:]) + 1; ie = float(es)
    o = outer(Z - z + 1)
    if not o or ie <= 0:
        continue
    n, ll = o
    C[(Z, z, ll)] = (n - z * math.sqrt(R / ie), q, n)

print(f"  FACES:  A filler {len(A):,}   B Theodosiou {len(B)}   C ladder {len(C)}\n")

keys = sorted(set(A) & (set(B) | set(C)))
tri = sorted(set(A) & set(B) & set(C))
ab = sorted((set(A) & set(B)) - set(C))
ac = sorted((set(A) & set(C)) - set(B))

print(f"  CELLS WITH ALL THREE FACES : {len(tri)}")
print(f"  A+B only                   : {len(ab)}")
print(f"  A+C only                   : {len(ac)}")
print(f"  total multi-face cells     : {len(keys)}\n")

SYM = {1:"H",2:"He",3:"Li",4:"Be",5:"B",6:"C",7:"N",8:"O",9:"F",10:"Ne",
       11:"Na",12:"Mg",13:"Al",14:"Si",15:"P",16:"S",17:"Cl",18:"Ar",
       19:"K",20:"Ca",21:"Sc",22:"Ti",23:"V",24:"Cr",25:"Mn",26:"Fe",
       27:"Co",28:"Ni",29:"Cu",30:"Zn",31:"Ga",32:"Ge",33:"As",34:"Se",
       35:"Br",36:"Kr"}
ROM = {1:"I",2:"II",3:"III",4:"IV",5:"V",6:"VI",7:"VII",8:"VIII",9:"IX",
       10:"X",11:"XI",12:"XII",13:"XIII",14:"XIV",15:"XV",16:"XVI"}

if tri:
    print("  THE THREE-FACE CELLS — every one read three ways\n")
    print(f"    {'cell':<12}{'l':>2}{'A filler':>10}{'B asympt':>10}"
          f"{'C ground':>10}{'A-B':>8}{'B-C':>8}   verdict")
    for k in tri:
        Z, z, l = k
        a = A[k][0]; b = B[k]; c = C[k][0]
        nm = f"{SYM.get(Z,Z)} {ROM.get(z,z)}"
        dab = a - b; dbc = b - c
        v = "AGREE" if abs(dab) < 0.05 else "A OFF"
        print(f"    {nm:<12}{'spdf'[l]:>2}{a:>10.4f}{b:>10.3f}{c:>10.4f}"
              f"{dab:>+8.3f}{dbc:>+8.3f}   {v}")

content.text:
**Nine cells entered, not twelve — and the multiplicity key is what stopped the other three.**

The index is keyed on **(Z, charge, ℓ, 2S+1)**, and Theodosiou's values are, in the paper's own words, *"an average over the multiplet and fine-structure components of a configuration."* For one electron outside a closed shell that average is over a **single term** and the doublet key is exact. For anything else it's a weighted mean with no single key.

    Na I     Ne core + 1 electron    doublet, unambiguous   → 4 cells  ENTER
    Fe VIII  Ar core + 1 electron    doublet, unambiguous   → 3 cells  ENTER
    Ca X     Ne core + 1 electron    doublet, unambiguous   → 2 cells  ENTER
    Ca I     TWO valence electrons   singlet AND triplet    → 1 cell   REFUSE
    Ca III   a hole plus an electron "open-shell core begins" → 2 cells REFUSE

Ca III's exclusion comes from **the paper's own remarks column**. A mean entered under a single 2S+1 key would fabricate precision the source doesn't have.

**And entering them exposed a provenance fault that was already there.** `coords.py` labelled *every* measured cell "captured levels" — true while every measured cell came from our own captures, false the moment one didn't. Provenance is now per-cell:

    328  captured levels
      9  Theodosiou, Manson & Inokuti 1986, PRA 34 943, experiment column

**The index moves from 328 measured to 337, verified from 1,257 to 1,266** — 7.82% to 8.03% of the reachable set.

Everything rebuilt from source rather than edited, which is register 1572's lesson applied *before* the mistake this time. Both gates pass.

Registers to 1576, checkpointed at `2_2p`. **Next on your order: row 1, H1.**

`coords.py` calls every cell above charge 10 improbable because there is *"no analysed data at this charge."* **The index itself holds twelve measured cells above it** — Ti XI at charge 11, Fe XV at 15, Fe XVI at 16, all from our own captures, all graded measured and verified. **The gate is contradicted by the file it gates.**

And Theodosiou reaches past it by design: its stated scope is *all* positive ions of *all* atoms to Z = 37 — that's 1 ≤ z ≤ Z, not z ≤ 10. Its Fe XVI row is charge **sixteen**, and we've already entered the neighbouring Fe VIII and Ca X.

**No — and testing it found something better.** Counting which gate actually fires over all 56,168 (Z, charge, ℓ) triples:

| gate | cells | share | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| no analysed data above **charge 10** | 34,968 | **62.3%** | **falsified by the index itself** |
| element too short-lived, Z > 103 | 13,320 | 23.7% | a physical bound — real |
| series unresolved above ng | 2,955 | 5.3% | an observational bound — real |
| **open-shell core, several parents** | 2,760 | **4.9%** | ← the multiplicity problem |
| already possible | 2,025 | 3.6% | open |

**Multiplicity is the fourth gate at 4.9%.** What it actually limits is *entry*, not reach — it's what stopped three of twelve Theodosiou cells, because a value averaged over several terms has no single 2S+1 key. Real, but narrow.

**The first gate is the key, and it's an assumption rather than a fact.**

`coords.py` calls every cell above charge 10 improbable because there is *"no analysed data at this charge."* **The index itself holds twelve measured cells above it** — Ti XI at charge 11, Fe XV at 15, Fe XVI at 16, all from our own captures, all graded measured and verified. **The gate is contradicted by the file it gates.**

And Theodosiou reaches past it by design: its stated scope is *all* positive ions of *all* atoms to Z = 37 — that's 1 ≤ z ≤ Z, not z ≤ 10. Its Fe XVI row is charge **sixteen**, and we've already entered the neighbouring Fe VIII and Ca X.

**So 62% of the index sits behind a cutoff that was true when written and isn't true now.**

Fixing it is one line. **The honest part isn't the line** — it's establishing what the new bound actually *is*, rather than moving the number and hoping. That's now **row 0** on the board, ahead of H1.

The two problems are different in kind: **multiplicity limits what a measured value can be keyed to; the charge cutoff limits what the index admits as reachable at all.**

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"def run(placement, higher_n=True, a0=1.0):
    """a is placed on the RUNNING INTERSECTION, not on the current element's own
    corridor. That is the structure that reproduces R 1401's fourteen forced
    moves exactly (balance.py); placing against each element separately makes a
    leave its bracket constantly and is not what the record describes."""
    a, moves, hits, misses = None, [], 0, []
    lo, hi = -1e9, 1e9
    for Z in STEPS:
        Lo, Up = IVL[Z]

        if placement == "handshake":
            nlo, nhi = max(lo, Lo), min(hi, Up)
            if nlo >= nhi or a is None:                  # the intersection empties
                lo, hi = Lo, Up
            else:
                lo, hi = nlo, nhi
        else:                                            # per-block ascent
            # R 1409 exactly: at a block opening a takes the block's OWN floor;
            # inside a block a takes max(itself, floor). Floors only — no
            # ceiling is intersected, so a only ever rises within a block.
            if Z in OPENS or a is None:
                lo, hi = Lo, Up
            else:
                lo, hi = max(lo, Lo), 1e9

        # the tightest finite non-zero bound: L where it is a real surd, U where
        # it is not. Lithium's window is (0, +inf) and determines nothing, so a0
        # is declared arbitrary there and its effect is measured below.
        want = lo if (lo > EPS and lo < 1e8) else (hi if hi < 1e8 else None)
        newa = want if want is not None else (a if a is not None else a0)
        if a is None or abs(newa - a) > EPS:
            moves.append(Z)
        a = newa

        prev = occ(Z - 1)
        pick = choose(candidates(prev), prev, a, higher_n)
        if pick == OBS[Z]:
            hits += 1
        else:
            misses.append((Z, OBS[Z], pick))
    return hits, moves, misses

"""trajectory.py — the walk with the leak closed, on the witness principle.

THE PROBLEM (registers 1440 and 1445 together).

    the LAW admits         at least 100 of 106   (midpoint placement, R 1440)
    the trajectory delivers    99 of 106 fitted  (R 1413)
    held out                   90 of 106         (R 1445)

So there is a gap of at least ten between what the corridor system ADMITS and
what any walk has DELIVERED without leaking. Closing it is "solve for
trajectory".

THE LEAK, EXACTLY. `scorer.py` at step Z reads IVL[Z] — the corridor for the
CURRENT element — places a on it, and only then predicts that element. But
`brack.py` builds IVL[Z] FROM the observed entrant at Z. The answer sets the
